15-year-old girl dies after getting hit while riding e-scooter, police say
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) - A 15-year-old girl died after she was hit while riding an electric scooter, according to authorities.
Police said the crash happened Oct. 21 at around 3:08 p.m. on Racetrack Road. The family identified the victim as Torrianne Mortensen.
Torrianne was riding from the Saguaro Park Trail and crossing in a marked crosswalk, police said.
Police said vehicles in the adjacent lane had slowed or stopped as she crossed. A southbound 2012 Nissan Rogue approached from behind, passed those vehicles and entered the crosswalk without stopping, hitting the 15-year-old.
The girl was taken to the hospital where she died.
Police identified the driver as Michael Stanton, 64. He has been charged with vehicular manslaughter, failure to exercise due care for a pedestrian, and overtaking a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk, police said.
Police said impairment and speed were not factors. The driver remained at the scene and cooperated with investigators, police said.

title: Waterville writer remembered as a storyteller
text:
WATERVILLE — In the last week of his life, legendary Waterville writer and award-winning columnist J.P. Devine told his daughter Dawn that for his whole life he had only wanted one thing: to be loved.
Devine, 94, who died Oct. 16 was an artist in every sense of the word. He spent his early adulthood in New York and Los Angeles acting and writing, and in Waterville he’s remembered as a storyteller.
When people talk about J.P. Devine, they mention his commanding presence on stage, his humor, his exceptionally good writing and his great hair.
Someone once asked Devine what his favorite role was. His daughter Dawn waited for him to mention an episode of “The Bob Newhart Show,” or the McDonald’s commercial that people used to stop him on the street over. She thought about the famous actors who told him his plays moved them, and the painting he sold.
But Devine said being a father and a husband was his favorite role.
In his own words, Devine landed in Waterville in 1984 “for love of a Maine Catholic girl,” and left about a year ago to be with his daughters in California because, after his wife died in 2024, he had “no desire to be covered with snow.”
After growing up in St. Louis, Devine joined the U.S. Air Force and was stationed in Japan during the Korean War to work in intelligence before his passion for acting took him to New York, then Los Angeles, where he and his wife, Katherine, raised their two daughters.
“We had a wonderful childhood,” Devine’s daughter Jillana Devine-Knickel said. “They both raised us with so much love and support and … encouragement to be whatever we wanted to be.”
Although Dawn Devine said her father was like a cat in the sun when he returned to the Golden State after 40 years, Devine-Knickel said Waterville really became his home.
Devine was already a Morning Sentinel columnist when Scott Monroe, now managing editor for the Maine Trust for Local News, arrived in Maine as a reporter in 2008. He said Devine’s work was the “talk of the town.”
“J.P. was so much more than an entertaining writer,” Monroe said. “J.P. was a Waterville celebrity who immediately brought energy and laughter to a room, and his writing was no less exuberant. His tales were legendary, cinematic and always brought a smile to my face.”
Ken Eisen, co-founder of the Maine International Film Festival and former Railroad Square Cinema, said Devine’s audience relied on him for his enthusiastic movie reviews.
Devine and Katherine Joly Devine put on productions at the Waterville Opera House that drew crowds. As a theater and improv teacher, particularly of his wife’s students, he found a creative outlet in Waterville he’d never had in New York, Devine-Knickel said.
Nothing fueled Devine like when people told him they loved him in a play, or stopped him at the grocery store to say his writing made them laugh.
Devine-Knickel said she never questioned how her adventurous, creative father managed to be such a hit in rural Maine. Although her mother was originally his in with people — Katherine Joly Devine, a teacher, was a Waterville celebrity in her own right — Devine-Knickel said her father could relate to anyone because he loved learning about them and their lives.
“He was so curious about people, and he loved to talk to people and get to know them,” Devine-Knickel said. “And he loved my mom so much, and he knew it was her town.”
Devine had coffee at least once a week with his best friend Joseph Jabar. Jabar is a Waterville native, but he said Devine quickly became more connected than he was.
“He really made an impression on Waterville,” Jabar said.
Former Morning Sentinel reporter and columnist Amy Calder used to keep candy in her desk drawer to give Devine when he stopped by the office. Red licorice was his favorite.
Calder interviewed Devine live on stage for part of the Community Voices series. She said she anxiously prepared questions, but she soon realized she wouldn’t need them.
“After the first question, he just ran with it, commanding the stage and sending the audience into fits of laughter,” Calder said. “I don’t think it is overstated to say we’ve lost a legend.”
In any given room, Dawn Devine said her father held court. He was the youngest of 10 children and always wanted to be heard. But he also shined the attention he craved onto others.
“Because he wanted to be loved, he wanted other people to feel heard and loved too,” Devine said. “He was still cool at 94 … I have a picture of him in the hospital. He’s got his aviators on and his Starbucks, looking out the window and giving me a thumbs up.”
But Devine was also sensitive, and Dawn Devine said there was always a little boy inside him who wanted to be loved.
After Katherine died, Devine thought people expected him to finally grow up. He refused.
“It won’t work,” he wrote. “She adored the little boy she married, as I did her.”
Devine-Knickel said both she and her sister believe their father is with their mother now. Devine-Knickel remembers them as a “wonderful team.” Dawn Devine remembers them as a “great love story.”
Devine-Knickel said she always knew their house and family was full of love and fun, but it wasn’t until her mother’s health struggles later in life that she realized how special that was.
“He stayed strong … and took amazing care of her,” Devine-Knickel said. “After all that time, I really saw what they were.”
After Katherine died, Devine wrote, “Each night before bed, I turn out the lights and kiss all the shadows around each room hoping one of them is She, and whisper, ‘Let’s stop saying goodbye, OK?'”
At the end of his life, Devine was a published author — his book “Will Write For Food – True Stories, Half Truths, and 3 Lies,” was one of his proudest achievements — an actor, an artist and a devoted father. He was still cool and he had hair that made everyone jealous. He was missed by his friends in Waterville, he was cherished by his daughters.
He was loved.

title: I’m pulling for you, Kylie Boardman
text:
A couple of weeks ago I read an article in this newspaper about a young Gardiner woman named Kylie Boardman who needs a kidney transplant.
My first thought was “I should get tested to see if I’m a match.” My second thought was “I already donated a kidney and I only have one left.”
Today is the fourth anniversary of my kidney donation surgery. As you can gather, these days it affects my life so little that sometimes I forget I did it. In fact, the other night in bed I was staring at my torso with a flashlight trying to figure out where the third scar from the laparoscopic surgery was and if it had somehow vanished. That’s how much it has faded. (If my wife noticed what I was doing, she didn’t say anything.)
I always assumed that pregnancy and birth would be a lot harder than donating a kidney, where basically all I had to do was show up and a team of specialists took care of everything else and here I am four years out from a nephrectomy and one year out from a baby and can officially, journalistically confirm: yeah, the birth and recovery was way harder.
Birth permanently damaged my body in a way that the kidney removal didn’t. This is just one of the many reasons I get so pissed off when politicians want to force women through pregnancy and childbirth because “a life is at stake” but nobody ever suggests mandating kidney donation even though a dozen people die every day waiting for one. That’s not to say there’s no pain or risk in donation — there is — but let me put it this way: if I could, I would choose to donate a kidney again. I would not choose to get pregnant or give birth again.
I always feel a little weird talking about how I donated a kidney to a stranger; I worry people will think I’m bragging or something. The truth is I didn’t do it for clout or to flex on other people, and I certainly didn’t do it for money (although I admit and disclose here that the Maine Transplant Organization gave me a really nice bathrobe).
I chose to donate a kidney to a stranger because I looked at the data, weighed the potential risks to myself against the potential benefits to the recipient (another decade or two of life) and decided the numbers added up to making a donation.
You don’t have to be a saint in order to do an altruistic donation; I’m certainly as selfish and crabby as anyone else and possibly more so depending on how much sleep I’ve gotten. (For a full list of my faults, please reach out to my wife, mother or any regular commenter on my articles.) You don’t have to be young or particularly fit. I’m actually in better shape now than I was before I got rid of the kidney. You just have to decide to do it.
I was looking for data on what percentage of living kidney donations are “non-directed” or “altruistic” — i.e., donations to someone the donor doesn’t know. (Personally I think it’s pretty altruistic to donate an organ to someone already you know; I didn’t make up this terminology.) I couldn’t find any solid numbers but the general indication seems to be it’s a small percentage. Which is weird to me, because I consider myself a pretty average person and I did it. Maybe I do have a screw loose after all.
That’s not to say I didn’t benefit from the donation. In addition to the aforementioned bathrobe (terry cloth!), the decision to donate a kidney did wonders for my mental health. First of all, any lingering anxiety I had about doctor’s visits or blood draws got hammered out of me through exposure therapy.
I also felt more confident than ever about my health, because I got a complete workover, inside and out, looking for any potential medical vulnerabilities, and all the medics found was that I snore sometimes.
Most importantly, it helped me heal a bit more from my father’s death. For years, I felt this intractable bit of guilt constantly poking at my mind that I couldn’t save him from his cancer. But I was able to save someone else’s dad. That really did help me move on with my life.
I hope Kylie Boardman gets a kidney. If you’re interested in getting tested to see if you’re a match, you can go to kidney4kylie.com. I hope at least one person reading this considers becoming a kidney donor (living or deceased, honestly, both are good). If I can do it, anyone can do it.

title: Trump to rally for Hyde-Smith in Mississippi as Senate race tightens
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is scheduled to hold a campaign rally in Mississippi on Monday to support Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) as the midterm elections approach.
The president is set to rally at Crossroads Arena in Corinth, Miss. Monday.
“They’ve asked me to go. I’m going there, I think, on Monday. And I look forward to it,” Trump said.
The rally is focused on bolstering support for Hyde-Smith, the state’s incumbent Republican senator, as well as other GOP candidates. It comes as polling suggests the Senate race is becoming more competitive despite the state’s Republican voting history.
Republican Party officials say their strategy is focused on turnout for their party.
“This president knows how to turn out these low propensity voters. And the midterms, historically, it’s all about turnout,” RNC Chair Joe Gruters said.
Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom suggested the visit is a sign of concern among Republicans. Colom wrote on X, “Cindy High Prices is scared and that’s why she’s sending Donald Trump down here. She’s scared to answer why she voted to cut healthcare, why she betrayed our farmers and why she blocked the release of the Epstein files.”
The president is scheduled to begin speaking at the rally at 6 p.m. Central Time Monday.

title: Obituary: James Bruce Johnson
text:
AUGUSTA – J. Bruce Johnson, 88, formerly of Saddleback, West Gardiner, and Farmington, passed away on Oct. 4, 2026, at the Maine Veterans’ Home in Augusta, Maine with his daughters Erin and Kate, and many loving, caring staff members by his side.
Bruce was born on April 4, 1938, in Farmington, son of Miriam “Babe” Barker (1910-1979) and Delmar Harold Johnson (1908-2001) and brother to Maria Holt (1929-2023), Neil Johnson (1932-1995), and Peggy Adams (1934-2016). A 1956 graduate of Farmington High School, he fondly remembered growing up in a small town where he could walk home during a Red Sox game without missing a single pitch, because every porch he passed had the game on the radio.
He was a 1960 graduate of the University of Maine with a Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering and a proud member and alumni of the Phi Kappa Sigma fraternity. He worked for the Maine State Highway Commission in Augusta, and the New York State Department of Public Works in Poughkeepsie, N.Y. He was always very happy to hear when friends and family drove through the Cloverleaf he helped design in New York.
Bruce served in the United States Army from 1961 to 1964 and was stationed in Orleans, France, for most of this time with his lifelong friends, Al Scheeren, Bob Kroupa, and Bob Heitman. He made the most of this time and traveled all over Europe, running with the bulls, drinking espressos in Paris cafés, driving his Porsche on the Autobahn, driving a VW bug to the 24 hours of LeMans, and hosting many parties. His knee was severely injured during this time, but he did not let that stop him from being extremely active for the rest of his life.
He was Saddleback Mountain General Manager for a few years in the late ’60s to early ’70s and volunteered and worked with the mountain for most of his life. He was inducted into the Maine Ski and Snowboard Hall of Fame in 2023 for his instrumental work designing and building Saddleback’s first snowmaking system, with a million-gallon retention pond, “First for a large ski area in Maine”. Bruce loved being at Saddleback, and one of his cherished memories was when his dear friend Jud Strunk came to play at the Lodge in August of 1968 with many family and friends in attendance. Is there anyone still out there who was at that event?
Bruce worked several different jobs before he settled at Superior Concrete for many years. In 1987, together with his childhood friend Rod Stewart, they created Eco-Tec, a company that distributed the first preformed products used for septic systems, in New England and Atlantic Canada.
Bruce “Pops” is survived by three daughters; nine grandchildren; and five great-grandchildren; and many nieces and nephews who love him dearly – Daughter, Catherine Roze, born in 1963 in Orléans, France, her husband, JeanFrancois, and grandsons Marc-Antoine and Pierre-Hadrien of Versailles, France; Daughter, Kate Taylor, born in 1968 in Augusta, and her husband, Don “Bud” of Manchester, granddaughter Ashley Freccia and her husband, Sam, and great-grandchildren Avery, Taylor, and Colby of North Yarmouth, granddaughter Mary Taylor and her wife, Colleen, and great-grandchildren William and Grace of Portland, granddaughter Madison Taylor of New London, N.H., granddaughter Maura Taylor, of Patchogue, N.Y.; Daughter, Erin Johnson, born in 1974 in Augusta, and her husband Matthew Byrd of Sandy River Plantation, grandson Tristan Byrd of Portsmouth, N.H., granddaughter Reid Johnson of Hallowell, and grandson Ben Byrd of Sandy River Plantation.
All gatherings with Bruce included storytelling, and over the years the stories likely were embellished? Here’s a sampling of the stories: Snowshoe races with Folger; Grandpa Johnson crashing the boat at Clearwater; Bruce waterskiing to a wedding; Withywindle; Halloween walks for Erin; golf and caddying for Laurel Kean; Nantucket bluefish runs, trips to Coatue to see the shipwreck, crazy hat dinners, and 3 p.m. swims with Al; holiday gatherings, ice skating, and lobster feeds on Cobbossee; Amazon boat cruise; New Year’s Eve at Saddleback with Diane, Rod, Vicki, Ronald, and Jean; West Branch Pond Camps walks to Jack’s bridge; Cook family visits; Tuesday ski group at Saddleback, golf league at Mingo, and performing Ishbel’s marriage in France.
A celebration of Bruce’s life will be held at the Pub (Painted Pony) at the Saddleback base Lodge on Saturday, Nov. 21, from 1 to 4 p.m. Military Honors will be held at 1 p.m. Bruce’s wish is for this to be a happy occasion to celebrate his life and remember the good times. Bring your favorite stories, your best memories, play some cribbage and pitch, and let’s honor Bruce the way he wanted with good company and lots of laughter!
His family extends their heartfelt gratitude to the dedicated staff of the Maine Veterans’ Home in Augusta for the exceptional care, kindness, and compassion they provided during the final six months of his life.
Wiles Remembrance Center is honored to be caring for the family of J. Bruce Johnson, please visit his Book of Memories at http://www.wilesrc.com to leave words of care and comfort.

title: Volunteers plant bulbs to commemorate three years since the Lewiston mass shootings
text:
Volunteers plant bulbs to commemorate three years since the Lewiston mass shootings
Later in the day, a vigil will be held at Simard-Payne Park to remember the 18 lives lost
Volunteers plant bulbs to commemorate three years since the Lewiston mass shootings
Later in the day, a vigil will be held at Simard-Payne Park to remember the 18 lives lost
Flags were at half-staff on Sunday across Maine, marking three years since the Lewiston mass shootings that killed 18 people and injured several others.
Oct. 25, 2023, was the deadliest mass shooting in Maine history. Eighteen people were killed and several others were injured. Three years later, the community has found different ways to remember the lives lost.
The "I Love You" gardens, represented by a sign word in American Sign Language, are a memorial project that was started by local artist Tanja Hollander in October 2025.
"My idea is to bring the community together to plant, and planting is one way that you can heal," Hollander said.
What started as a small community project quickly grew. Throughout the spring and summer of 2026, more than 100 volunteers continued planting bulbs in flower beds at Simard-Payne Park and Bonney Park.
On Sunday, Hollander said her goal was to plant 1,500 bulbs in the ground with help from the community. Now she and volunteers are adding two new sites to the list, one at the intersection of Oxford Street and Cross Street and another at the Maine Museum of Innovation, Learning and Labor.
"I'm just so proud and so happy that so many volunteers from all over the state have come to help Lewiston," Hollander said.
Volunteers can sign up through the art project's website.
Later in the day, the Maine Resiliency Center will be holding a candlelight vigil at Simard-Payne Park to remember the victims of the mass shootings. Participants will gather at the park entrance at 6 p.m. before walking together to the Longley Bridge for the vigil.

title: These 5 buildings in Bangor are said to be haunted
text:
As the former longtime home of Stephen King and the inspiration for several elements in the author’s horror novels, Bangor is no stranger to spooky stories — and not all of them are purely fictional.
As Halloween approaches, the Bangor Historical Society offers tours that tell the stories of unsolved mysteries, murders and spirits that some believe still linger in some of the Queen City’s most well-known buildings and sites.
Here are a few of the many stories featured in the Ghostly Bangor Walking Tour, which the historical society offers throughout October.
Bangor House
Built in 1835, the Bangor House on the corner of Main and Union streets opened as a luxury hotel during the city’s time as the lumber capital of the world. It hosted notable guests ranging from U.S. presidents to famous athletes and musicians and was a setting for grand parties and dinners.
However, it was also home to several murders including one of Bangor’s most notable cold cases.
On March 18, 1965, a chambermaid named Effie MacDonald was found strangled with her own stockings in a vacant hotel room on the third floor.
This occurred just after the heyday of the Boston Strangler, a serial killer who murdered more than a dozen women, leading people to wonder whether the killer had traveled north to continue the spree. Investigators from Boston came to Bangor to investigate MacDonald’s murder, but ultimately deemed it to be the work of a copycat.
No one was ever charged with MacDonald’s murder, but she’s reportedly still seen roaming the halls of the second and third floors of the building closest to Union Street.
The building’s time as a hotel ceased in 1968 and the building was converted into apartments, which is still what it’s used for today.
Bangor Opera House
The predecessor to the Penobscot Theatre Company building on Main Street was built in 1882 and was one of several music houses throughout the city. The Bangor Opera House hosted many well-known entertainers, including John Wilkes Booth’s brother, Edwin Booth, who was a renowned Shakespearean actor.
The building escaped destruction in the Great Fire of 1911 only to ignite on Jan. 15 three years later.
Firefighters responded quickly and began pouring water on the building, but the opera house was quickly encased in ice due to the freezing temperatures. The weight of the ice caused the roof to collapse, killing two firefighters who were inside clearing the building.
The theater was rebuilt in the same location in 1920, but actors and employees have reported seeing shadowy figures in two locations that are believed to be the two firefighters who died in the fire. In several cases, a figure has been spotted on the balcony while photographers have captured another that appears to be sitting on the edge of the stage.
There have also been reports of the spirit of a young child being seen running through the lobby, though there’s no record of a child dying on the property.
On one occasion, a lighting technician said he was working in the building alone one night and brought a cookie wrapped in plastic to the light booth in the back of the theater. After stepping away to turn a few lights on, he returned to find the plastic had been ripped open and a small bite had been taken out of the cookie.
Thomas A. Hill House
Located on the corner of Union and High streets, real estate investor and businessman Thomas A. Hill commissioned a house to be built for him in 1835. However, he lost his fortune a few years later and sold the house in 1845 to Samuel Dale, another local businessman and politician, who lived in the house with his wife, Matilda, and their son, George
Samuel Dale served as Bangor’s mayor for two terms, including in 1871 when the Great Chicago Fire broke out. Bangor residents raised roughly $10,000 to support relief efforts for the victims and, as mayor, it was Samuel Dale’s job to bring the money to Chicago.
It was also customary at the time for the recipients to take ads out in the local newspapers thanking Bangor residents for their contributions. But, Bangor never received any receipt for the donations, leading residents to question whether Samuel Dale embezzled the funds.
That same year also marked the completion of the European and North American Railroad, and family President Ulysses S. Grant visited Bangor to celebrate. The Dale family hosted a lavish party at their home to welcome the President in October 1871 and made significant upgrades to the house in anticipation of the event.
Again, residents questioned where the money the mayor was using to fund the party came from, especially considering the party favors included watches and jewelry.
A few months later, Samuel Dale became ill and died in a bedroom in the home while his wife and son were at church. His stomach contents were sent to Boston to be tested for poison but his cause of death was ultimately ruled a stroke.
Matilda Dale continued living in the home until she died in the same room as her husband in 1894. The house remained a private residence until the Sons of Union Veterans bought it in 1942 before the house was gifted to the Bangor Historical Society in 1974.
To this day, Bangor Historical Society employees and volunteers report inexplicably smelling cigar smoke, even in sealed, climate controlled rooms. This, they believe, is the spirit of Samuel Dale, who was a habitual smoker.
Employees have also reported seeing a woman in a Victorian dress when changing exhibits, cleaning or decorating for the holidays. This, they believe, was Matilda Dale, as she would’ve overseen such work as the lady of the house.
Phenix Block
Located in West Market Square in downtown Bangor, the Phenix Block has been plagued by fires since its construction in 1873.
On one occasion, William Bracket was walking through downtown on his way to work when he noticed smoke pouring out of the top of the building. People were carrying items out of the ground floor, which held a dry goods shop at the time.
Bracket began making trips into the building to help salvage items, but masonry from one of the building’s upper floors fell and hit him while he was inside, killing him.
The building was later rebuilt and now serves as the Phenix Inn, continuing its long legacy of operating as a hotel or apartments of some kind. However, guests have reported strange electrical occurrences and feeling unexplained cold spots on the building’s third floor, which is where the masonry that killed Bracket is believed to have fallen from.
Thomas Hill Standpipe
Built in 1897, Bangor’s iconic standpipe that looms over the city consists of an iron tank that holds 1.5 million gallons of water surrounded by a wood frame jacket. A staircase to the observation deck runs between the two structures.
For years the standpipe was open to the public and unattended until 1940 when a group of children climbed up the standpipe, not using the stairs, but by climbing up the support beams that run between the water tank and wood exterior.
A 12-year-old boy slipped while jumping from beam to beam and fell roughly 20 feet down into the gap between the metal tank and wooden shell. He died from his injuries two days later.
Today, those climbing to the top of the standpipe on the rare occasions it’s open report hearing children’s voices, laughter and footsteps.

title: Obituary: Catherine Folan (Doane) Knudsen
text:
FALMOUTH – Catherine Folan Doane Knudsen, 70, of Falmouth, passed away peacefully Saturday Oct. 17, 2026, surrounded by family and friends.
She was born May 2, 1956 to Don and Barbara Doane. A lifelong resident of Falmouth, she and her brothers grew up swimming and water skiing in Mussel Cove. She met her husband, Erik, in the third grade. It would be another seven years before they began dating, and another six before marrying.
Cath graduated from Falmouth High School in 1975, attended UMaine Orono, and graduated from USM with a degree in elementary education in 1981. One week after graduating, her first son, Neils, was born. Cath loved every minute of motherhood and had another son, Kurt, in 1984. Later in life she delighted in being a grandmother to her four grandchildren.
Besides working in the family business, Cath was a proud volunteer in Falmouth’s Elementary School Library for over 30 years. She had a special knack for remembering details about every child who spent time in the library. In her free time, Cath was very athletic and moved from school sports into skiing, cycling, and running. She especially loved trail running and her many awards adorned home and camp. She could frequently be seen walking Route 88 with a friend, easily identifiable by her enviable amount of hair.
Anyone who knew Cath always remarked on her smile and perpetually cheery nature. Many people considered her as their best friend, and nurturing her many relationships brought her great joy. She was genuinely interested in other people’s lives and could spark a conversation with anyone who crossed her path.
Cath is survived by her husband of 47 years, Erik; sons Neils (Liz) and Kurt (Kaylee); granddaughters Olivia, Lydia, and Reese, grandson, Elliot; brothers Don (Susan), Jimmie (Beth), and Joe (Pauline), as well as many nieces and nephews. The family would like to express special thanks to Ali and Emma from Hospice of Southern Maine.
Celebration of Cath’s life will be held on Thursday, Dec. 17, from 3 to 7 p.m. at SMCC’s McKernan Center, 122 McKernan Dr., South Portland, ME 04106.

title: Caribou Sweeps Individual Titles, Boys Win Class B North Cross Country Championship
text:
Caribou Boys Win Class B North Cross Country Title as Gorneault and Graves Claim Regional Championships
Aroostook County runners had another outstanding Saturday, bringing home a team championship and both individual titles at the Class B North Regional Cross Country Championships in Belfast.
Caribou's boys captured the regional championship with 61 points, while Pierce Gorneault led the Vikings with a first-place finish in 16:01.03.
On the girls' side, Caribou's Emma Graves won the individual championship in 18:44.40, while Presque Isle finished second in the team standings and Caribou placed third.
Presque Isle's boys also had a strong afternoon, finishing third in a tightly contested team race.
With the top seven teams and top 30 individual finishers qualifying for the state championships next weekend, both County schools put themselves in a strong position heading into the next round.
Class B Boys: Caribou Captures Regional Championship
Caribou's boys continued their impressive postseason run Saturday, winning the Class B North regional championship with 61 points.
John Bapst and Presque Isle both finished with 83 points, with John Bapst taking second and Presque Isle third in the official team standings.
The Vikings placed three runners among the top four, led by Pierce Gorneault, who won the individual regional championship in 16:01.03.
Tewolde Stewart finished third in 16:59.73, while freshman Peyton Gorneault was fourth in 17:12.04.
Isaac Brissette placed 24th, and Xander Jamieson rounded out Caribou's scoring five with a 30th-place finish.
Presque Isle also put together an impressive afternoon.
Paxton Darrell led the Wildcats with a fifth-place finish in 17:15.20, followed by Jeremy Charette in 11th and Geonni Guevara in 17th.
Henry Clayton finished 22nd, while Connor Meile placed 29th to complete Presque Isle's scoring five.
The Wildcats' third-place finish came after a close battle with John Bapst, with both teams finishing on 83 points.

Obituary: Kim Alison Hebert
text:
EMBDEN – Kim (Bragg) Hebert, 67, passed away peacefully Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, after a courageous battle with leukemia. She was surrounded by her loving family at her home in Embden, Maine.
Kim was born Jan. 17, 1959, in Skowhegan, the daughter of Elmer “Bus” Bragg and Madalene “Sis” (Adams) Bragg. She graduated from Carrabec High School with the Class of 1977 and as a graduation present, took off traveling and made it to all 50 states. On June 30, 1984, Kim married Kerry D. Hebert, they met in 1978 and moved to Florida the following year. They spent 10 years there, building their first home in Port St. Lucie, Fla. and eventually returned to Maine where they built their “forever home” and raised their two daughters.
Throughout the years, Kim worked in many different occupations. Always known as hard working, she held various positions alongside lifelong friends- Goodwin’s Homewood Industry, Tropicana, and Precious Moments Childcare Center- to name a few. She also dedicated 25 years of work to children with behavioral disabilities, a true reflection of her patience and kindness.
Kim always enjoyed the simple things in life. Most important to her were camping trips, hunting season, snowmobiling, and ANY reason for a gathering or “house full of people”. She was partial to her house plants and flower gardens. She loved Embden Pond and all the memories of growing up on the water. It brought her joy to raise her family with the same values and traditions as her childhood. Although shy in her younger years, Kim was often the life of the party. She was most proud of her children, grandchildren and loved her family and friends so much!
Kim was predeceased by her parents; and brother-in-law, Jean Demers.
She is survived by her husband, Kerry, of 42 years; her sister, Corilee “Jo” Demers, brother, Kris Bragg and wife Kelly; daughters Kylee Hebert and her companion Mark Nichols and Kara Hebert; three grandchildren, Landon Whipple, Marshall Nichols, and Klaira Nichols; as well as numerous extended family and friends.
The family would like to thank Dana Farber Cancer Institute and Andwell Hospice for their care and dedication. They also extend their deepest and most heartfelt gratitude to the RFGH Oncology team, for treating mom like part of the family.
All are invited to attend her Celebration of Life at Diadema Golf Club 419 New Portland Rd., North Anson, ME 04958 on Saturday, Nov. 7, at 2 p.m.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to RFGH Oncology in Kim’s name.

Obituary: Sheila Millington Carmichael
text:
FALMOUTH – Sheila Millington Carmichael, 81, passed away on Oct. 19, 2026, in Falmouth, surrounded by the love of her family. Sheila was born on May 26, 1945, in Halifax, Nova Scotia, the daughter of the late Edward and Jerry (Gleeson) Mullins.
Sheila was immensely proud of her Canadian heritage. She grew up in Halifax, enjoying summers at the Waegwoltic Club and cherished family vacations spent at Pictou and Keltic Lodges, especially alongside her beloved best friend, Maureen. These memories remained close to her heart throughout her life.
Sheila attended Sacred Heart School in Halifax, completing her studies in just three years before continuing her education at St. Francis Xavier University in Antigonish, Nova Scotia. She graduated in 1965 and remained a proud and devoted alumna of St. FX. She loved returning for reunions and wore her cherished X ring with pride until the day she died.
It was at St. FX that Sheila met her soulmate, John Millington. They married shortly after John’s graduation in 1966 and began their life together. After brief stays in Massachusetts and Delaware, they settled in South Portland, Maine, where they raised their four children.
Sheila’s family was the center of her world, and she was their most devoted supporter. One of her greatest joys was watching her children compete at South Portland High School. She was their biggest fan and never missed a game. Through years of cheering from the sidelines, she formed many lifelong friendships that became an important part of her life.
Sheila enjoyed a fulfilling career as a clinical dietitian at Maine Medical Center, where she worked for more than 30 years. She loved her profession, the people she worked with, and the many friendships she made along the way. She held a special place in her heart for her colleagues, whom she affectionately called her “Maine Med girls.”
A dedicated runner, Sheila embraced fitness and routine throughout most of her adult life. She rose at 5:30 a.m. each morning to complete her familiar three-mile route along Fickett, Sawyer, Stillman, and Highland. She eagerly anticipated the annual Beach to Beacon Road Race in Cape Elizabeth, participating from 1998 through 2019 and missing only two races during those years. Her determination carried her through her 75th birthday, reflecting the energy, discipline, and enthusiasm with which she approached life.
Sheila was also a lifelong tennis player, spending many years competing at Foreside Fitness in Falmouth and Tennis of Maine in Portland. Running, tennis, and supporting her children were more than pastimes; they were ways she built lasting friendships and remained connected to the people and communities she loved.
Following John’s passing in 1998, Sheila was blessed to find love again with Herbert “Herb” Carmichael III. Together, they embraced retirement, traveled the world, and delighted in their role as doting grandparents. Their years together brought many wonderful memories and much happiness until Herb’s passing in 2016.
Sheila will be remembered for her devotion to her family, her deep pride in her Canadian roots and St. FX, her lifelong friendships, and her remarkable determination to remain active and engaged in the world around her. She lived with enthusiasm, cherished the people in her life, and leaves behind a legacy of love and treasured memories.
Sheila was predeceased by her first husband and the father of her children, John Millington; her second husband, Herbert Carmichael III; her infant son, John A. Millington II; and her brother, Edward Mullins.
She is survived by her children, Mark Millington, Scott Millington and his wife, Angela, Kevin Millington and his wife, Susan Manning, and Sarah Millington; Herb’s children, Mike and Josh Carmichael; her grandchildren, John A. Millington III, Matthew Millington, Shay Millington, Stone Carmichael, and Reade Carmichael; Ron Morton, her companion with whom she shared many happy years; her special niece and childhood friend, Maureen Mullins Buell; and many extended family members who will miss her dearly.
The family extends its heartfelt gratitude to the care team at Sedgewood Commons for the kindness, compassion, and support they provided to Sheila.

A funeral service will be celebrated at 11 a.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 4, at the funeral home, followed by a graveside service at Calvary Cemetery in South Portland.

title: 22 states have red flag laws. What that means and why it's unlikely to spread nationwide
text:
22 states have red flag laws. What that means and why it's unlikely to spread nationwide
Nearly a year ago, 63% of Maine voters approved a ballot measure to make the state the 22nd state with a red flag law, building on its yellow flag law.
The ballot measure came after the state’s deadliest mass shooting, which killed 18 people at a bowling alley and a bar and grill in Lewiston on Oct. 25, 2023.  An independent commission appointed by Gov. Janet Mills later concluded that Army officials and law enforcement had opportunities to intervene with the 40-year-old Army reservist responsible for the shooting.
What are yellow and red flag laws?
Extreme risk protective orders, also known as red flag laws, allow immediate family members or law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from someone who poses a serious risk of injuring themselves or others.
Yellow flag laws require police to take an individual into protective custody and hold them for a mental health evaluation, which can be problematic, said Josh Horwitz, the co-director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions. It could be difficult to take someone into custody or find a mental health provider when law enforcement needs to act immediately.
Yellow flag laws also do not allow family members to petition courts to restrict a potentially dangerous person’s access to guns. Red flag laws, however, allow immediate family, law enforcement or other community members to do so. Who can petition a court varies by state.
Connecticut was the first state to pass a red flag law in 1999. Since then, 21 states and the District of Columbia have passed red flag laws, with Maine being the 22nd state to join the list.
Other states have banned red flag laws. In 2020, Oklahoma was the first of six states to pass such a ban. Oklahoma lawmakers passed Senate Bill 1081, also known as the Anti-Red Flag Act, to protect residents' Second Amendment rights. The law also prohibits the state, or any city, county or political subdivision, from accepting grants or funding to enact a red flag law.
Tennessee, Texas, Wyoming, West Virginia and Montana are the other states with bans.
Twenty-two states have neither enacted nor banned red flag laws, but some, like Iowa, Missouri and South Carolina, have introduced legislation to ban them.
How many petitions have been filed since states passed the law?
Florida has had the most petitions filed since it passed its law in 2018. Florida legislators proposed the bill after a mass shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, killed 17 people.
New York passed a red flag law a year after Florida and had the second-highest number of petitions filed, with 19,401.
In 2025, Connecticut had the highest rate of petitions, with 46 petitions filed per 100,000 people. The state had nearly 1,700 petitions filed. New York had the second-highest rate, at 28 per 100,000 people.

Let’s do political campaigning the Irish way
text:
Regarding the Oct. 18 report “It’s not your imagination — you’re being bombarded with political ads this election,” I have an idea for Maine elections gleaned from my years of teaching in Ireland.
Paid political advertising is generally not permitted on broadcast media in Ireland. Thirty days before the election, candidates and parties may put up print ads, billboards, posters and signs. By seven days after the vote, all signs must be removed (or face on-the-spot fines of €250 for each sign).
If it’s possible for Maine to impose such a system, we would have our family time free of these ugly and demeaning ads for most of the year, and politicos would have a generous window to focus their arguments carefully on the issues, not on their opponents’ character.
Robert Smart
Saco

title: I’m pulling for you, Kylie Boardman
text:
A couple of weeks ago I read an article in this newspaper about a young Gardiner woman named Kylie Boardman who needs a kidney transplant.
My first thought was “I should get tested to see if I’m a match.” My second thought was “I already donated a kidney and I only have one left.”
Today is the fourth anniversary of my kidney donation surgery. As you can gather, these days it affects my life so little that sometimes I forget I did it. In fact, the other night in bed I was staring at my torso with a flashlight trying to figure out where the third scar from the laparoscopic surgery was and if it had somehow vanished. That’s how much it has faded. (If my wife noticed what I was doing, she didn’t say anything.)
I always assumed that pregnancy and birth would be a lot harder than donating a kidney, where basically all I had to do was show up and a team of specialists took care of everything else and here I am four years out from a nephrectomy and one year out from a baby and can officially, journalistically confirm: yeah, the birth and recovery was way harder.
Birth permanently damaged my body in a way that the kidney removal didn’t. This is just one of the many reasons I get so pissed off when politicians want to force women through pregnancy and childbirth because “a life is at stake” but nobody ever suggests mandating kidney donation even though a dozen people die every day waiting for one. That’s not to say there’s no pain or risk in donation — there is — but let me put it this way: if I could, I would choose to donate a kidney again. I would not choose to get pregnant or give birth again.
I always feel a little weird talking about how I donated a kidney to a stranger; I worry people will think I’m bragging or something. The truth is I didn’t do it for clout or to flex on other people, and I certainly didn’t do it for money (although I admit and disclose here that the Maine Transplant Organization gave me a really nice bathrobe).
I chose to donate a kidney to a stranger because I looked at the data, weighed the potential risks to myself against the potential benefits to the recipient (another decade or two of life) and decided the numbers added up to making a donation.
You don’t have to be a saint in order to do an altruistic donation; I’m certainly as selfish and crabby as anyone else and possibly more so depending on how much sleep I’ve gotten. (For a full list of my faults, please reach out to my wife, mother or any regular commenter on my articles.) You don’t have to be young or particularly fit. I’m actually in better shape now than I was before I got rid of the kidney. You just have to decide to do it.
I was looking for data on what percentage of living kidney donations are “non-directed” or “altruistic” — i.e., donations to someone the donor doesn’t know. (Personally I think it’s pretty altruistic to donate an organ to someone already you know; I didn’t make up this terminology.) I couldn’t find any solid numbers but the general indication seems to be it’s a small percentage. Which is weird to me, because I consider myself a pretty average person and I did it. Maybe I do have a screw loose after all.
That’s not to say I didn’t benefit from the donation. In addition to the aforementioned bathrobe (terry cloth!), the decision to donate a kidney did wonders for my mental health. First of all, any lingering anxiety I had about doctor’s visits or blood draws got hammered out of me through exposure therapy.
I also felt more confident than ever about my health, because I got a complete workover, inside and out, looking for any potential medical vulnerabilities, and all the medics found was that I snore sometimes.
Most importantly, it helped me heal a bit more from my father’s death. For years, I felt this intractable bit of guilt constantly poking at my mind that I couldn’t save him from his cancer. But I was able to save someone else’s dad. That really did help me move on with my life.
I hope Kylie Boardman gets a kidney. If you’re interested in getting tested to see if you’re a match, you can go to kidney4kylie.com. I hope at least one person reading this considers becoming a kidney donor (living or deceased, honestly, both are good). If I can do it, anyone can do it.

title: Suspect arrested after fire “completely engulfed” Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest mountain retreat in Germany
text:
BERLIN (AP) — A fire swept through the mountaintop retreat built for Adolf Hitler and known as the Eagle’s Nest as emergency services struggled to tackle the blaze in snow and wind, and a man was arrested on suspicion of arson, authorities said Saturday.
Emergency services in the Berchtesgaden district, in the Bavarian Alps in Germany’s southeastern corner, were alerted to the fire by an alarm at about 9:15 p.m. Friday. Firefighters and police rushed to the scene — located at the end of a narrow road that winds up the mountain, in part through a series of tunnels — and could see the flames as they approached.
They stopped and arrested a man on a motorcycle driving the other way down the road.
Prosecutors said the 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn’t currently live there, was questioned. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building’s history. Police said there were no current indications that anyone else was involved.
Rain that turned into the season’s first significant snow, accompanied by strong wind, complicated the already difficult task of tackling the blaze and firefighters had to pull out overnight after several hours, officials said. No one was injured in the fire, and firefighters hoped to finish their work on Saturday though they weren’t able to enter the building because of a danger of falling material.
The building, known in German as the Kehlsteinhaus, is located on a cliff 1,834 meters (6,017 feet) above sea level. It is reachable by an elevator built inside the rock from the end of the mountain road, which is closed to public traffic but used during the day by buses for visitors.
It has been operated as a cafe and restaurant since 1952 and contains an exhibition on its history. The Nazi dictator himself rarely used the Kehlsteinhaus — unlike the Berghof residence, also in the Berchtesgaden area, the ruins of which were blown up in 1952.
The Obersalzberg Documentation Center, further down the mountain, is home to the area’s main historical exhibition and was unaffected by the fire.
Officials indicated that the Eagle’s Nest would be restored, though they were vague so soon after the blaze about how exactly that would be done.
“We’re not going to leave a ruin there,” Bavaria’s interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, told reporters in Berchtesgaden. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.
“I think we will be able to find a sensible solution,” Herrmann added. Bavaria’s state government owns the building.
The minister stressed that “it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance.”

title: The “Lewiston is Our Hope” Project Brings Together a Community
text:
Bates Professor and psychologist Yun Loh began working on the art installation Lewiston is Our Hope in the fall of 2025. “As a psychologist, I have witnessed people suffering, but also, I have witnessed their commitment to hope, values and a fully engaged life,” Loh explained. Inspired by this sense of hope in the Lewiston community, even in tough times, Loh sought to create a project for and by the Lewiston people that would portray this hope.
On Oct. 24th, 2026, Loh and her team unveiled the Lewiston is Our Hope mural to the community at the Lewiston Public Library. The unveiling was a community event, which included a buffet of food, musicians, and other art activities.
The Lewiston is Our Hope art installation contains 403 wooden circles arranged in a spiral shape. Each wooden circle has a drawing on it, done by a member of the Lewiston community. For the project, people drew images that represented what makes them feel hope in Lewiston and the hope that they have for Lewiston’s future.
For the art pieces, Loh and her team worked to gather materials such as the wooden circles, which come from local Maine trees. In describing why she chose this medium, Loh explained that the wood is special because, “not every circle shape is the same, which signifies that hope doesn’t need to look the same. Everybody has different shapes and forms of hope.”
Drawings depicted family, friends, a sunset on a river, Lewiston Strong written out in blue letters, a soccer ball and more. Describing this process, Loh said, “I thought that it would take some time for people to think about what they wanted to draw. Yet, when I invited them to think about hope and visualize it, it didn’t take more than three seconds. They get so excited thinking about hope. Some of them really shared very moving stories.”
The process of making this mural involved organizing 47 community drop-in art tables and workshops. These workshops took place at many different spaces, including the ArtVan, Le Ronj, Bates psychology classes, the University of Southern Maine and the Lewiston Farmers Market, among others.
The unveiling event on Oct. 24, 2026, began with several members of the Maine Music Society singing “I Walk in Beauty.” Then attendees were invited to participate in another art project and have some food from the buffet.
In addition to Loh, Lewiston resident Fowsia Musse played a key role in this project as community steward. In her speech at the event, Loh shared that Musse, “one year prior to the Lewiston shooting, lost her sister to gun violence.” Loh led the event attendees in twenty seconds of silence, to honor Musses’s loss and enabling attendees to reflect on Musse’s resilience and hope in a tough time. As community steward, Musse worked with Loh, alongside Bates psychology students, including Reynolds Huard, Kelly Saldana, Claudia Klingbeil, Sophia Ramsey, Anna Luka and Mo Mcguire.
At the unveiling, community members also had the chance to attempt to correctly answer questions about the project, including the age range of people that participated, by placing a slip of paper with their name on it in the box of their guess. Before the mural was unveiled, four lucky winners, who had guessed correctly that the participants ranged from 2 to 95 years old, had their names pulled from the box and won a handmade grocery bag.
Attendees were also invited to participate in a second art project. Developed by some of Loh’s psychology students already working on Lewiston is Our Hope, the project invited attendees chose one of four stamps to put onto a map of Lewiston and Auburn. The stamps represented different ways that hope is created, such as through nature, animals or connections. As the event went on, people began to fill up the map with stamps, placing them in areas that made them feel hopeful, like Bates College, the Androscoggin river, or Thorncrag Sanctuary.
When it was time to unveil the mural, attendees counted down and two Lewiston residents dropped the black sheet covering the mural to reveal the colorful spiral, to wide applause.
As the event drew to a close, I got some food from the buffet, also collecting a complimentary rose and postcard with an image of the mural on it. Then, I exited the library and walked into the sunshine, my heart filled with hope.
Editor’s note: This story was previously published in an incomplete form. The story has since been edited to include details about the art installation.

title: Hearty Roots Plans to Transform Former Bangor Savings Building into Youth-Centered Third Space
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new banner hangs outside of what was formerly the Bangor Savings Bank in downtown Damariscotta, marking a new beginning for the building.
Hearty Roots, a nonprofit organization dedicated to nature-based learning, is set to move into 100 Main St. by the end of this year. The transition was first announced during Pumpkinfest when a Hearty Roots banner was placed outside of the building. Executive Director Haley Bezon said the goal is for the organization to have a “downtown presence.”
“I mean, a property like a once in a lifetime opportunity for an organization,” Bezon said.
The organization is currently located at 18 Water St. in Damariscotta in one of the First National Bank offices. Since its founding in 2017, Bezon said Hearty Roots has grown tremendously and now has a 15-person staff. With the expansion of the employee roster, she said the downtown location will provide more space.
In recent years, Bezon said the organization has also been thinking about creating a “youth-friendly” space in an easily assessable area like downtown. She said third spaces allow young people to connect outside of their homes and school. The location at 100 Main St. is in walking distance from Lincoln Academy in Newcastle and Great Salt Bay Community School in Damariscotta.
There is not a shortage of third spaces in the area but that more can be done, according to Bezon.
“We feel like as we’ve been planning in our strategic vision, we feel like we’re really well poised to not only acquire this property and first, host our 15-person staff team, but then do some visioning and discovering around what this space could become for young people that’s walkable from two schools in our area,” Bezon said. “Through our lens of being a relationship-based organization, how could we bring our approach to youth development to downtown Damariscotta?”
As they prepare to open this space to the public, Bezon said the plan is to research other organizations’ approach to youth-dedicated third spaces, including Midcoast Youth Center and Skatepark in Bath, the Augusta Teen Center, and The Landing Place in Rockland.
The goal is for the new space to be something where young people can stop by that is not “pay to play,” requiring membership or financial obligation to receive services, Bezon said. The organization will also be reaching out to parents, caregivers, and school administrators to further their research on how to make the new space successful.
“You can come in, you can have a snack, you can connect, you can do an activity, and so I think we have a lot of learning to do and we’re going to be leaning on first and foremost, the voices of young people themselves,” Bezon said.
Hearty Roots set eyes on the property when it first went on the market in March, after Bangor Savings vacated the space. The closure of the branch came after the bank’s decision to consolidate it with its location at 619 St. in Damariscotta, according to December 2025 reporting from The Lincoln County News.
In addition to the 4,600-square-foot building, there is a 37-space parking lot in the back that overlooks the Damariscotta River. For the past three years, the organization has been set up in a donated office space from First National Bank. Before that, it did not have a dedicated office and staff members worked from home, according to Bezon.
The goal with the move is to have staff members transferred over to Main Street by the end of the year. Once settled in, Bezon said the organization will focus on fundraising and brainstorming how it plans to transform the property. The process will include seeking community feedback, as the organization plans to host listening sessions in February 2027.
As Hearty Roots steps into its next chapter, Bezon said she is proud of the work the organization has accomplished. In 2026, Hearty Roots has served 1,700 kids so far and partner with 13 schools in Lincoln County.
The acquisition of a new building continues their youth development efforts in a way where they can “catch kids right where they are,” Bezon said. The acquisition of the space will allow children and teenagers to stop in after school for a snack, connect with friends, or go outside to fish.
“I think the most important thing to highlight is just that we’ve been building the programs and the people and the partnerships for almost a decade and this is a really natural next step for us,” Bezon said.

title: Obituary: Michael Dana Worden
text:
WESTBROOK – Michael Dana Worden, 84, passed away peacefully Tuesday evening, Oct. 20, 2026.
Mike was born in Jay, Maine, and lived in Canton Point and Wilton throughout his childhood. He graduated from Wilton Academy and served in the Army at Fort Belvoir in Virginia, after graduating from SMVTI with an Associates Degree. He married Betty Lou Mosher, also from Wilton, in 1967, and they moved to Cape Elizabeth where they raised their family and were married for 50 years. During that time, Mike was food service manager for the correctional center in South Windham and went on to found the Prison Industries Program there.
Mike was the definition of a social butterfly, commenting after a recent high school reunion, “I talked with every person there!” He was known for being a good dancer (Wilton Academy’s 1961 “Jitterbug King”), and for his wide smile and deep summer tan. Mike was happy to coordinate church suppers, and in doing so he made a number of cherished, lifelong friends. He loved spending time as a ride-along bird-hunter with his brother, Jon, who was his best friend. Mike was a runner, camper, fisherman, and hiker. He was happiest when traveling around the country by motor home with Betty, reaching Branson, Key West, Campobello Island, and the Grand Canyon, among other destinations.
Mike took great pride in watching his grandsons, Harry and Sully, thrive. Grampy towed them around the Cape in a bicycle trailer, and they toasted marshmallows at Lily Bay State Park. A trip to Grammy and Grampy’s often included walks to the pond, sorting change, “new” bikes, and peanutbutter-and-Fluff sandwiches. Mike and Betty enjoyed sitting on bleachers and sidelines for soccer, basketball, baseball, and ultimate frisbee.
Mike dedicated many years of his life to caring for Betty, who was diagnosed at 47 with Parkinson’s disease, until she passed away in 2017. While it took its toll, that profound act of devotion is forever revered in the hearts of our family.
Michael was predeceased by his parents, Homer and Velda Worden, and he is survived by his brother, Jon (Diane) Worden, sister, Sue (Jim) Gurney, sister, Betsy Bransky; daughters Kristi (Tim) Worden and Dena (Doug) McFarland; and grandsons Harrison Worden McFarland and Sullivan Michael McFarland.

title: Survivors of Lewiston mass shooting mark anniversary, honor victims with cornhole tournament
text:
LEWISTON — Jason Barnett tossed a beanbag in the air. It hit the cornhole board opposite him with a thud. He threw another that flew into the hole, earning the familiar nod of his teammate, John Petrocelli.
Barnett and Petrocelli were cornhole partners Saturday, like they were nearly three years ago at Schemengees Bar & Grille in Lewiston when they survived the mass shooting that killed 18 people and injured 13. They played this weekend at Just-in-Time Recreation, the bowling alley the shooter attacked on Oct. 25, 2023, before he headed to Schmengees.
Just-in-Time closed after the tragedy but reopened six months later, while Schmengees permanently shuttered. This was the third year TB Events held a cornhole tournament around the anniversary of the attack to raise funds for Maine Resiliency Center — an organization dedicated to helping people navigate the impacts of the shooting — and to unite survivors, families of victims and others who were affected.
“It gets us all back together, it keeps that alive, and it heals us at the same time,” Barnett said.
In April, Just-In-Time owners Justin and Samantha Juray began ripping out six bowling lanes to create a carpeted space for cornhole. The change combines the two activities many of the survivors of the shooting love, but found too painful to participate in, in the months and years after the attack. Survivors of the shooting wore shirts that said “Survivor” on the back and “Lewiston Strong” on the front.
“To see people get over that fear and walk through those doors for the first time again is pretty awesome,” said Justin Juray, who survived the attack while running the bowling alley.
Danielle Jasper said she and a group of other survivors who endured watching other cornhole players die in the shooting regularly get together to play weekly, not just on the anniversary.
“People that I didn’t know before that night are like family now,” Jasper said.
Tyler Babb, owner of TB Events, said turnout at the event exceeded his expectations — he had laid out eight games, but added two more to accommodate the nearly 170 people who signed up across the afternoon and evening tournaments. Entry was $20 per team, which the Maine Resiliency Fund uses to help connect people affected by the shooting with counseling and other resources.
It was not only survivors and the immediate family members of victims who came to play — some drove multiple hours because they enjoy cornhole and wanted to support the fund.
Kathy Bartley, of Houlton, organizes a weekly cornhole league at home and tries to travel to other Maine towns to play, too — she has a friend who was injured in the shooting at Just-in-Time. And Trina Cayford, a professional cornhole player from Bangor who competes nationally with her husband, Phil Cayford, said she came just to connect with people and support the cause.
“Everyone grieves in their own kind of way,” Babb said. “For a lot of people, they’re die-hard cornhole players and community members. And I think that means more to them than anything else ever would.”

title: Family files lawsuit after 50+ middle schoolers served pretzels coated with oven cleaner at lunch
text:
TIGARD, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A family has filed a nearly $1 million lawsuit against an Oregon school district after pretzels seasoned with crushed oven cleaner were served to more than 50 middle school students last year.
The lawsuit, filed Sept. 9, centers on an incident that took place at Fowler Middle School on Oct. 20, 2025, when about 37 pretzels coated with crushed Alto-Sham concentrated oven cleaner — a caustic industrial chemical containing sodium hydroxide — were served during sixth-grade lunch.
More than 50 students ate all or part of the tainted pretzels, according to Tigard-Tualatin School District records.
The school district has described the incident as “human error,” saying a kitchen staff member mistook the oven cleaner for salt. Tigard Police reviewed the case and did not file criminal charges.
The family’s lawsuit names the school district, the lead kitchen worker who put the oven cleaner on the pretzels and Fowler Middle School Principal Cindy Pellicci. It lays out seven claims, including strict liability, negligence, unlawful confinement and violations of civil rights and seeks up to $950,220.85.
Student who ate tainted pretzel felt burning in mouth, throat
The student at the center of the case, identified only as L.L., ate one of the tainted pretzels and immediately felt burning in his mouth and throat, according to the lawsuit, along with chest pain, stomach upset and lingering anxiety about eating at school.
The filing lays out a minute-by-minute timeline of the response. It says Poison Control was not contacted until 11:03 a.m., about 27 minutes after staff realized what happened, and the first email to families did not go out until nearly two hours after students ate the pretzels.
The lawsuit alleges L.L. was then kept in a room for roughly an hour, examined and monitored without his parents being told, denied requests to call home and later sent back to class after staff said he was asymptomatic — even though his mother says he came home with a sore throat and stomach pain.
That account is part of a broader negligence claim. The suit alleges the district failed to store caustic chemicals away from food, failed to train staff on handling them and allowed a crushed cleaner puck to be left on a prep counter and then used as seasoning.
Substitute kitchen worker’s account
The lawsuit leans heavily on the account of substitute kitchen worker Chloe Larson, whose story KPTV first reported. According to the suit, Larson tasted the seasoning, felt a burn, tracked down the discarded packet and had to push the kitchen lead to flip it over to reveal it said “oven cleaner.” The complaint says the kitchen lead first described it to administrators as soap.
KPTV previously reported that the school district’s outside attorney never interviewed Larson, and police only did so after she contacted them about her concerns. The lawsuit makes the same allegation, saying the district interviewed seven staff members but not the substitute who was in the kitchen that day.
Police closed their investigation the same day after speaking with the kitchen lead by phone, saying they had no kitchen photos or video and could not establish probable cause. The lead told police the salt had gotten “cakey,” police said; although that account was never documented in police reports, nor was it heard in the interview police had with the kitchen lead, which KPTV obtained.
The lawsuit says the kitchen lead gave differing explanations — that she was in a rush and, later, that she had crushed the cleaner to use on a steamer and left it out.
The complaint also brings three federal civil rights claims, arguing L.L.’s family was cut out of medical decisions, and the student was exposed to a known danger. Legal experts note those “shocks the conscience” and Monell policy-or-custom arguments are difficult to prove.
An attorney, Barrett Mersereau, has appeared for the defendants but, as of Oct. 23, had not yet filed a substantive answer.
When reached for comment, the school district said it cannot comment on pending litigation but confirmed that the kitchen lead still works in the district.

Maine officials and candidates release statements on the third anniversary of the Lewiston mass shooting
text:
(WABI) - On the third anniversary of the mass shooting in Lewison, elected officials, and candidates released statements.
Lewiston’s mayor Carl L. Sheline:
“Three years ago today, we endured an unimaginable tragedy that forever changed the fabric of our community. In the aftermath, we saw the very best of our community: people caring for one another, showing up in moments of unimaginable grief, and reminding us that we are stronger when we look out for each other.
In the days and weeks that followed, we saw that spirit in countless acts of kindness and generosity. I remember how people showed up for one another, the compassion that carried us through those first difficult weeks, and the determination to keep moving forward. That strength is part of who we are and can never be taken from us.
Today, as we remember those we lost and the lives forever changed, hold your loved ones close. Please check on one another and continue to show each other the same kindness that helped us move forward,”
Governor Janet Mills: “Today we remember and honor the eighteen people who were taken from us on Maine’s darkest day. We keep in our hearts the loved ones they left behind, and we offer our deepest gratitude for the heroes and first responders who saved countless lives. As we pause to remember those we lost, may we find strength in remembering the outpouring of love and support that Maine people showed for one another - from everyday acts of kindness to the sea of blue hearts in store windows that conveyed our love for our Lewiston neighbors. Three years later, we will never forget the hard moments, and we will always remember the humanity and compassion that Maine people found in one another. Hug your loved ones and keep in your hearts those who are no longer able to hold in their arms those who perished,”
Senator Susan Collins: “Three years ago, a horrific shooting in Lewiston claimed 18 innocent lives, injured more than a dozen others, and affected countless members of the greater Lewiston-Auburn community.
“On this solemn anniversary, we remember those who were taken from us and stand with all those who still carry the scars from that devastating night.
“In the years after, the people of our state have done what we always do: law enforcement officers, first responders, health care workers, local leaders, community volunteers, and neighbors came together to support each other through unimaginable grief.
“Since the shooting, I have worked with Lewiston to ensure the community has resources to help them heal and recover, including by strengthening mental health services and supporting the Maine Resiliency Center.
“We will continue to remember the victims, support their families and loved ones, and stand with the people of this community,”
U.S. Senate Candidate Troy Jackson: “Three years ago, 18 of our neighbors were murdered in Lewiston.
I had grown up with guns and at the time, I opposed some gun laws. That day, I learned those 18 people deserve more than our grief.
We need to make sure what happened in Lewiston never happens again.
From then on, I fought to protect the people we love by fighting for stronger gun laws.
Today, I’m thinking of all of the families who lost someone that day.
My heart is with them, and I will not stop fighting for them,”
Congressman Jared Golden: “Three years ago today, 18 Mainers were killed and 13 more injured in the deadliest shooting in our state’s history.
It shook our community, our state and the entire nation. While time has passed, the painful sense of loss remains, especially for the families and friends who lost loved ones and for the victims who still carry the scars of that awful day.
But while the grief remains, my pride in my hometown does too. In the days and weeks after the shooting, Mainers showed up for one another. In the midst of the crisis, we had each other’s backs.
Today, Izzy and I are keeping the victims and their loved ones in our prayers. We will never forget the horror of October 25, 2023. But as we were then, we will remain: Lewiston Strong,"
Congresswoman Chellie Pingree: “Three years ago, Maine suffered one of the deadliest mass shootings in American history.
Eighteen people lost their lives that day. An entire city was shaken to its core. For all of Maine—and especially for the people of Lewiston-Auburn and the families whose hearts were shattered by the loss of a loved one—it’s a tragedy that will never be forgotten.
Today and every day, we remember the victims. We are deeply grateful to the first responders for their service and bravery. And we hold all those who continue to live with the pain of that day in our thoughts.
But let us also honor the incredible support and resilience that the Lewiston-Auburn community showed, and continues to show, in the wake of that terrible tragedy. Their courage. Their compassion. Their kindness.
And let us commit—to these families, this community, and all our fellow Mainers—to doing everything in our power to ensure nothing like this ever happens again,"
Gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles: “Three years ago, 18 innocent Mainers were taken from us on the darkest night in our state’s history. Tonight, in Lewiston, we remember every life lost, pray with the families whose grief never fades and stand shoulder to shoulder with the survivors who still carry the physical and emotional scars of that tragic day.
“Standing with these families also means refusing to stay silent while they are robbed a second time. After the shooting, generous people across Maine and America donated millions because they were promised in writing that 100 percent of their money would help the victims and survivors rebuild their lives. Instead, nearly $2 million meant for those victims was siphoned off to 29 politically connected nonprofits—many of which never helped a single survivor—without even requiring full spending reports on where the money went. The State leadership and Governor Mills - and her top policy staffer Hannah Pingree - should have insisted on accountability; that was their moral and legal responsibility. They did not, deepening the tragedy through indifference.
“While survivors like Jennifer Zanca are left fighting $93,000 in uncovered hospital bills, activist nonprofits cashed $65,522 checks—more than double what victims received on average—and the Attorney General in Augusta refuses to investigate. Taking money raised on the backs of murder victims is a betrayal of the most sacred trust. As governor, I will audit every dollar, expose who signed off on this scheme and fight until the Lewiston victims and their families get every dime that was taken from them,”
Gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree: “Three years ago today, 18 people were taken from us in Lewiston, and 13 more were wounded.
Families lost the people they loved most. A community was changed forever, and all of Maine grieved with them. Today, we remember those we lost. We hold their families, the survivors, and the Lewiston-Auburn community in our hearts, knowing that for many, the pain has never gone away.
We also remember how Maine responded. First responders ran toward danger. Neighbors opened their doors and took care of one another. People across our state came together to show that, even in our darkest hour, we acted as Mainers and we acted as a community.
That compassion is who we are. It is what I will carry with me, and it is what we must all carry forward: by standing by the survivors and families still healing, and by continuing the work to make our communities safer and prevent future tragedies in our state,"
Gubernatorial candidate Rick Bennett: “Three years ago tonight, everything changed in a city that had never imagined this.
Eighteen of our neighbors did not come home. Thirteen more were injured. Many more carry wounds that do not show.
To the families, we have not forgotten. We will not forget.
To the first responders, and to the neighbors who ran toward the tragedy, thank you.
And to anyone carrying this alone tonight, asking for help is not weakness. Our state should make that help easy to find, close to home, and there when someone reaches for it.
Maine is at its best when we hold each other up.
May the fallen rest in peace, and may we prove worthy of their memory,"

title: Simone Biles cries following sale of million-dollar home
text:
Simone Biles breaks down in tears following sale of million-dollar home
Simone Biles, an Olympic gymnast, and Jonathan Owens, a safety for the Indianapolis Colts, have been married since 2023.
The athletic couple stunned on the runway at celebrity events and show support for each other in their games and meets.
Video above: Star gymnast Simone Biles donates her Kentucky Derby hats to charity auction
One of their biggest accomplishments, though, may come away from the turf and balance beam — it was calling their beautiful house a home.
But like in any stage of life, there comes a time for change.
In a video posted to TikTok, Biles offered a tear-filled goodbye to her beloved home. In what took nearly five years to custom-build, Biles and Owens moved into their beautiful 3,998-square-foot property in a gated community near Houston, Texas, in 2020.
"This house will be on the market for the first time, and I don't know why I'm boohoo crying," Biles said. "I was here for six years, and I feel like there were just so many good memories, so many bad memories. "But I feel like I grew up in this house. It's made me a real adult, so I'm going to miss it. I didn't think I'd be emotional about a house."
Biles, 29, a native of Columbus, Ohio, grew up in the foster care system when her birth mother was unable to care for her or her three siblings. She moved to Texas and was adopted by her maternal grandfather, Ron Biles, and his second wife, Nellie Cayetano Biles, in 2000.
She met Owens, 31, on a dating app in March 2020 when he was playing football for the Houston Texans. They moved in together a short time later.
"Whoever buys this house, I hope it brings you as much joy as it did for me," she said.
The house was listed at $1.275 million.
Video below: Simone Biles, Martha Stewart amongst keynote speakers at Boston women's conference
In her video, Biles gave a quick tour of the four-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bath home that featured a spacious kitchen and a waterfall island with quartz countertops, according to the Houston Association of Realtors.
The couple was used to moving around the country, although they still maintained this home while Owens was playing for several NFL teams.
Owens, a Missouri native, went undrafted after playing college football at Missouri Western University from 2013-17. In 2018, he signed a free-agent deal with the Arizona Cardinals. He played for the Texans from 2019-22. He spent one year with the Green Bay Packers in 2023, played with the Chicago Bears from 2024-25, and has been with the Colts on a one-year contract.
As an Olympic gymnast. Biles has collected seven gold medals, two silver medals and two bronze medals.
Biles and Owens were married in April 2023.
In September, Biles posted on social media that another home she lived in while in Chicago was broken into, and her car was stolen.
Biles said the vehicle, a Porsche GTS, was later recovered, but she and her husband decided to replace it. She also indicated that the couple acquired a Doberman after the incident.
