title: Independent candidates hold the key to our democracy
text:
Sam Hunkler of Beals was a 2022 independent candidate for Maine governor.
It’s a squeal I often heard while collecting signatures to get on the ballot.
“You’re going to split the vote,” a political party cry. One woman was beside herself, irate that I was going to get a share of the pie. Later, she drove by shaking her fist at me. I wondered which party she belonged to.
Democracy implies splitting the vote. The vote is always split among candidates, like a pie. If unopposed, you get the whole pie. No splitting. But the concept takes on a different color with party politics.
Parties claim entitlement to the pie. In their world, a vote outside the two parties is considered “splitting” because it splinters from the party machine where one must choose sides.
When I ran in Maine’s last gubernatorial election as an independent, both of my opponents were party, not electorally, chosen. The Maine Republican and Democratic parties each selected their candidate so there would be no splitting of the vote. They imposed their will to stymie other candidates, the will of party members and democracy.
The advent of political parties, which occurred during his time in office, greatly disturbed George Washington. He was the first and only independent president, the only president to have not belonged to a party. During his farewell speech in 1796 he foresaw that “the spirit of party …serves always to distract the public councils and enfeeble the public administration. It agitates the community with ill-founded jealousies and false alarms, kindles the animosity of one part against another, foments occasionally riot and insurrection.”
The “spirit of party.” How prophetic.
Imagine what it would be like if everyone was an independent, including candidates for office. Imagine if everyone had to decide for themself what was important and how to vote without a party dictating importance and loyalty of their candidates, if elected officials acted upon the voices of the people who elected them and not on the party that enshrined them. We’d have a different outcome and perhaps get beyond the right/left politics, black/white thinking and for/against dogma that divide us.
Even though independents make up a third of Maine voters, we rarely have a voice in our state government. An independent cannot afford to run for higher office unless they are wealthy. They cannot compete financially with party candidates who are bankrolled by parties in exchange for party ideology devotion, where there is little leeway to think and act independently.
Take this year’s U.S. Senate race with Susan Collins and Troy Jackson. Approximately $400 million is expected to be spent in this race, more than $400 per each voting-age resident. How can an independent candidate of ordinary means possibly compete? Consequently, democracy and the voices of at least a third of Mainers are thwarted.
In Maine, we’ve taken that a bit further. The two parties have legislated themselves to be the only ones recognized. The other parties are collectively called “independents,” though we have multiple other parties, including the Green Independent and Libertarian parties.
I am not affiliated with any party, so I am considered an “unenrolled” independent. Again, exclusivity by the two parties in control opposes democracy. This inequality has become more evident over time, especially since Citizens United, which allowed virtually unlimited independent political expenditures by corporations and labor unions — from who knows where. Unfortunately, the party that spends the most often wins. Our elections are being bought.
The party system “kindles the animosity of one part against another,” fermenting fear. In 2022, it seems that I met as many who planned to vote against Mills or LePage as for them. I frequently heard, “I’m afraid to vote for you because Mills (or LePage) might win.”
Is there a remedy, a solution to this assault on democracy?
A step in that direction would be to vote for change rather than out of fear. Consider voting for an independent. We have an opportunity this year to make a significant vote to do just that in our highest Maine office, the governorship.
The independent in this race, Rick Bennett, running a grassroots campaign on a low budget, is the most qualified candidate, with the most experience and with a good heart. Take a look. George Washington would smile.

title: Let’s do political campaigning the Irish way
text:
Regarding the Oct. 18 report “It’s not your imagination — you’re being bombarded with political ads this election,” I have an idea for Maine elections gleaned from my years of teaching in Ireland.
Paid political advertising is generally not permitted on broadcast media in Ireland. Thirty days before the election, candidates and parties may put up print ads, billboards, posters and signs. By seven days after the vote, all signs must be removed (or face on-the-spot fines of €250 for each sign).
If it’s possible for Maine to impose such a system, we would have our family time free of these ugly and demeaning ads for most of the year, and politicos would have a generous window to focus their arguments carefully on the issues, not on their opponents’ character.
Robert Smart
Saco

title: Obituary: Elaine Marie (Coyne) Kitchen
text:
DEFREESTVILLE, N.Y. / PORTLAND – Elaine Marie (Coyne) Kitchen, 89, passed away peacefully surrounded by her family on Oct. 22, 2026.
Born on June 16, 1937, she was the beloved daughter of the late Martin Henry Coyne and Claudia Gould (Crowley) Coyne. Elaine grew up in South Portland and graduated from South Portland High School in the Class of 1956.
On June 12, 1960, just one week after her husband, T. Robert “Bob” Kitchen, graduated from the University of Maine at Orono, the two were married. Two weeks later, they embarked on a new journey together, moving to the Albany, N.Y. area. They settled in Defreestville, N.Y. in 1963, where they built a warm and loving home and life together. Although New York was her home for over six decades, Elaine remained a true Mainer at heart throughout her entire life.
Early in her career, Elaine worked as a secretary for the Engineering Department of Portland Pipe Line. After raising her three children, she returned to the workforce with the New York State Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Third Judicial Department. She earned immense respect for her professionalism, concluding her career as the confidential secretary to the Presiding Justice, Hon. A. Franklin Mahoney and retired on Dec. 31, 1993.
Elaine was a very private person, yet deeply liked and respected by all who had the pleasure of knowing her. Her primary devotion was always her family and friends. In retirement, she and Bob loved to travel, taking road trips across the United States and Canada, vacationing in Europe, and making memorable trips to Ireland, tracing the heritage of the Coyne family.
Above all, they cherished the considerable time spent at their condo at Whistler Landing in Scarborough where they shared special memories with family and dear friends.
Elaine is survived by her devoted husband of 66 years, T. Robert “Bob” Kitchen; her three loving children, David B. Kitchen (Lori), Stephen Kitchen, and Annemarie Kitchen Spada (Eric); and her two cherished granddaughters, Lidia Spada and Julia Spada.
She was predeceased by two brothers, John Coyne and James Coyne.
At Elaine’s request, there will be no calling hours. A private graveside service and burial will be held at the convenience of the family.

title: Man cooking chicken for roadside barbecue finds dead snake in charcoal bag
text:
NAHIKU, Hawaii (HNN/Gray News) - A Hawaii man was cooking chicken for lunch at a roadside grill when he noticed a slithery surprise in a bag of charcoal.
Roy Hanks was in for a surprise while cooking huli huli chicken just before lunch last Saturday for Hana Hawaiian BBQ, a roadside barbecue at Nahiku Marketplace on the island of Maui.
“My husband was running the grill. He went to throw charcoal on the fire. He opened the charcoal bag and found the snake on top of the bag,” said Sharon Fillazar-Hanks, Roy’s wife and the manager of Hana Hawaiian BBQ.
She said she did not believe her husband at first.
“He sent a picture,” Fillazar-Hanks said. “I thought it was a prank, but it wasn’t. It was real, but it was dead.”
Fillazar-Hanks called the Maui Police Department, who responded and then contacted the Hawaii Department of Agriculture Quarantine Division.
MPD officials said the department told officers the snake could be disposed of.
The department confirmed the charcoal bag was packaged outside of Hawaii.
“It was likely already deceased during the packing process in its state or country of origin,” said Jai Cunningham, Hawaiʻi Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity public information officer. “DAB has seen similar cases with baled hay, where snakes seek shelter in the unprocessed product, are killed during processing and are then unintentionally shipped to Hawaiʻi.”
The snake’s species is unclear. Based on photos, state officials said it is likely a nonvenomous rat snake.
“Some people say possible juvenile copperhead snake. Then, one said a rat snake. I’m like, ‘A snake is a snake. We don’t need it here,’” Fillazar-Hanks said.

title: Is it Nov. 4 yet? What about now?
text:
Eddie Adelman is a writer who lives in Belfast. His book of columns and short essays is titled “Don’t Get Me Started.”
I don’t know about you, but I’ve got Wednesday, Nov. 4, circled on my calendar. That’s the day after Election Day, when all the political ads expire, the lawn signs begin to come down and the robocalls cease and desist. And let’s not forget the political junk mail.
I am neither a Democrat nor a Republican. As a proud independent, you could say I’m an equal opportunity skewer.
But before I do any skewering, let me say how blessed I am to live in a country where I can write a piece like this without fear of being abducted from my home in the middle of the night and imprisoned, tortured or killed.
For the brave citizens in places like Russia, North Korea and Iran willing to risk everything standing up to tyranny, I can only bow my head in humility and utter veneration.
And with that, back to the skewering. As far as I can tell, the No. 1 goal of every elected official is simple: Get reelected at all costs.
Power is intoxicating, as the senators in ancient Rome knew all too well while they luxuriated in their executive bath houses. Nowadays, getting reelected is a full-time job. There’s always a new gunslinger ready and willing to face off in the middle of town. And let’s face it, we all love a “Gunsmoke” moment.
Sadly, it’s the moments leading up to that face-off that cause trouble.
Let’s start with political advertising. It’s been estimated that the total cost for the 2024 presidential and congressional election campaigns was about $16 billion. Sixteen billion dollars. And that doesn’t even take into account the cost of local and state elections.
Who knows what the total price tag will be for the 2026 campaigns?
Think about how much low-income housing all this money could buy. In a single election cycle, we could take a significant bite out of the homeless crisis here in America.
Of all the billions of dollars raised and spent, a sizable chunk will be spent on TV ads.
If I’m not mistaken, there was a time when TV ads didn’t mention the competition. Tide never mentioned Cheer. Ford never mentioned Chevy. Pepsi never mentioned Coke.
I believe the same was true for political ads. We were content to see the candidates posing in the backyard with his or her family in front of a swing set, surrounded by impossibly cute kids and stout, hard-working immigrant parents. Kiss those days goodbye.
Nowadays, candidates take turns disparaging, even demonizing, their opponents. Not only do these ads cancel each other out, but they ruin the TV watching experience. It’s enough to drive the average citizen to pick up a book.
And political junk mail? Please. Has anyone ever read one of those mailings and thought, “That does it. I’m changing my vote.” Hello, recycling bin.
Road signs. Lawn signs. Hats. T-shirts. Bumper stickers. Don’t get me started. Election Day is just around the corner. And as far as I’m concerned, it can’t get here soon enough.
I’m Eddie Adelman and I approved this column.

title: Central Maine residents are using citizens’ petitions to change public policy. Here’s what to know
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
During this election season, voters across Maine will choose candidates to represent them at local, county, state and federal levels.
They will also weigh in on local referendums, ballot questions that will set policy for the communities where they originated. The Maine Trust for Local News voter guide lists 11 local initiatives; most were put there by elected officials, but in about 15% of the cases, proposals came from residents through a citizens’ initiative.
The municipal petition-backed referendums on November’s ballot are mostly simple. Four seek to stabilize lot rent in mobile home parks, where rapidly rising rent has been an issue across the state. Two call for a town to withdraw from a school district. One looks to ban automated license plate readers.
While initiatives are a tool that allows residents to have a direct influence on policy when other avenues haven’t worked, there are some pitfalls and there’s no guarantee of success. Some municipal and policy experts warn it should be used as a last resort.
CREATING A PETITION
Dan Shea, a Colby College professor of government and a Mount Vernon selectman, said ballot initiatives that are carefully and cleanly written find much more success at the state level.
A year ago, Maine voters supported the so-called Red Flag Law, which started as a citizens’ petition, by 2-to-1 margin. It allows family or household members or law enforcement to petition courts to temporarily bar someone from having dangerous weapons if the person poses a significant danger of causing injury to themselves or others.
A decade ago, Maine voters narrowly legalized adult-use marijuana. That also started as a citizens petition.
A good referendum question, Shea said, is one a voter can understand on a “gut level.” These initiatives don’t typically find success along party lines; they generally have broader appeal.
Kate Dufour, director of advocacy and communications at the Maine Municipal Association, a voluntary membership organization for cities and towns that offers services to local governments and advocates for municipal interests, said the best way to ensure a citizens’ initiative works is to have conversations with governing officials before moving to a petition.
“I think sometimes we’re, as a society, too quick to say ‘well, this is not working, it has to be done this way,'” Dufour said. “When we avoid having those conversations, which can be uncomfortable, and they can take time and effort, we set stages that don’t necessarily need to be set.”
In 2023, the Maine State Legislature repealed a property tax stabilization program for senior citizens and Carol Carothers took action.
Carothers tried discussing the issue with her state legislators. When that didn’t work, she moved straight to a citizens’ initiative. She drafted an ordinance to give seniors property tax relief in Belgrade, where she lives.
In hindsight, Carothers said going to Belgrade’s selectboard first to ask how they could work together to create an ordinance may have been a better approach.
The selectboard told Carothers her first proposal was not legal. It said the same about the next one she drafted, also focused on tax rebates for residents. She said she felt brushed off, but Anthony Wilson, who sits on Belgrade’s budget committee, said the ordinances posed a financial danger to the town — Belgrade couldn’t afford them.
Sometimes, citizens’ initiatives can result in unintended consequences for towns, said Wilson, who is also Winthrop’s town manager. Equally, town governments sometimes don’t act as residents would like them to because they’re bound by state law.
“There is a method to the madness, and from the outside looking in, it’s not always apparent,” Wilson said. “Unless you’re engaged in the process, you may not fully appreciate that.”
Carothers is now on her third petition and perhaps one step closer to having her ordinance. She’s focused on budgeting transparency and how the town approves spending. Residents will vote on her proposed policy at Belgrade’s next town meeting in June.
Carothers said she was emboldened to pursue a citizens’ initiative after she spoke to people about her dissatisfaction with Belgrade’s property taxes.
“So many people said to me, ‘there’s nothing you can do,'” Carothers said. “I think the best thing about this country … is that we do have the ability to change something we think isn’t working and that there’s a process for that. I believe in that wholeheartedly.”
At least one clause of her new proposed ordinance conflicts with state law, but Carothers added a clause allowing the town to sever any illegal sections. Some selectboard members argued passing an ordinance they know needs to change is bad public policy.
In the meantime, the budget committee is working to adopt some of the conditions in the ordinance proposal as policy, something Wilson thinks could have happened already if the petitioners had first consulted with the selectboard.
Carothers said that is to the board’s credit, but she had her reasons for pursuing collecting signatures first. Carothers was working with a group of Belgrade residents who had voted on whether to involve the board, and most said no.
Some, she said, felt burned by her previous petitions being dismissed and others had their own experiences where they felt the board hadn’t heard them. So they went straight to the people.
Carothers said she knows the selectboard could repeal her ordinance even if it passes, but she still believes in her own power to make a difference.
“It’s always Sisyphean. You have to say to yourself, ‘I’m in this for the long haul because I’m going to roll the rock up the hill, but this rock could roll back down,'” Carothers said. “This is the process, and I need to be willing to roll that rock up there again.”
HOW TOWNS RESPOND
In Belgrade, selectboard members consulted with an attorney, held a public hearing and spent a few meetings discussing the ordinance before they agreed to put it on next year’s town meeting warrant despite their concerns.
The process isn’t always so simple.
Earlier this year, 270 Sidney residents signed a petition aimed at putting a 180-day moratorium on “large-scale industrial facilities” and creating an oversight board to review such projects. Petitioners wanted to prevent a new Amazon facility, which had already been approved by the time the public hearing on the petition was held, and to create oversight for similar future projects.
In this case, the selectboard was frustrated. A provision in the proposed ordinance required a special town meeting, which costs the town. Sections of the Sidney petition also conflicted with state law.
At a public hearing for the initiative, selectboard and planning board members criticized the petitioners for not coming to more meetings. They argued residents’ concerns could have been addressed without an expensive public process — it cost about $3,000 — and voters rejected the ordinance in August.
In other Maine towns, petitioners are involved with an issue before they resort to petition.
Oakland residents asked town officials earlier this year to consider an ordinance to stabilize rent in mobile home lots after one mobile home park increased lot rents by more than 50% in less than two years.
Oakland officials established a committee to review health and safety in the parks and promised to consider a rent stabilization ordinance. But the Town Council later disbanded the committee and said it would not pursue an ordinance.
That’s when residents started a petition, and the proposed ordinance is now on Oakland’s ballot.

title: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visits China to inaugurate a new cross-border bridge
text:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visits China to inaugurate a new cross-border bridge
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited China on Saturday, inaugurating a new bridge that connects the two countries and vowing to expand cooperation with his powerful neighbor.
Related video: Trump says US won't put brakes on AI following Xi visit
Kim’s visit to China is his latest move in an increasingly assertive foreign policy as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a “new Cold War.” It's his first visit in a year.
Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong Saturday after crossing the newly opened bridge, according to South Korea’s Unification Ministry and China's official Xinhua News Agency.
Both sides promise to strengthen cooperation
In Dandong, Kim visited a memorial marking China's support of North Korea during the 1950-53 Korean War and met with Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of China’s Communist Party.
At the memorial, Kim said that North Korea will “firmly carry forward the invincible DPRK-China friendship forged at the cost of blood all the time,” according to the North's official Korean Central News Agency. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, the North's official name.
During their meeting, Kim reaffirmed a resolve to develop bilateral cooperation, while Wang conveyed Chinese President Xi Jinping's greetings and said Kim's visit to the memorial was “of great significance” in carrying forward the friendship between the two countries, KCNA said.
The two toured a car factory as well, before Wang accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, according to KCNA and Xinhua.
New bridge was built to help expand trade between the countries
Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge this month was a key symbol of strengthening ties between North Korea and China and reflected their intent to expand trade, as it is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks. The bridge was opened after more than a decade of delay.
While returning home via the bridge, Kim said “the bridge would undoubtedly and correctly fulfill its historic mission of linking the two countries and firmly joining the minds of the peoples of the two countries,” KCNA reported.
Kim has recently taken steps to bolster ties with China, the North’s traditional main ally and economic lifeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia. China, for its part, has sought to restore its unique influence over North Korea.
North Korea has sent thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for military and economic assistance.
Kim's visit timed to key battle anniversary in Korean War with China
Kim’s latest visit to China is his sixth since taking power in late 2011 following the death of his father, Kim Jong Il. The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of his ties with Beijing ahead of the Oct. 25 anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean War, which was days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950.
The war began with North Korea’s surprise attack on the South in June 1950, prompting a U.N.-led coalition headed by the United States to intervene and push back the offensive. North Korea was backed primarily by Chinese forces, with assistance from the then-Soviet Union’s air force, before fighting ended with a 1953 armistice that left the peninsula technically at war.
Xi traveled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit, Xi expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.
Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025, when he met with Xi and watched a military parade alongside Putin and other foreign leaders.
Kim has maintained a hard line toward Seoul and has so far rebuffed a proposal from U.S. President Donald Trump to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019 during Trump’s first term. Kim’s government has called for Washington to abandon its “hostile policy” and drop demands for the North’s denuclearization as a precondition for renewed talks.
South Korea’s liberal government, which favors engagement with the North, hopes renewed talks between Washington and Pyongyang will thaw inter-Korean relations, and has also urged China to play a “constructive” role in resolving the standoff. Seoul's spy agency told lawmakers last month that it saw a 50% possibility of a meeting between Trump and Kim on the sidelines of next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, summit in Shenzhen, China.
“From Seoul’s perspective, if North Korea focuses more on economic development than military buildup and threats, that would be positive for diplomacy and security,” said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“But if Kim can extract ever more benefits from China and Russia, it is unclear what Seoul could offer that would be worth the political risks Pyongyang attaches to exchanges with a more prosperous, globalized, and free Korea.”
___
Wu reported from Bangkok. Associated Press journalists Hyung-jin Kim in Seoul and Mayuko Ono in Tokyo contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: Monica Natalie (Kowalski) Vanderburg
Family files lawsuit after 50+ middle schoolers served pretzels coated with oven cleaner at lunch
text:
TIGARD, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A family has filed a nearly $1 million lawsuit against an Oregon school district after pretzels seasoned with crushed oven cleaner were served to more than 50 middle school students last year.
The lawsuit, filed Sept. 9, centers on an incident that took place at Fowler Middle School on Oct. 20, 2025, when about 37 pretzels coated with crushed Alto-Sham concentrated oven cleaner — a caustic industrial chemical containing sodium hydroxide — were served during sixth-grade lunch.
More than 50 students ate all or part of the tainted pretzels, according to Tigard-Tualatin School District records.
The school district has described the incident as “human error,” saying a kitchen staff member mistook the oven cleaner for salt. Tigard Police reviewed the case and did not file criminal charges.
The family’s lawsuit names the school district, the lead kitchen worker who put the oven cleaner on the pretzels and Fowler Middle School Principal Cindy Pellicci. It lays out seven claims, including strict liability, negligence, unlawful confinement and violations of civil rights and seeks up to $950,220.85.
Student who ate tainted pretzel felt burning in mouth, throat
The student at the center of the case, identified only as L.L., ate one of the tainted pretzels and immediately felt burning in his mouth and throat, according to the lawsuit, along with chest pain, stomach upset and lingering anxiety about eating at school.
The filing lays out a minute-by-minute timeline of the response. It says Poison Control was not contacted until 11:03 a.m., about 27 minutes after staff realized what happened, and the first email to families did not go out until nearly two hours after students ate the pretzels.
The lawsuit alleges L.L. was then kept in a room for roughly an hour, examined and monitored without his parents being told, denied requests to call home and later sent back to class after staff said he was asymptomatic — even though his mother says he came home with a sore throat and stomach pain.
That account is part of a broader negligence claim. The suit alleges the district failed to store caustic chemicals away from food, failed to train staff on handling them and allowed a crushed cleaner puck to be left on a prep counter and then used as seasoning.
Substitute kitchen worker’s account
The lawsuit leans heavily on the account of substitute kitchen worker Chloe Larson, whose story KPTV first reported. According to the suit, Larson tasted the seasoning, felt a burn, tracked down the discarded packet and had to push the kitchen lead to flip it over to reveal it said “oven cleaner.” The complaint says the kitchen lead first described it to administrators as soap.
KPTV previously reported that the school district’s outside attorney never interviewed Larson, and police only did so after she contacted them about her concerns. The lawsuit makes the same allegation, saying the district interviewed seven staff members but not the substitute who was in the kitchen that day.
Police closed their investigation the same day after speaking with the kitchen lead by phone, saying they had no kitchen photos or video and could not establish probable cause. The lead told police the salt had gotten “cakey,” police said; although that account was never documented in police reports, nor was it heard in the interview police had with the kitchen lead, which KPTV obtained.
The lawsuit says the kitchen lead gave differing explanations — that she was in a rush and, later, that she had crushed the cleaner to use on a steamer and left it out.
The complaint also brings three federal civil rights claims, arguing L.L.’s family was cut out of medical decisions, and the student was exposed to a known danger. Legal experts note those “shocks the conscience” and Monell policy-or-custom arguments are difficult to prove.
An attorney, Barrett Mersereau, has appeared for the defendants but, as of Oct. 23, had not yet filed a substantive answer.
When reached for comment, the school district said it cannot comment on pending litigation but confirmed that the kitchen lead still works in the district.

title: Once adrift, Graham Platner’s fleet of volunteers finds new purpose
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On a recent October evening, Kelly Millikan was among a half-dozen volunteers sitting on repurposed church pews inside a small storefront in Portland’s Arts District.
Hunched over a clipboard, Millikan dutifully scrawled a note on the back of a postcard.
“Last we spoke you told us of your plan to vote early at City Hall,” she writes. “Thank you for being an active participant in our Democracy + making your voice heard. Best, Kelly + PPM.”
Each postcard is pre-printed with “People Powered Maine. Organized money always wins. Until organized people show up.” — the calling card of an organization founded by former volunteers for Graham Platner.
When Platner’s meteoric bid against Republican Sen. Susan Collins came crashing down in July, thousands of people inspired by the political newcomer and his progressive policy agenda were set adrift.
But many, like Millikan, are still engaged in the consequential election.
Some have signed on to the Maine People Powered Movement, which rose from the ashes of Platner’s implosion. A few are working independently of any organized group. And others have joined up with the Maine Democratic Party.
Many of those disappointed by Platner’s exit say they have found a renewed purpose their organizing.
“I think it was difficult for a lot of people, not just me,” said Michelle Lesperance, a 69-year-old retired special education teacher from Portland who’s working independently for progressive causes. “We had so many reservations about the party itself, and I continued to have reservations.”
But in the short term, she and the party share the same goals.
“The bottom line is: We all are completely, completely and totally 100% around getting rid of Collins,” Lesperance said.
Volunteers with People Powered Maine are sending the postcards to residents their group has already met through canvassing efforts. Their notes don’t advocate for a specific candidate on the Nov. 3 ballot. That’s by design, said Bente Lundh, a lead organizer with the group.
“Most of the time, as you will see in the instructions, we’re not pushing people one way or another,” Lundh told the assembled volunteers. “We’re trying not to be obnoxious that way.”
With less than two weeks before the midterm elections, People Powered Maine’s softer approach is distinct from other progressive organizing efforts in the state.
Democratic Party organizers are mustering canvassers to ask Mainers to vote for Democrat Troy Jackson over Collins. But People Powered Maine isn’t being quite so blunt. They’re betting that fostering relationships beyond the transactional nature of asking for a vote will lead to lasting change.
Those close to these efforts insist there is no tension between the voter outreach efforts of the Democratic Party and independent groups. But they’re undeniably approaching the campaign in different ways.
PEOPLE POWERED MAINE
Last fall, Platner’s campaign held a series of “Grahamcamps” that trained volunteers in relational organizing, which seeks to build relationships within a community and identify a common concern before trying to persuade someone to support a certain issue or candidate.
A core group of lead organizers attracted to Platner’s theory of politics decided to formalize his approach in August, incorporating People Powered Maine as a 501(c)(4), a type of nonprofit that allows for lobbying and public issue advocacy.
“Graham was much more focused on building that connection with the person you’re knocking at a door with,” said Gioachinno Brennan, a 26-year-old Cumberland resident and former Platner volunteer who now works with People Powered Maine. “The whole message was — the campaign is listening … this is a candidate that wants to address the concerns of the people.”
However, the group isn’t staying agnostic in the state’s biggest race. Last month, organizers created a federal political action committee, Maine People Powered Movement, to advocate for specific candidates who pledge to support the group’s platform and who pass muster with its members.
The group is backing Jackson, co-founder Crystale Lapham said, because he signed onto their policy platform and took questions from members.
Within the last couple of weeks, the group worked the crowds at rallies with Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.
At the Warren rally in Portland’s Deering Oaks, Lapham said the group focused on “tripling.” That’s where volunteers ask attendees to call or text three friends urging them to vote and telling them what issues they find important.
Lapham said the group has a core of 250 or so volunteers and more than 2,000 others who have signed up on its website.
The 501(c)(4)’s canvassing approach is largely one of persuasion. Rather than knocking on the doors of Democrats, hoping to fire up the anti-Trump base, People Powered Maine is reaching out to people who are not enrolled in a political party ahead of the midterms. Unenrolled voters comprise nearly a third of the state’s registered voters, making them the second-largest voting bloc behind Democrats in Maine.
Lapham said nearly a third of those unenrolled voters are undecided about the U.S. Senate race, according data from the group’s canvassers. (Formal polls show a far lower share of undecided voters.)
“A lot of the people are saying, ‘This is the first time anybody’s knocked on my door to talk about Troy,'” said Lapham, a 44-year-old Falmouth resident. “So we know that we’re talking to the right doors.”
The group is being assisted by Ronnie Cho, a former statewide organizer for Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign. Cho said Obama had a field operation that was separate from the Democratic Party — and it was key to his resounding victory in Maine.
“One of the biggest takeaways I got from that campaign was how important it was to talk to people beyond party affiliation,” Cho, 43, said.
“We had offices that were not co-located with the Maine Democratic Party, because we knew that we needed to make this place welcome and open for folks of all political stripes. … And I haven’t seen enough of that kind of intentionality when it comes to organizing.”
PARTY EFFORTS
The Maine Democratic Party says it has built the largest canvassing operation in state history.
On Tuesday, the party announced it has made more than a million attempted voter contacts, with canvassers knocking on more than 230,000 doors and making 790,000 phone calls. The party has opened 25 field offices in all 16 counties, trained more than 290 volunteer leaders and surpassed 18,000 volunteer shift sign-ups, it said.
The party said more than 2,200 former Platner volunteers have signed up for at least one volunteer shift.
That effort is geared toward electing Democrats up and down the ballot on Election Day. The party says 30% of their canvassing targets are unenrolled voters — meaning their efforts aren’t strictly partisan, either.
Collins’ campaign did not respond to specific questions about its canvassing operations. But spokesman Shawn Roderick said in a written statement that canvassing is being done by both campaign volunteers and the Maine Republican Party.
An outside group, Stronger Maine, has also been canvassing on Collins’ behalf for months.
SOME STILL ADRIFT
Some former Platner volunteers say they haven’t found a home since the campaign ended.
Among this group of expats is Erin Evans, who has offered her Portland house as a base for canvassing and making homemade campaign throughout the political season.
Evans wanted Nirav Shah to replace Platner on the Democratic ticket, but her candidate was out-organized by Jackson with the help of labor unions during the Democrats’ second, truncated mini-primary in July. But she’s still engaged in campaigning.
“I am 50,000% onboard with Troy Jackson and Matt Dunlap,” Evans said, also referring to the Democrat running for the 2nd Congressional District seat. “And so are all of my Graham friends.”
Evans and some other like-minded former Platner volunteers said they didn’t like the top-down approach of the Maine Democratic Party’s campaign apparatus. Instead, they preferred the flexibility, creativity and community that infused Platner’s campaign.
“I’m not satisfied with either party,” said Jeanne McCliment, a 76-year-old independent who volunteered for Platner. “For me, the Democratic Party is the least worst.”
PLAYING THE LONG GAME
With so much at stake in November, it may seem strange to some how, in many ways, People Powered Maine is already looking beyond the midterms. But this outlook is part and parcel with the group’s theory of politics. They plan to stay active after the election so they can try to make inroads with people who don’t share their views.
“We have a huge resource,” said 24-year-old volunteer Lucy Climer-Kennedy, a Portland transportation planner. “People power.”
On a recent fall day, their unorthodox approach took them to Jonesport, a small Down East town more than 200 miles from Portland. There, Donald Trump and Collins each won their most recent elections with nearly 70% of the vote.
The group did not go there to talk politics or gin up support for Jackson or any other candidate. It was there to provide financial assistance to lobstermen at a local cooperative.
After a long morning of hauling lobster traps, Maurice Alley was greeted at the docks by Suzanne Carver, a fellow resident of nearby Beals and a People Powered Maine member.
As Alley’s crew sorted lobsters into crates and topped off his fuel tank, Carver told the 78-year-old skipper of the F/V Renegade that her group provided up to a couple hundred dollars for each member of the Beals-Jonesport Co-Op to help with the high cost of diesel.
For Alley, it was a pleasant surprise. Oftentimes, lobstermen arrive at the docks only to find that gas prices have gone up and the price of lobster has gone down.
Barely audible over the loud rumble of his diesel engine, Alley lamented that people in power are eager to help farmers affected by high prices, but lobstermen are often forgotten.
Nearby, the organizing group unfurled a banner reading “Working Mainers left holding a bill.” It detailed the increased costs of diesel, heating oil, gasoline and health insurance. Another volunteer offered Alley and his crew slices of pizza and cold drinks, which he accepted.
Before shoving off, Alley was asked about the assistance he received.
“Well, I like that,” he said. “It’s not that farmers’ aid, but at least it’s something.”
Carver, a former Platner volunteer, was careful not to talk politics or specific candidates on the docks. She said she’s only there to help her community.
Tensions rose when more reporters arrived with cameras. One reporter asked Carver about the upcoming elections and specific candidates. Within 30 minutes, journalists were asked to leave the docks by the manager.

title: Registered sex offender accused of posing as teenage girl to enroll in high school
text:
MAPLE GROVE, Minn. (Gray News) - A 29-year-old registered sex offender is accused of pretending to be a teenage girl to try to enroll in a high school.
According to KARE, Maple Grove Police Department was notified by a Maple Grove Senior High School staff member about a person who was trying to enroll at the school as a “homeless youth.” The person, later identified as Makayla Craig, allegedly said they were a 17-year-old named Molly from Oregon.
Craig, who was still claiming to be Molly, allegedly told police they had never attended school before and wanted to “get the full experience.” They also allegedly told investigators they were worried they might get mistaken for “Makayla Craig, a registered sex offender from Oregon.” When it was determined that they were in fact Craig, they were arrested.
“Craig never completed enrollment with Maple Grove Senior High School, and he was never present on campus as a student or in any online classes,” police said in a press release. “The Maple Grove Police Department credits the school district staff for their alertness with the incident, quick action to notify a school resource officer, and collaboration in the investigation. The case remains an active and ongoing investigation.”
KGW reports that in 2024, Craig was sentenced to 40 days in jail after claiming to be a “15-year-old homeless teenager named Madison” and enrolled at a high school in Oregon.
Craig was previously convicted of fraudulent use of a credit card, forgery and false swearing in 2025, and sexual abuse of a minor in 2023. They have a warrant out for their arrest in connection with an open theft case from May after failing to appear in court in July, according to KARE.
Craig’s bail was set at $200,000 without conditions and at $100,000 with conditions. Those conditions include a mental health evaluation, no contact with minors and staying three blocks away from K-12 schools, KARE reports.

title: Trump escalates rhetoric against El-Sayed as he tries to undermine Democrat in Michigan Senate race
text:
PORT HURON, Mich. (AP) — President Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security and questioning his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally.
Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists” and would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.” He also repeatedly invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93.
El-Sayed, who would become the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country “shameful” and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups. The Republican president’s remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, the group that helped lead the president’s outreach to Arab American voters in 2024.
“The president’s statements are out of line,” he said in a phone interview. “They are crossing a red line. They are racist.”
With Republicans on the defensive over inflation, soaring fuel prices and the Iran war, the president has been trying to generate turnout by claiming that El-Sayed and other Democrats are existential threats to America, instead of electoral rivals. Michigan’s Senate race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is among a handful of contests that could determine control of the chamber.
Trump made his remarks in Port Huron, a Canadian border city about an hour north of Detroit and near communities where he made significant gains among Arab American voters in 2024. He became the first Republican presidential candidate since 2000 to win Dearborn, a city with one of the nation’s largest concentrations of Arab Americans.
Trump, who imposed a travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries during his first term, has increasingly leaned into anti-Muslim rhetoric as Election Day approaches. He also attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota at Sunday’s rally, where he declared that he had come to Michigan “to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator.”
Responding to Trump, who also regularly mocks his name, El-Sayed told supporters at a rally in Grand Rapids later Sunday that he doesn’t care how Trump pronounces or misrepresents it.
“I don’t even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me ‘senator’ after November,” El-Sayed said, drawing cheers. “I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro.”
El-Sayed’s faith, associations and past statements become campaign flashpoints
Central to Republicans’ strategy against El-Sayed in the final weeks of the campaign has been an effort to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic movement with branches that the U.S. government has designated as terrorist organizations.
There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. His half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, wrote on social media in 2012 that “my family has long been MB” and described a conversation with her mother about her involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1970s.
El-Sayed was born in the United States to Egyptian immigrant parents who divorced when he was young. He was raised by his father, not his biological mother.
Trump on Sunday also targeted El-Sayed’s ties to popular streamer Hasan Piker, who appeared alongside the Democrat multiple times during the primary campaign, including at his election night event.
Piker in the past has said that “Hamas is a thousand times better” than Israel, describing some Orthodox Jews as “inbred” and that “America deserved 9/11.”
El-Sayed has faced criticism for his own rhetoric. He has repeatedly refused to answer questions about whether Iran or Israel poses a bigger threat to the country. Earlier this year, he said “hurt people hurt people” after an attack on a synagogue in the Detroit area. The attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week earlier. El-Sayed later apologized, saying he was not trying to justify what happened.
“To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I’m really sorry,” he said. “That was not my intention.”
Founder of Arab Americans for Trump calls the president ‘racist’
Bahbah, whose organization has since changed its name to Arab Americans for Peace, said Trump’s remarks were unacceptable to Arab and Muslim communities, including Christian Arabs.
“The remarks are out of line and crazy. I mean, no sane individual would say these things,” Bahbah said.
Dearborn helped Trump win Michigan in 2024 after many voters in the city were outraged by the Biden administration’s handling of the war in Gaza.
“The president of the United States saying that about a person because of his religion, that is just not acceptable,” said Bahbah. “And people are going to remember that on Nov. 3.”
Sen. Bernie Sanders, speaking at the Grand Rapids rally, said Trump and his allies were using Islamophobia because they have “nothing to say” about the issues most important to working people, such as health care, housing and income inequality.
“All they can do is foment hatred and divisiveness,” Sanders said.
The campaign has been one of the most contentious this year
Rogers and El-Sayed have been locked in a bitter race to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
During their second and final general election campaign debate, Rogers questioned El-Sayed’s loyalty to the United States.
“Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers asked.
El-Sayed said that questioning was “shameful.”
“I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray,” he said.
Speaking before Trump’s appearance Sunday, Rogers repeated his allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood.
“The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year,” Rogers said on stage. “Abdul El-Sayed’s.”
Rally doesn’t deliver a new economic handout, but gets boost from Minaj
Trump has routinely announced new investments in factories at his campaign rallies, but he did not do so as part of his speech in Michigan, a state defined by the auto industry.
The president instead repeated investments already being made by domestic automakers. Those automakers could see their finances slump if the president expands his trade war with Canada, which has been an essential partner for the U.S. automotive sector.
While it lacked a fresh promise for Michigan’s economy, Trump’s rally did deliver a bit of star power.
Rapper Nicki Minaj appeared on stage and urged people to get out and vote for the state’s Republican ticket. Her appearance followed an awkward moment from Trump, who has increasingly been fixated on commenting about other people’s body parts.
After praising the body of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican in a close election contest, Trump turned his eye toward Minaj and commented on her posterior.
The president then signaled for Minaj to stand for the crowd and she did, after which Trump said, “I hope Nicki wasn’t insulted, but we love Nicki. She’s been with us for a long time.”
___
Cappelletti reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Josh Boak in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Possible ammonia contamination prompts evacuations after Oregon seafood plant fire, officials say
text:
Possible ammonia contamination prompts evacuations after Oregon seafood plant fire, officials say
Potential ammonia contamination after a seafood plant fire prompted recommended evacuations in a coastal Oregon city, local officials said Sunday morning.
The incident occurred at Pacific Seafood in Newport, Oregon, officials said in a city update as of 10:34 a.m. PT.
“The evacuation is due to a potential ammonia contamination in the area from the plant,” the update said. “We recommend staying inside if you are in Newport today. If you must go outside, you should wear a mask. Updates will continue to be made on this post.”
Footage of the scene posted by the city on social media showed firefighters spraying the building down. See that video below:
John Fuller, a city spokesperson, estimated hundreds of people have been evacuated within the expanded one-mile evacuation radius surrounding the processing plant in the city of just over 10,000 people. Officials said the evacuations were strongly recommended but not mandatory.
An initial half-mile evacuation zone was in the city’s Bayfront area, which is mostly commercial and has some popular tourism areas with fewer homes, Fuller told CNN. It is currently the off season for tourists, he said, though the city still sees some visitors on weekends.
The expanded mile radius now encompasses nearby residential areas, Fuller said.
City officials established a shelter for evacuees at Sam Case Elementary School, the update said.
The Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office said in a morning update Level 3 evacuations are underway in a one-mile radius of the plant. Level 3 is the highest level, meaning residents in the affected area should leave immediately. People were told to stay clear of the scene because of a possible fire. US 20 from Harney Street West to US 101 is closed, the sheriff’s office said.
The Oregon State Fire Marshal is responding to the incident with a hazmat team because of chemicals at the facility, the state agency announced in a social media post.
A spokesperson for Pacific Seafood said in a statement the company was not aware of injuries and all employees have been accounted for.
“However, the situation is still ongoing and we are focused on supporting emergency responders to help ensure everyone is safe,” the statement said.
Fire crews were still working on putting out the fire, Fuller said. The cause of the fire and possible ammonia contamination are still under investigation. There are no reported injuries at this time, Fuller confirmed.
Oregon resident Coby Bertalotto shared videos with CNN showing a thick cloud of billowing smoke over Newport.
“Driving through that thick smoke … It was thick enough that I couldn’t see the side of the road,” Bertalotto said. “I was very cautious.”
He described the smell outside as “rubbery,” affecting an area with several tourist attractions such as candy stores, bars and Ripley’s Believe It or Not.
“There are probably about three or four blocks that are just getting smoked out,” Bertalotto said.
Exposure to high levels of ammonia in air may cause irritation to the skin, eyes, throat, and lungs and cause coughing and burns, according to the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry. Some people with asthma may be more sensitive, the agency said.
_______
This is a developing story and will be updated.
CNN’s Nic F. Anderson and Maria Aguilar Prieto contributed to this report.

title: Venezuela's opposition leader Machado returns after months in exile, as doubts over democracy deepen
text:
Venezuela's opposition leader Machado returns after months in exile, as doubts over democracy deepen
Opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado reappeared in Venezuela Sunday for the first time since December, returning from exile at a time when doubts about the country's democratic future — and the role of the U.S. — are growing.
Previous video coverage above
It was her first appearance since the U.S. military deposed the country’s then-President Nicolás Maduro, replacing him with an interim president who has exceeded the time she was authorized to serve, with no election scheduled.
Machado announced her arrival on social media, writing, “I am here. With you.”
Another leading figure in the Venezuelan opposition, Edmundo González, wrote on X confirming that Machado had arrived and that he would be next to her “very soon.”
“Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!” he wrote. “You know it, this is until the end.”
Venezuela run by Maduro ally backed by the Trump administration
On Sunday afternoon, Machado strode into a church in the town of Lara, west of Caracas, to the applause of dozens gathered there as they shook her hand and hugged her, with cell phones aloft to record her return.
“María! María!” someone cried out.
“Welcome to Venezuela!” another person shouted.
Asked by reporters Sunday about Machado’s return to Venezuela, U.S. President Donald Trump said, “I don’t know anything about it, but I think she’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize. So how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe. She’s a very nice woman. But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”
Since Maduro’s ouster, Venezuela has been run by acting President Delcy Rodríguez, a longtime Maduro ally who received the Trump administration’s blessing to succeed him.
Rodríguez was initially supposed to serve only 90 days as acting president, but has remained in office and has made no move to call an election.
Machado was briefly detained in January 2025, following a protest against Maduro’s planned swearing-in ceremony, and went into hiding in Venezuela for 11 months. After making a clandestine escape from the country, she reappeared that December in Norway, where she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her peaceful challenge to Maduro’s authoritarian government.
Machado and her allies have been demanding a date for a presidential election in Venezuela, but U.S. officials have emphasized economic stabilization first.
Credible evidence shows the opposition won the last election
In October 2023, Machado won an opposition primary and intended to challenge Maduro in the 2024 presidential election, but the government barred her from running for office.
González took her place on the ballot, and ample credible evidence showed that he defeated Maduro by more than a 2-to-1 margin. But the National Electoral Council, which is stacked with ruling-party loyalists, declared Maduro the winner.
The lead-up and aftermath of the election were marked by widespread government repression, including forced disappearances, torture and other human rights violations. More than 2,000 people, including poll workers, were detained in the days after the vote.
In January, the U.S. military captured Maduro in Caracas and whisked him to New York to face drug-related charges, which he has denied. Many Venezuelans were stunned by the Trump administration’s decision to work with Rodríguez, instead of Machado, to try to revitalize the crisis-racked country.
Machado has demanded a date for a presidential election
Machado had repeatedly vowed to return to Venezuela and, according to her party, she made seven unsuccessful attempts.
One of the efforts would have seen her take a charter boat, but the operator canceled the trip, alleging the vessel was unfit for navigation. In another attempt, her team said, Machado tried to fly to the Caribbean island of Curacao, from where she could take a speedboat to Venezuela, but her plane was denied landing permits.
Opposition activists have accused Venezuela’s government of blocking Machado’s return, a claim denied by Venezuelan authorities. Others have also questioned whether the Trump administration has also been involved in the efforts to stop her from returning.
Trump administration officials deny they are holding Machado back but have said that, on some occasions, they have advised her against returning due to safety concerns.
After Maduro was deposed, Venezuela’s highest court said Rodríguez could serve as acting president for up to 90 days — an interim appointment that could be extended by the National Assembly for an additional 90 days. But the ruling party-controlled assembly never voted to extend her term.
Machado and her allies have demanded that the Rodríguez government set a date for a presidential election. Rodríguez told the U.N. General Assembly in September that Venezuelans will determine the “right moment” for the next election.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has argued that before holding new elections, Venezuela must stabilize its economy and rebuild its institutions, including its courts and electoral council. But he said in a news conference earlier this month that Machado has “every right to enter her country whenever she wants to return.”
Supporters of Machado have held demonstrations in Caracas demanding her return.
Coto reported from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Associated Press reporter Josh Boak in Washington, D.C., contributed to this report.

This story was originally published in October 2021.
People often ask where I find the inspiration to write a different column every week. Sometimes I get inspiration from alert readers. For instance, I recently received mail, asking me to explain why owls are hooting in October.
My first answer is that they like to make Halloween spookier. Messing with humans makes them giggle. However, my second answer may be closer to the mark.
Mating season has already begun.
Maine has three common nesting owls. One of them, the tiny northern saw-whet owl, generally leaves Maine during the coldest months. The other two don’t migrate. In fact, great horned and barred owls don’t even wander very much. They always have some notion of their territories, and are apt to proclaim it periodically. The hootin’ and hollerin’ starts in August, but intensifies in October.
Nesting season starts early. Baby owls must be able to hunt soon after they fledge. They must be fully developed by the time they leave the nest. This means that the owls have to start making babies early, since the youngsters spend a long time on the nest before departing. Barred owls sit on the eggs for about a month, then tend the nestlings for another month. For great horned owls, it takes even longer — 10 weeks or more before the chicks are ready to leave the nest. Once off the nest, barred owl chicks may stay in the area for up to half a year, before wandering off to make their fortunes elsewhere.
Great horned owls start nesting earliest, usually in late winter. Barred owls nest a little later. Both begin announcing territories in autumn, and not just for mating purposes. Competing owls don’t like to intrude on each other, lest a fight break out. By announcing their territories, they can stay out of each other’s way.
Owls hoot to attract mates, although that’s often a foregone conclusion. Great horned owls mate for life. Barred owls probably do. In the offseason, both mates remain in the same general area, although they don’t typically roost together. Barred owls are typically cavity nesters, though they sometimes use open nests. They identify a number of potential nesting sites within their territories, and may switch from year to year within the same area. Great horned owls will often reuse the same nest. Once the pairs reunite in connubial bliss, it doesn’t take long to set up housekeeping.
Another reason that owls nest early, especially great horned owls, is that they don’t build their own nests. They generally take over the nests of other large birds, such as great blue herons and red-tailed hawks. By the time the rightful owner returns to the nest in the spring, the owl is already on it.
Perhaps the better question is this: why do the owls quiet down in early summer? Because they’re busy. They’re sticking close to the nesting site. They’re feeding the kids. They’re not keen on announcing where the babies are, in case some predator might be listening. Great horned owls don’t have to worry about predators very much. They are so ferocious, not even eagles will mess with them. Only unattended nests are vulnerable. But barred owls must be a little more cautious. Great horned owls, some hawks and even raccoons can raid their nests.
Now that you’re eavesdropping on owls, let’s make sure you know who you’re snooping on. The hoot of a barred owl is famously described as “Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?” It’s basically a nine-note phrase, though sometimes embellished with a few screeches and cat-calls. The great horned owl booms a deeper five-note phrase, often described as “Who’s awake? Me, too.”
Listen also for call and response. Owls often answer each other. Female voices are higher in pitch.
It’s not a total shock to see owls out in the daytime, especially in winter. When food is scarce, they may be forced to hunt in daylight. Sometimes, they’ll perch out in the morning just to warm up in the sun. However, they’re not likely to linger in daylight. Crows are apt to take exception and harass them. This mobbing behavior becomes more aggressive as crow nesting season approaches.
Of course, owls can also be aggressive as nesting season approaches, especially when they perceive that you’re the threat. A great horned owl defending its territory can get quite impatient with humans. Attacks by barred owls are rarer, but not unheard of. Hmmm. Maybe they really are making Halloween spookier.

Obituary: James B. Harmon
text:
SCARBOROUGH – James “Jimmy” B. Harmon, 83, of Scarborough, passed away peacefully on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, at his home.
Jim was born in Portland on April 20, 1943, a son of John and Thelma (Baker) Harmon. He grew up in Scarborough and graduated from Scarborough High School. As a boy, he spent countless hours on Scarborough Beach and fostering his love of animals. Jimmy was known to bring home a wide variety of animals including a recued pet seal named “Suzie”. Jim made neighborhood deliveries for Harmon’s Market, a local family market owned by his parents.
After graduation Jim enlisted in the United States Navy and faithfully served our country from 1968 to 1970. Soon afterwards, he attended both the Boston School of Art and Portland School of Art, in his ability with watercolors focusing on landscapes. Jimmy was a phenomenal cook and enjoyed entertaining which came very natural to him.
Jimmy worked for 32 years at Weyerhauser, a local manufacturing company, but his heart and passion was always in his artwork. Many of his paintings will be enjoyed by his family and friends for many generations.
Jimmy married the love of his life, Peggy Rioux, on Sept. 2, 1984, in the home where he grew up. The couple settled in that very same home where they raised their daughter, Aili. As a young family they enjoyed traveling to their rustic cabin in Stratton, which they affectionately called “Pukin Mauna.” For many years they spent every weekend cross country skiing, walking in the woods, downhill skiing and simply enjoying quality time together. During the summer months Jimmy found peace and satisfaction in creating elaborate flower gardens on his property, and in watching the many birds that paid daily visits to his birdfeeders.
Jimmy and Peggy were fortunate to have traveled together throughout the U.S. and abroad, visiting places like South Carolina, Mexico, Costa Rica, and Spain. One of the most memorable trips he took with his family and dear friends, was a road trip throughout the midwestern states. He also had the opportunity to ski in Colorado with his best friend Michael Reid and family, and to experience a once-in-a-lifetime trip to Alaska where he and Mike fished for salmon.
Jimmy was immensely proud of his daughter, Aili and of her husband, Matt, for all their accomplishments and giving him his most important role, becoming a Papa. His four grandchildren, Henley, Waylon, Wade and Willis were his world. He and Peggy’s days soon became filled spending countless hours at the beach, cheering them on in their various activities, taking yearly vacations with the family and teaching them life is always better with a sweet treat and sandy toes.
If Jimmy were to describe himself in just two words, it would be “Beach Bum”. He absolutely loved the sun, sand, surfing, and simply sharing this passion with his family and friends.
Jimmy will be sadly missed by all who knew and loved him.
Jimmy was predeceased by his parents, John and Thelma Harmon; brother, Steve Harmon, brother-in-law, Robert Abbott; and by his nephew, Robbie Abbott.
He is survived by his loving wife, Peggy Harmon, of 42 years; by his daughter, Aili Desrochers and husband Matt; by his grandchildren, Henley, Waylon, Wade and Willis Desrochers; by his brother, John Harmon, by his sister, Judy Williams and husband Ernie; and by his niece, Stacey Abbott and her boys Tucker, Sayler and Sullivan Conley.
Friends and family are invited to a celebration of life beginning at 2 p.m., on Saturday, Nov. 14, at Jimmy’s homestead in Scarborough.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in Jimmy’s name to Camp Sunshine at Sebago Lake by clicking on the following link: https://www.campsunshine.org/donate-today

title: Obituary: Camillo Raymond Aceto
text:
VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. – Camillo Raymond Aceto, 85, passed away peacefully on Oct. 21, 2026, in Virginia Beach, Va., surrounded by his loving family.
Born to Daniel Aceto and Edna Swasey Aceto on April 21, 1941, Camillo grew up in Portland, and graduated from Deering High School. A hardworking brick mason and general contractor, Camillo devoted his life to building with his hands. He took great pride in his work, leaving behind not only the buildings and projects he helped create but also lasting memories for his family, friends, and all who knew him.
Camillo was predeceased by his wife, Miriam P. Eldridge Aceto; his son, John Aceto, his daughters Irene Landry, Susan Bryant, and Marion Allen; and his siblings Daniel Jr. and Mary.
He is survived by his children, Richard (Linda) of Windham, David (Jodi) of Severn, Md., Camilla (James) of Virginia Beach, Va., Michael (Laurie) of Gorham, Joseph (Tracy) of Westbrook, and Cathi (Paul) of Monhegan. He also leaves behind his siblings, Ralph, Teddy, Chucky, Dorothy, and Linda; many grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and great-great-grandchildren; and extended family and friends who will cherish his memory.
Services will be held at a later date.

title: BACK-TO-BACK! Houlton Boys Win Regional Title, Four County Girls Head to States
text:
Houlton Boys Repeat as Class C North Cross Country Champions, County Runners Advance to States
For the second straight year, the Houlton/GHCA boys are Class C North regional cross country champions.
And Saturday in Belfast, the Shires didn't leave much room for doubt.
Houlton placed four runners among the top five and finished with just 30 points to capture another regional championship. George Stevens Academy was second with 47 points, followed by Orono with 67.
While the boys celebrated another team title, several other Aroostook County runners earned their own opportunities to compete at the state championships on October 31 at Cony High School in Augusta.
The Houlton/GHCA girls finished fifth in the team standings and did not qualify as a team, but Charlotte Estabrook and Isabella McCarthy both advanced individually. Washburn's Eleanora Streeter and Maine School of Science and Mathematics runner Sadie Wigmore also qualified.
Houlton Boys Make It Back-to-Back
Winning a regional championship is impressive enough. Coming back and doing it again the following season says a lot about a program.
Houlton/GHCA accomplished that Saturday, capturing its second consecutive Class C North boys championship with five runners finishing among the top 16.
Malachi Witmer led the Shires with a second-place finish in 16:52.80, just over four seconds behind Orono's Brady Cox, who won the individual title in 16:48.44.
Brayden Drake finished third in 16:59.00, followed by Wyatt Quint in fourth at 17:01.89 and Logan Witmer in fifth at 17:13.72.
That gave Houlton four of the first five finishers in the race.
Freshman Stephen Cormier rounded out the scoring five, placing 16th in 18:49.57.
Lucas McPhee also competed for Houlton, finishing 34th in 20:29.95.
The Shires' six regional runners are part of a boys team that has earned its place at the state championships, where they'll look to build on another impressive postseason.
Houlton Girls Place Fifth, Two Earn Individual State Berths
Houlton/GHCA's girls finished fifth in the Class C North regional standings with 106 points.
George Stevens Academy won the team championship with 46 points, narrowly edging Orono, which finished with 48. Calais was third with 73, followed by Narraguagus with 77.
Only the top four Class C North girls teams qualified for states, leaving Houlton outside the team cutoff.
But that doesn't mean the Shires won't be represented in Augusta.
Charlotte Estabrook finished 19th in 24:25.61, while Isabella McCarthy placed 22nd in 24:57.91. Both earned individual state championship berths by finishing among the top 30.
April Mazur placed 31st, Dalylah Mincey finished 32nd and Alaina Locker was 42nd to complete Houlton's scoring five.
The individual regional championship went to George Stevens Academy's Ripley King-Ofsiany in 20:43.77.
Washburn and MSSM Also Sending Runners to States
Two more County athletes will represent their schools at the state championships.
Washburn's Eleanora Streeter finished 25th in the girls race with a time of 25:16.15, earning an individual qualifying spot.
Sadie Wigmore, a freshman at the Maine School of Science and Mathematics, finished 29th in 25:50.33, also advancing individually.
That gives the County four individual qualifiers from schools that did not earn girls team berths, joining the Houlton/GHCA boys team in Augusta.

text:
Florida man who swallowed nearly $1M in stolen jewelry found guilty of robbery
A jury found a man guilty of stealing nearly $1 million in jewelry from the Mall at Millenia in Orlando, according to the Florida State Attorney’s Office.
The incident happened Feb. 26, 2025, when Jaythan Lawrence Gilder allegedly posed as a representative for an Orlando Magic player interested in purchasing jewelry at a Tiffany & Co. store.
Gilder was taken to a private room to see the jewelry.
According to the affidavit, Gilder grabbed the jewelry and fled the store, injuring an employee in the process.
Florida Highway Patrol troopers later stopped him and said Gilder swallowed the jewelry to hide the evidence.
Officials later recovered the jewelry, which they confirmed matched the stolen items.
“This verdict sends a clear message that violence and theft will not be tolerated in our community,” State Attorney Monique Worrell said in a statement.

title: Why this Massachusetts independent is traveling for Troy
text:
Charlie Welch of Northampton, Massachusetts, holds a bachelor’s degree in American history from Harvard College and an MBA in finance and economics from New York University. He runs a real estate agency.
I have never before spent my time on politics, yet in addition to canvassing for Troy Jackson, I phone bank for him three nights a week and I will be in Maine on Election Day to serve as a poll observer.
On Saturdays, I phone bank for Roy Cooper, the Democratic Senate candidate in North Carolina. I have donated money to the campaigns of Chris Pappas in New Hampshire and of Cait Conley in New York, both Democratic candidates running to flip or defend a seat in Congress. This is a radical departure for me, a person who has had no political party affiliation and has rarely voted outside of presidential elections.
It’s clear to me that this election is different. In this midterm election, our democracy is on the line. This is a crisis that demands the attention of every voter in this country and transcends our state borders and party affiliations.
In this election, we have two choices. We can endorse one man’s progress in dismantling our democratic form of government or we can defy it and reaffirm our commitment to the principles upon which this nation was founded 250 years ago.
We are immersed in a war with Iran of great consequences, including a higher cost of living and a world economy thrown into turmoil. Far graver is the estimated deaths of more than 9,000 people, including more than 1,700 civilians. More deaths will come as the war lumbers on with no end in sight. Although our nation chose this war, and our nation will inherit its legacy, whose war is it? Our Congress has never approved or supported it, yet we started it and are in it, based on the decision of one man.
Without congressional approval, our current president is feverishly remaking our nation’s capital to his liking. In addition to tearing down the East Wing of our White House and constructing a monstrous addition that will be nearly twice the size of the White House itself, he has begun site work for an arch that will be more than twice the height of our Lincoln Memorial.
He threatens to tear down our Kennedy Center unless he is allowed to put his name on it. Past presidents resisted having their names put on government projects while in office. Our current president insists on it.
He has weaponized our government agencies against us. The examples of this are many, but one of the most outrageous is the arrest of an Olympic athlete to deflect the blame for a botched paint job on our Reflecting Pool.
Recently, he has attacked our free press by banning three media outlets from the White House because he considers their news coverage too negative. He is currently running taxpayer-funded ads that are unequivocally intended to sway voters before the midterm elections, a brazen and illegal use of taxpayer money for partisan propaganda and self-aggrandizement.
Prior to 2024, any one of these events would have set off alarms warning us that the guardrails of our democracy had been breached, but overwhelmed by the sheer volume of abuses and so immersed in the bitter partisanship incited by this man, we have hardly noticed that we have surrendered a large portion of our democracy to him, and what remains is rapidly slipping through our fingers.
On Jan. 6, 2021, the ultimate assault on our democratic form of government took place. Never in our nation’s history has there been a violent attempt to overturn the results of a presidential election. Our current president reaffirmed his disdain for our democracy by pardoning over 1,500 people involved in this attack on our nation’s capital.
Mindful of these events, his relentless attempts to influence our upcoming midterm elections are ominous. The peaceful transfer of power is the very soul of any democracy. Without it there is no democracy.
For the time being, we are all able to vote and our votes are meaningful. The vote you cast on Nov. 3 will be more meaningful than any midterm vote cast in our nation’s history.
We all have our beliefs and our priorities. On Nov. 3, I implore you to be clear on what you are prioritizing, what you are endorsing. Your vote will either encourage the slide of our government into the clutches of a man fond of posting pictures of himself as a king, even a god, or it will defy it.
Our nation has faced and defeated great threats before, and regardless of the outcome of this election, we will do it again. But this Nov. 3 is crucial. Without a Democratic victory, the road back to our democracy will be much longer and more arduous.
Despite the distorted image of American greatness that has been peddled to us in recent years, there is only thing that makes our nation great and that is that our founders introduced to this world a revolutionary form of government, a form of government that we have defended for more than 250 years with our blood and our treasure, a government through which the people themselves guide their destiny, instead of a monarch or a king.
It is our unwavering commitment to that democracy that makes us great. Without it, we are ordinary, at best.
Indeed, I am urging you to vote for the Democratic Party in this election, but please do not make the mistake of thinking that I am merely a Democrat in disguise. As an independent, I have voted with both parties. Currently both parties share some of my views; neither of them share all.
I am well aware that a Democratic victory in November will not cure our wounded democracy, but it will stem the bleeding and keep it alive.
For that, I’m willing to drive a lot longer than three hours.
