Prolonged dry conditions continue across Maine, worsening drought concerns and keeping fire danger at a medium level across the state. With little relief from the dry weather, fallen leaves, dormant grass, and other seasonal debris can become fuel for fires, making fire prevention especially important this time of year.
Even when fire danger is not classified as high, dry vegetation can ignite quickly under the right conditions. Residents are urged to use caution with anything that could spark a fire, including outdoor burning and improperly discarded smoking materials.
The Freeport Fire Rescue Department recently shared an important reminder about cigarette disposal, highlighting how even a small discarded cigarette can pose a significant risk when conditions are dry.
“All joking aside, this serves as an important reminder to properly extinguish and dispose of smoking materials,” the department noted. “With dry leaves, grass, and other debris accumulating this time of year, something as small as a discarded cigarette can quickly become a fire hazard.”
Fire officials encourage everyone to take a moment to ensure smoking materials are completely extinguished and disposed of properly. Cigarettes should never be tossed onto the ground, into dry vegetation, or out of vehicle windows.
The department also added a bit of humor to its public safety message, signing off with: “Freeport Fire Rescue, protecting our community above ground, below ground, and apparently keeping an eye out for clowns along the way.”
As Maine's dry conditions persist and drought concerns grow, residents are encouraged to remain vigilant and take simple precautions to help prevent fires. A little extra care now can go a long way toward protecting homes, property, and communities across the state.
With dry conditions continuing across Maine, properly putting out fires is an important step in preventing accidental fires. Even when a fire looks like it’s out, hot embers can remain hidden beneath the ashes and reignite hours later.
If you’re enjoying a campfire, make sure to check local fire restrictions before lighting it, and never leave it unattended. When it’s time to put it out, slowly pour water over the flames, remaining wood, and embers. Use a shovel or stick to stir the ashes and mix them with the water, making sure to reach the material underneath and around the edges. Continue adding water and stirring until everything is thoroughly soaked and there are no glowing embers or remaining heat. The fire should be completely cold before you walk away. Simply covering a campfire with dirt or sand isn’t enough, as hot embers can remain underneath and reignite when exposed to oxygen.
Wood stoves also require care, especially during dry conditions. Let the fire burn down naturally when possible, keep the stove door closed, and use the air controls according to the manufacturer's instructions. Never pour water into a hot wood stove, as the sudden temperature change and steam can cause serious injury or damage.
When cleaning out a wood stove, never dump hot ashes onto dry grass, leaves, or other combustible materials. Instead, place them in a covered metal container and keep it outdoors on a noncombustible surface, well away from your home, decks, woodpiles, and other flammable materials. Ashes can hold enough heat to start a fire for several days, even when they appear to be completely cold. Keeping your stove and chimney properly maintained and ensuring combustible materials are kept well away from the stove can also help prevent a fire.
If a fire escapes its designated area or begins spreading into nearby grass, leaves, or woods, call 911 immediately rather than putting yourself at risk trying to contain it. With Maine's dry conditions and growing drought concerns, taking a few extra minutes to make sure every fire is completely out can make a real difference in protecting homes, property, and the surrounding environment.

title: The University of Maine in Orono celebrates homecoming weekend

ORONO, Maine (WABI) - On Saturday, the University of Maine in Orono celebrated their annual home coming game.
Current students, alumni, family, and friends came from all over the state and beyond to take part in the home coming tailgate event.
Katie Fletcher and Connor Magliozzi spoke with tailgaters about the excitement of the day, and their personal connection to the university.
“It’s my 20th homecoming. It’s just a great feeling of camaraderie. Last time I was on the campus was last homecoming,” said one tailgate attendee.
“My kids went here. My father went here. We’re a legacy family. So it’s just kind of tradition now,” he said.
One attendee traveled from Scotland to visit friends, enjoy the live football game and experience his first tailgate event.
" I love the sport. I’m a huge Chicago Bears fan, and I know people from Maine," he said.
The crowd was filled with positive energy and Black Bear pride. One tailgater expressed his hope for a UMaine win.
“Oh, we’re going to smoke them. No doubt. Let’s go Maine. Go Black bears,” he said.

title: Obituary: Bruce Cantley Morrison
text:
PORTLAND – Bruce Cantley Morrison passed away during his 100th year due to natural causes on Oct. 16, 2026. He was born in Augusta to Raymond D. and Miriam L. (Washburn) Morrison on June 29, 1927. He graduated from Cony High School, while there he participated in football, basketball, and baseball. In 1945, shortly after graduating and turning 18, he enlisted in the Army and served in the 24th Infantry Division Occupation duty in Japan in Southern Island and Kyushu. He was honorably discharged as a corporal. When he returned to Maine, he then attended Maine Central Institute post graduate program where he played football and was part of the State Championship prep school team. While at MCI he also played hockey.
As you can see, sports were a major part of his life and continued to be during his entire life by either playing, umpiring or being an enthusiastic fan. He attended Red Sox games in Fenway Park as a child with his grandfather while staying with his beloved grandparents, Laura and Percy Ford in Massachusetts. As an adult, he took his youngest daughter, Nancy and her friends to Red Sox games – one of which they were lucky enough to catch a foul ball. He hung onto that ball for over 30 years and eventually passed it on to his grandson, Alex. Although his professional team loyalties could change depending on how poorly he considered their play. At one point he was even a Yankees fan much to his family’s horror. He died a Red Sox fan.
After MCI he then attended Bates College where during his sophomore year, he was recalled to the Army to serve in the Korean Conflict. He was in the 8th Army 8204th CIU unit (graves division) identifying those who perished during battle. He was proud to have received letters of Commendations for his service. It was a horrific assignment which he rarely spoke about other than to say war was hell. He was honorably discharged as Staff Sergeant. He very proudly wore a Korean War veteran cap or World War II veteran cap whenever he left his home. After Korea, he returned to Bates and graduated with a Bachelor of History degree. During his senior year he served as a freshman line coach for football after being injured while playing. One of his injuries resulted in him having his nose broken. He loved to fold his nose toward his cheek to get a reaction from new people in his circle. His love for Bates was undeniable, and he attended every reunion he could. As life would have it, he outlived most of his friends and classmates.
After Bates, he went to work for SD Warren/Scott Paper Company (now Sappi Paper). He was in Supervisory and Management positions in the Finishing Department and Customer Service. He married Judith H. (Pinkham) Morrison in 1959, they divorced in 1979. When he took an early retirement, he started volunteering for CASA (court appointed special advocate) for children placed in the court system by DHHS. He spent the next 20 years serving and protecting children in Southern Maine. He cared deeply for the children in his charge and would buck DHHS and the judge if he did not feel the child’s best interest was being met. He considered CASA” a most rewarding endeavor of a lifetime by helping those who could not protect themselves”. Bruce was awarded the Governors’ Maine’s 100 in 2000 by Governor Angus King in recognition of outstanding achievements and dedication to community and state through volunteerism and community service for his work with CASA. He was awarded the 6 Who Care award in 2003 also for his work with CASA and received a national CASA achievement Award in 2007.
He liked to travel in his “younger” years and was part of the Portland sister city trip to Archangel, Russia which was a highlight. During that trip he gave a young doctor who was going to an interview but did not have a jacket to wear so he gave him one of his so he would be properly dressed.
He also traveled to Finland, Switzerland, and Italy, which was his favorite country. Although he never got to Scotland, he was proud of his Scottish heritage. He owned a small plot of land in Scotland, a gift from his children, so he could be officially called Laird Bruce Morrison.
In keeping with his love of sports, he was an ASA umpire from 1975-1986 for fast, modified, and slow pitch for the South District. He was district umpire-in-chief and district commissioner for the Southern District. He enjoyed attending his eldest grandson Zach’s games be it soccer, basketball, or baseball when Zach played for Windham, travel, and college teams. He was asked to and did umpire one of Zach’s Little League games when they were short of an umpire when he was in his mid-70’s. He also greatly enjoyed watching his grandson Luke play lacrosse and football, as football was a shared passion, for them both. Luke would become his roommate and caretaker until he moved to assisted living at 98. He would happily tell anyone how proud he was of all his grandchildren and their successes.
After a heart attack in the fall of 1980, he started at the Heartline at the USM gym and continued in the Lifeline program. He loved the gym! It was his favorite place to be. He would be there as soon as they opened at least three days a week until the pandemic hit. He made some of his best and most loyal friends there. He wanted to acknowledge the Gym Rats: Jim P., Steve, Ray H., Arthur J, Andy, Katherine, Annette, Fran and all the rest. He greatly enjoyed and treasured his friendships with them. He felt the program provided him with a longer and healthier life and has many thanks to those involved. Dad never looked or acted his age. Whenever he met someone new, they would never believe he was as old as he was. His youthful attitude along with being active was his fountain of youth. No matter where he traveled, he would run into someone he knew whether during family travels to Williamsburg or shopping at the Mall. He loved to shop but had to get a bargain or deal which was a source of a family nickname of Bargain Basement Bruce. He was also a long-time blood donor.
In addition to the gym, he found joy in reading a good book, eating breakfast out with his friends, and yelling at the TV while watching game shows, football, or baseball. Dad also loved to eat out at F Parker Reidys, Tortilla Flats and Brea Lu Café being three of his favorites along with trying ethnic restaurants in the Greater Portland area. He loved to cut out articles from newspapers or magazines with information he thought you would enjoy. That’s how he showed he was thinking about you.
He lived in his home on Forest Avenue in Portland from 1962 until the Fall of 2025 when he moved to assisted living. His son Andy and daughter-in-law Paula along with Luke were the reasons he was able to be independent so long. Many thanks to them! He enjoyed the companionship and pleasure of cats. His current constant companion, Freddie, survives him.
He was predeceased by his parents; infant grandson, Andrew “AJ” H. Morrison, Jr. in 2001; his sister, Ann (Dr. James) McCullum in December 2017; his nephew and godson, Peter McCullum in October 2021; and son-in-law, Robert Conrad in 2000.
Bruce is survived by his children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, about whom he said he was “extremely proud of their growth and achievements”, Beth (Steven) Cantor of Denmark, and Youngsville, N.C., grandson Zachary (SarahMaura) and great-grandchildren, AvaMaura and Owen Bruce Cantor, all of Raleigh, N.C., Andrew (Paula) Morrison of Westbrook, grandson Luke and partner Genevieve Leonard of Portland, Nancy (Thomas Cooney) Conrad-Cooney, grandchildren, Alex Conrad-Cooney and fiancé Lexi Glasgow, and Brooke Cooney, all of Coral Springs, Fla. He is also survived by his niece, Catherine McCullum of Brunswick.
His family would like to thank the VA in Togus and Portland along with his medical team which included Dr. Wadland, Dr. Moore, and Dr. Danforth for helping him to live a long healthy life. His family would also like to thank Stacey, Taylor and Odessa at Birchwoods for their kindness and care. He always spoke highly of them. His niece, Catherine, was a dedicated visitor and caretaker during his last years for which his family is most grateful.
Per his request and honoring his giving back to the community his body has been donated to the UNE School of Medicine.
A celebration of his life will be held at Allagash Brewing “Great Room” in Portland on Nov. 14 from 2 to 5 p.m., to tell Bruce stories. Please dress casually as he would want everyone to be comfortable. Interment will be private for the family at a later date.
In lieu of flowers, please consider contributing to the Animal Refuge League in Westbrook, where four of his cats came from, a veteran’s services organization or making a blood donation in his memory.

title: Following the Horizon—Coast to coast with Ford & Brinkley, part IV
text:
As America celebrates its 250th Birthday, we continue to push westward to take in the 100th Birthday of America’s Main Street, Route 66.
In Oklahoma, the terrain becomes flatter, more open. The visual expanses are greater. Yet, the roadside examples of old gas stations, almost a constant of new “museums,” gift shops and repurposed attractions, as well as the diners and other hospitality stations, continue to shout about Route 66 for a new generation of visitors. “Come see our small town, come visit us and experience America” is their cry.
Our F-350 Super Duty continues to work easily pulling our Brinkley travel trailer. Thankfully, we have the eight-foot bed with ample space to hold our supplies and travel accessories; like a generator and fuel, wood blocks to level the camper, a cooler for extra drinks in the warm climate (so far), outside chairs, someone’s golf clubs, extra DEF fluid, an air compressor, tools, even a shovel and tow straps are somewhere in the bed just in case one of us wanders off the original Route 66 into a cow pasture, right, Tim…
Our daily stops continue to be an eclectic collection of historical visits, mixed with the whimsical and the downright ridiculous. Most of the Route 66 museums have been downright impressive, with the “official” #66 Museum in Clinton, Oklahoma, outstanding. Its chronological presentation of the creation, constructio, and use of Route 66 clearly defines how this national asset redefined significant parts of America.
Pushing towards Amarillo, Texas, the horizon is filled with wind towers. Filled. There aren’t just hundreds, there have to be thousands spread out in every direction. The old versions of the Mother Road become harder to find in sections, often right beside I-40 or there and then gone, replaced by the new road, or transitioning to a rancher’s access road. Tumbleweeds and tall grass signal that some sections see little traffic at all, despite the popularity of Route 66 purists looking to drive every single mile that can be found.
After a heavy thunderstorm sweeps over Amarillo, flooding the streets upon our departure, we witness a Jeep Wrangler chasing the Route 66 dream, bounding through wash-outs next to the highway. They didn’t need Route 66 decals — they were wearing the red patina of the run-off dirt.
The Ford is staying relatively clean, but we also see the red dirt occasionally, but with less vigor having the camper in tow. A 20-mile dirt road diversion in Oklahoma and a very sketchy run over Sitgreaves Pass in Arizona as the remains of Hurricane Paulo chased us proved that the Super Duty can handle not only the winds on the highway, but it also has the nimble handling necessary to handle 180-degree switchbacks up and down a narrow mountain pass.
But there are other highlights. The 1699 Catholic Mission in Laguna Pueblo, with a private tour; the couple who run the gift shop in Adrian, Texas (the halfway point on Route 66), that used to belong to the woman who was the Flo character in the CARS movie; plus, the three young women who were running the U-Drop Inn café. Each was a memorable visit because of the people we met.
Yet, the most ironic visit took place in Winslow, Arizona, the infamous corner where Jackson Brown and Glen Frey wrote the hit song for the Eagles about “the girl with the flat-bed Ford looking at me.” It seems a little sketchy, but the throngs of people gathered there on a Sunday, each respectfully waiting to take their own photos of this bally-hooed spot, proves that Winslow is more than a line in a song.
We stopped to get an ice cream at the corner shop, looking at this square. The table next to us had two couples who’d been riding Harleys all over the Southwest for over two weeks. We learned they were from New Hampshire. Then we learned that one of the couples had a camp on Graham Lake, five miles from where each of us lives. Route 66 is truly small-town America.
Our camping has really been more “parking” each night. We have gone to just-in-time reservations, which have been working well. The Route is full of visitors each day, but few are pulling RVs. But the ones that are traveling via RVs have some absolutely stunning homes on wheels that are the direct opposite of what the original Route 66 travelers were used to. We think of that contrast often.
By day 14, we had been over 3,200 miles, and we were headed to Flagstaff, AZ. The truck was scheduled for service at Babbit Ford, the third-oldest Ford dealer in America. The only Ford franchise in an 80-mile radius in the Arizona high country — Flagstaff is at 7,000 feet — Babbit’s service people took great care of us on short notice in their downtown location, next to Route 66, of course, while we played at the Grand Canyon for the day.
Next up: California and the end of phase one of our journey.

title: Large fire at seafood processing plant prompts evacuations in Oregon city
text:
NEWPORT, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A large fire at a seafood processing plant prompted evacuations in Newport, Oregon, over concerns that the smoke contained ammonia.
Crews battled a large structure fire that broke out at a freezer building in the Pacific Seafood plant on the historic Newport Bayfront Sunday morning. According to the City of Newport, about 30 to 40 people were at work in the building at the time, but all were able to get out safely.
One firefighter was taken to the hospital and treated for exhaustion.
The City of Newport issued an evacuation order for people within a 1-mile radius of the processing plant. However, later in the day, officials said crews mitigated the risks of a tank leaking ammonia and reduced the evacuation zone to just a couple of blocks because of smoke.
Ammonia is a colorless gas with a sharp odor. High levels of exposure can cause skin, eye and throat irritation, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Authorities said the main concern now is toxic smoke created by the fire.
Authorities urge everyone in the area to stay inside if possible, and to wear a mask if they have to go outside.
An evacuation shelter had been set up at a local church.
Fuller said the cause of the fire has not been identified yet, but crews remain on the scene.
No civilian injuries have been reported at this time, according to city officials.
Newport is located about 132 miles southwest of Portland, Oregon, and has a population of about 10,000 people. Its bayfront is a popular tourist attraction featuring shops, restaurants and tours.
Fuller said a “good chunk” of the small town was impacted by the evacuation, including businesses and residences. The Newport aquarium announced it was closing for the rest of Sunday as a result of the evacuations.
Pacific Seafood released a statement about the fire on Sunday evening, in which Vice President Ashton Meier thanked the emergency responders who have been working to knock down the flames:
“Pacific Seafood is devastated by today’s fire in Newport. Although we are still working with emergency response officials to determine the full extent of the damage, we expect that it will be a major loss.
Our focus going forward will be on supporting our team members, our neighbors, and the people of Newport. In the days ahead, we will continue to work with public safety officials to make sure they have the access and information necessary to determine the cause of the fire, the extent of the damage, and any ongoing hazards or effects,“ the statement reads in part.

Houlton Survives Penalty Kicks, Caribou Scores Six as County Soccer Playoffs Continue
Saturday brought plenty of playoff excitement for Aroostook County soccer teams, including a penalty-kick thriller, a six-goal performance and another shutout victory for one of the region's top seeds.
Houlton's boys survived a dramatic shootout against Penquis to advance in the eight-person tournament, while Caribou's boys rolled past Medomak Valley 6-2 in Class B North.
On the girls' side, top-seeded Fort Kent continued its postseason run with a 3-0 victory over Maine Central Institute, while Katahdin's season came to an end in a penalty-kick loss to Penquis.
Three County teams are moving on, and the regional quarterfinals are bringing some interesting matchups.
Houlton Boys Survive Penalty-Kick Thriller Against Penquis
It doesn't get much more dramatic than deciding a playoff game from the penalty spot.
Ninth-seeded Houlton traveled to eighth-seeded Penquis on Saturday for an eight-person boys preliminary matchup, and neither team was able to break through during regulation or overtime.
With the game still scoreless, it came down to penalty kicks.
The Shires converted three attempts to Penquis' two, giving Houlton the victory and a place in the regional quarterfinals.
The result goes into the books as a 1-0 win for Houlton, with the Shires taking the shootout 3-2.
For a team that entered the tournament as the No. 9 seed, it's a big road victory and another opportunity to keep playing.
Caribou's Three Two-Goal Scorers Lead Win Over Medomak Valley
Caribou's boys made the most of their home playoff opportunity Saturday, defeating Medomak Valley 6-2 in a Class B North preliminary matchup.
And the Vikings didn't have to rely on just one scorer.
Louie Hebert, Declan Miller and Carter St. Pierre each scored twice for eighth-seeded Caribou, accounting for all six goals.
Liam Doughty scored both goals for ninth-seeded Medomak Valley.
The victory sends Caribou into the regional quarterfinals, where the Vikings will face top-seeded John Bapst.
It's a familiar opponent for Caribou, but the stakes are considerably higher this time around. The Vikings will need another strong performance to keep their tournament run going.
Fort Kent Girls Shut Out MCI to Advance in Class C North
Top-seeded Fort Kent opened its Class C North postseason with a 3-0 quarterfinal victory over eighth-seeded Maine Central Institute.
The Lady Warriors took care of business at home, earning the shutout and advancing to the regional semifinals.
Fort Kent entered the tournament as the No. 1 seed following a strong regular season, and Saturday's victory keeps the Lady Warriors in the hunt for a regional championship.
With the field narrowing, the competition will only get tougher from here.
Katahdin Girls Fall to Penquis in Penalty Kicks
Katahdin's girls were involved in another dramatic eight-person preliminary matchup Saturday.
The ninth-seeded Lady Cougars traveled to eighth-seeded Penquis, and the two teams remained scoreless through regulation and overtime.
The game eventually went to penalty kicks, where Penquis came away with the victory.
The final is recorded as a 1-0 win for Penquis following the shootout.
It was a difficult way for Katahdin's season to end, especially after keeping Penquis off the scoreboard throughout open play and overtime.
Three County Teams Move On
Saturday's results leave three more County teams advancing in the 2026 MPA Soccer Championships.
Houlton's boys are moving into the eight-person quarterfinals after their shootout victory, while Caribou's boys will take on No. 1 John Bapst in Class B North.
Fort Kent's girls have already secured a place in the Class C North semifinals after their shutout win over MCI.
For Katahdin's girls, the season comes to a close following a hard-fought preliminary matchup.
There's still plenty of tournament soccer ahead, and I'll have more County results, updated brackets and previews as the postseason continues.

title: Judge asked to compel Trump administration to disclose emails and texts about Kennedy Center plans
text:
Judge asked to compel Trump administration to disclose emails and texts about Kennedy Center plans
President Donald Trump's administration is withholding records documenting the scope of his influence over management of the Kennedy Center, according to attorneys for a Democratic lawmaker challenging the Republican president's plan to close the performing arts center for renovations.
A list of records in the Kennedy Center's possession suggests that Trump has been in “near-constant contact” with the center's management, either directly or through intermediaries, plaintiffs' lawyers said in a court filing on Sunday.
Attorneys for Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, are seeking a court order for the administration to turn over documents, emails and text messages that it has withheld based on its claims that they contain privileged presidential communications.
“These communications directly bear on the issues before the Court, and the claim of privilege cannot stand,” Beatty's lawyers wrote.
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper didn't immediately rule on their request to compel disclosure of the records.
The list of withheld documents includes 19 text messages between Kennedy Center executive director and CEO Matt Floca and Trump executive assistant Natalie Harp regarding Kennedy Center-related matters. They exchanged 11 of those messages on Sept. 15, when the center's board voted for a third time to close the facility, according to Beatty's lawyers.
The list also includes approximately 180 center-related texts between Floca and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who was acting as Trump's “go-between,” Beatty's lawyers say. The plaintiffs' attorneys suspect the administration is engaging in impermissible "gamesmanship."
“Without access to these materials, (Beatty) will lack a complete picture of Defendants’ actions,” they wrote.
The White House didn't immediately comment on the court filing.
Cooper, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama, ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump’s name to the building and ordered it removed.
Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center’s chairman last year by loyalists on its board, has said the building is in dangerous condition that will require it to be “ripped down.” The board voted to close the center after Cooper blocked the institution from returning Trump’s name to the building.
On Sept. 16, Floca ordered a temporary closure of the center's main building. A day later, Cooper ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building.

title: Independent candidates hold the key to our democracy
text:
Sam Hunkler of Beals was a 2022 independent candidate for Maine governor.
It’s a squeal I often heard while collecting signatures to get on the ballot.
“You’re going to split the vote,” a political party cry. One woman was beside herself, irate that I was going to get a share of the pie. Later, she drove by shaking her fist at me. I wondered which party she belonged to.
Democracy implies splitting the vote. The vote is always split among candidates, like a pie. If unopposed, you get the whole pie. No splitting. But the concept takes on a different color with party politics.
Parties claim entitlement to the pie. In their world, a vote outside the two parties is considered “splitting” because it splinters from the party machine where one must choose sides.
When I ran in Maine’s last gubernatorial election as an independent, both of my opponents were party, not electorally, chosen. The Maine Republican and Democratic parties each selected their candidate so there would be no splitting of the vote. They imposed their will to stymie other candidates, the will of party members and democracy.
The advent of political parties, which occurred during his time in office, greatly disturbed George Washington. He was the first and only independent president, the only president to have not belonged to a party. During his farewell speech in 1796 he foresaw that “the spirit of party …serves always to distract the public councils and enfeeble the public administration. It agitates the community with ill-founded jealousies and false alarms, kindles the animosity of one part against another, foments occasionally riot and insurrection.”
The “spirit of party.” How prophetic.
Imagine what it would be like if everyone was an independent, including candidates for office. Imagine if everyone had to decide for themself what was important and how to vote without a party dictating importance and loyalty of their candidates, if elected officials acted upon the voices of the people who elected them and not on the party that enshrined them. We’d have a different outcome and perhaps get beyond the right/left politics, black/white thinking and for/against dogma that divide us.
Even though independents make up a third of Maine voters, we rarely have a voice in our state government. An independent cannot afford to run for higher office unless they are wealthy. They cannot compete financially with party candidates who are bankrolled by parties in exchange for party ideology devotion, where there is little leeway to think and act independently.
Take this year’s U.S. Senate race with Susan Collins and Troy Jackson. Approximately $400 million is expected to be spent in this race, more than $400 per each voting-age resident. How can an independent candidate of ordinary means possibly compete? Consequently, democracy and the voices of at least a third of Mainers are thwarted.
In Maine, we’ve taken that a bit further. The two parties have legislated themselves to be the only ones recognized. The other parties are collectively called “independents,” though we have multiple other parties, including the Green Independent and Libertarian parties.
I am not affiliated with any party, so I am considered an “unenrolled” independent. Again, exclusivity by the two parties in control opposes democracy. This inequality has become more evident over time, especially since Citizens United, which allowed virtually unlimited independent political expenditures by corporations and labor unions — from who knows where. Unfortunately, the party that spends the most often wins. Our elections are being bought.
The party system “kindles the animosity of one part against another,” fermenting fear. In 2022, it seems that I met as many who planned to vote against Mills or LePage as for them. I frequently heard, “I’m afraid to vote for you because Mills (or LePage) might win.”
Is there a remedy, a solution to this assault on democracy?
A step in that direction would be to vote for change rather than out of fear. Consider voting for an independent. We have an opportunity this year to make a significant vote to do just that in our highest Maine office, the governorship.
The independent in this race, Rick Bennett, running a grassroots campaign on a low budget, is the most qualified candidate, with the most experience and with a good heart. Take a look. George Washington would smile.

title: Suspect arrested after fire “completely engulfed” Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest mountain retreat in Germany
text:
BERLIN (AP) — A fire swept through the mountaintop retreat built for Adolf Hitler and known as the Eagle’s Nest as emergency services struggled to tackle the blaze in snow and wind, and a man was arrested on suspicion of arson, authorities said Saturday.
Emergency services in the Berchtesgaden district, in the Bavarian Alps in Germany’s southeastern corner, were alerted to the fire by an alarm at about 9:15 p.m. Friday. Firefighters and police rushed to the scene — located at the end of a narrow road that winds up the mountain, in part through a series of tunnels — and could see the flames as they approached.
They stopped and arrested a man on a motorcycle driving the other way down the road.
Prosecutors said the 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn’t currently live there, was questioned. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building’s history. Police said there were no current indications that anyone else was involved.
Rain that turned into the season’s first significant snow, accompanied by strong wind, complicated the already difficult task of tackling the blaze and firefighters had to pull out overnight after several hours, officials said. No one was injured in the fire, and firefighters hoped to finish their work on Saturday though they weren’t able to enter the building because of a danger of falling material.
The building, known in German as the Kehlsteinhaus, is located on a cliff 1,834 meters (6,017 feet) above sea level. It is reachable by an elevator built inside the rock from the end of the mountain road, which is closed to public traffic but used during the day by buses for visitors.
It has been operated as a cafe and restaurant since 1952 and contains an exhibition on its history. The Nazi dictator himself rarely used the Kehlsteinhaus — unlike the Berghof residence, also in the Berchtesgaden area, the ruins of which were blown up in 1952.
The Obersalzberg Documentation Center, further down the mountain, is home to the area’s main historical exhibition and was unaffected by the fire.
Officials indicated that the Eagle’s Nest would be restored, though they were vague so soon after the blaze about how exactly that would be done.
“We’re not going to leave a ruin there,” Bavaria’s interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, told reporters in Berchtesgaden. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.
“I think we will be able to find a sensible solution,” Herrmann added. Bavaria’s state government owns the building.
The minister stressed that “it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance.”

title: Iranians fear a possible return to all-out war as US and Israeli elections approach
text:
Iranians fear a possible return to all-out war as US and Israeli elections approach
Many Iranians are bracing for a return to all-out war as Israeli and U.S. leaders sharpen their threats ahead of elections in both countries in the coming days, and as Iran’s leaders remain defiant despite mounting pressure.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces a close vote Tuesday, says Iran's leadership must be eliminated. U.S. President Donald Trump vows to “finish the job” in Iran eight months after the war began, as a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops make their way to the region. Some fear attacks just after the U.S. midterms on Nov. 3.
The Associated Press spoke with Tehran residents who described growing anxiety. Some were preparing to leave the capital. Iran's president has accused the U.S. of disrupting negotiations that have shown little sign of progress for months.
Fereshteh Hajipour, 35, the mother of a toddler, said she was stockpiling over-the-counter medicines and food for fear of a “possible war and bigger bombs.”
Iran threatens new targets as it feels growing economic pain
Iran's leadership believes that Trump likely will order new strikes regardless of the results in the midterm elections, and “they are planning for the scenarios so they can take remedial measures,” said a former government official and foreign policy professor at the University of Tehran, Sasan Karimi.
“They’ve accepted that he will attack us again, before or after the elections,” Karimi said.
Iran has again threatened U.S. military bases and allies in the Middle East, and has warned that it could attack new targets, including undersea data cables that snake through the Strait of Hormuz. This month has seen the highest number of reported attacks on commercial ships transiting the strait since the war’s opening weeks in March.
Meanwhile, a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports has restricted oil exports on which Iran's government depends, increasing the economic pain as each side tries to outlast the other. Trucks have piled up at borders as Iran's trade shifts to overland.
The blockade has caused medicine shortages in Iran, though there is no sign of shortages of food or other essential goods. Iranians have seen livelihoods and purchasing power crumble as their currency’s value has reached record lows, losing much of its value in the past year. Inflation has soared.
Iranian officials have accused the U.S. of aiming to foment unrest.
“Economic warfare is the main axis of the war against us,” Iran’s parliamentary chief and lead negotiator in past rounds of talks with the U.S., Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, told a gathering of officials this month.
President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran faces “a dangerous turning point” as the government seeks to manage growing economic problems and find consensus within the Islamic Republic’s fractious power structure.
Memories are fresh of the nationwide protests sparked by economic pressures that led to a deadly crackdown weeks before the war.
A supermarket trip can eat up half a month's salary
Even for middle-class Iranians, affording basic groceries has become difficult. Prices for staples have risen steeply since the war began. Rice is over 60% more expensive, and beef over 150%.
Mohammad Mohammadi, 36, said a trip to the supermarket can burn through half a monthly mid-range salary of 400 million rials (roughly $150).
Despite the high prices, Mohammad Abedi, 39, said the rising attacks on the Strait of Hormuz spurred him to buy extra supplies for his family, including dried dates, cooking oil and rice.
“I’m worried that the situation could get worse,” he said.
Political moderates are calling for a deal with the U.S. to salvage the economy.
“With the increase in the exchange rate, the conditions for governing the country have become difficult for the executive branch,” warned politician Mohsen Hashemi Rafsanjani in an editorial this month in the reformist daily Saazandegi.
But economic pressure won’t change Iran’s negotiating positions, said Karimi, the former official who served under Pezeshkian. “This is a tested thing. No economic pressure will convince people here to make a deal.”
Karimi added: “Tehran is calculating based on resistance, because they are convinced that will change the calculations of the other side.”
There has been little said publicly about negotiations via mediators after Trump rejected an Iranian proposal last month to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz within a week if Washington met certain conditions like lifting the blockade.
Some Tehran residents are preparing to leave the city
Tehran is dotted with bombed-out buildings from U.S. and Israeli strikes during the height of the war in March and April. Thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed.
Hashem Vajdani, 45, a gym trainer, said he plans to leave the city as anxiety grows.
“I have already packed my belongings to go to a safer town in the north of the country,” he said. “Today I bought more canned food, crackers and extra blankets.”
There are concerns that new fighting could bring a higher toll for Iranian civilians. Thousands have been killed in the war. Trump has repeated threats to take out power plants and other infrastructure.
Anger at the U.S. president has found expression in a billboard set up days ago at a major Tehran square. Passersby have gawked at a Trump impersonator languishing behind bars as footage airing behind him shows a deadly strike on a wedding party in southern Iran that was blamed on the U.S.
Staring up at the cage, Farzaneh Arabzadeh, 30, said she hoped the scene would happen in reality. Trump said he launched the war to help Iranians, she said, but he “put our people in a worse situation.”
The elections in Israel and the U.S. are expected to reflect voters' anger over the war and other issues. Trump’s political support could be weakened, while Netanyahu is in a tight race at a time of anger over Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack, and a series of inconclusive wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Israel's elections are especially important, Tehran-based analyst Rahman Ghahremanpour said. If Netanyahu stays, there is a higher chance of all-out war resuming because of his willingness to take major risks, he added.
Tehran residents said neither election is likely to improve relations.
“It makes no difference. Their hostility toward us remains unchanged,” said Rasool Ghanbari, 50.

President Donald Trump and former President Barack Obama hit the campaign trail in key battleground states on Saturday, delivering sharply different messages about the state of the economy and the direction of political discourse.
With Election Day just around the corner, both presidents appeared alongside candidates in closely watched gubernatorial races and Senate elections that will help determine control of Congress.
Former President Obama made his way around the Midwest, rallying support for Democrats during stops in Ohio and Michigan.
Obama critisized Trump's tariffs for raising costs on consumers and highlighted the impact on border state economies that have been hit especially hard by the trade war with Canada.
"The weirdest thing is that he's the toughest when it comes to tariffs and trade wars on that well-known evil empire, Canada," Obama quipped. "That's your neighbor. It's a few minutes' drive over the bridge. These are the people who gave us Martin Short and maple syrup."
Trump painted a very different picture while campaigning for Republicans in Georgia, arguing that tariffs have "made us rich" and powered American manufacturing.
Trump announced on Saturday that Audi will build a new automobile plant in the Peach State. The $4 billion investment is expected to create roughly 4,500 jobs, according to the company's press release.
"This will be the single largest investment in US auto industry history, modern history," Trump said.
In Ohio, Obama called for political leaders to demonstrate decency. He criticized an ad campaign from the state's Republican gubernatorial candidate, Vivek Ramaswamy, featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling her a liar. Acton has described facing homelessness as a child, and her stepfather was charged with raping her as a 12-year-old, after which her mother lost custody.
"I dont know what has happened. The standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that," Obama said.
The ad has divided Republicans, but Trump continued to defend it during an exchange with reporters on Saturday after he voted early in Florida.
"The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar and she's no good and, you know what? I don't think you can get a better reference on that," Trump said.
On Sunday, Trump is expected to campaign in Michigan, where Republican Mike Rogers is locked in a tight Senate race with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
During his speech in Georgia on Saturday night, Trump called El-Sayed a "radical" and once again referred to the self-described progressive using his middle name, Mohamed.
Obama likened comments on El-Sayed's name and background to attacks he faced during his political career. Trump has often referred to Obama using his middle name, Hussein, and promoted false theories that he was born overseas.
"We have seen this movie before. I starred in it. I have a long form birth certificate to prove it," Obama said. "This stuff didn't work on me, not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul."
El-Sayed has critisized Obama in the past, but the former president downplayed those differences on Saturday, telling the crowd, "Abdul shares my values.” It remains to be seen if that message can help win over Black voters who decisively backed El-Sayed's primary opponent earlier this year.

NASCAR race at Talladega was stopped after Joey Logano's car went airborne in scary 15-car wreck
The NASCAR Chase race at Talladega Superspeedway was stopped under the red flag with five laps remaining after a scary wreck involving three-time Cup Series champion Joey Logano, whose car went airborne and landed on its roof.
Safety crews needed several minutes to turn Logano's No. 22 Ford back over on its wheels, and Logano was able to climb from the car to cheers from the crowd.
Logano was running in fourth when he lost control off a push by Carson Hocevar and started a 15-car pileup on the frontstretch that also included Chase Briscoe, Brad Keselowski, Austin Cindric, Josh Berry and Riley Herbst, who appeared to lose the brakes in his No. 35 Toyota before hitting the inside wall at virtually full speed.
“I just got a push in the wrong spot there,” Logano said. “It was very much a ‘Talladega Nights,’ Oh no, I’m upside down, this is not good’ moment. I can’t thank the safety crew enough. They did an amazing job flipping that thing over."
Herbst, who missed the Daytona race in August with a concussion from a crash at New Hampshire Motor Speedway, was able to exit his car with help from safety workers. He took a moment to lean against his car before removing his helmet.
In a postrace interview with USA Sports, Herbst had a soft cast on his left hand and a wrap around his wrist and forearm.
“I’m OK; it was a big one,” Herbst said. "But just thank you to 2311 Racing and Toyota for the support. It’s been an up-and-down year, to say the least. I thought we had a shot at it there at the end. We got shuffled out a little bit, but came back and ultimately just got caught up in that wreck at Talladega.
“My dad always said, ‘If you’re going to be dumb, you better be tough.’ So, cheers.”
Logano is a three-time winner at Talladega. He has been involved in airborne crashes before at the 2.66-mile oval that is infamous for its big crashes.
After a similar incident in the April 2021 race at Talladega, Logano expressed frustration that his car had gotten up in the air and had its roof crushed. “I got a roll bar in my head,” Logano said. “That is not OK. I am one hit away from the same situation Ryan Newman just went through ( in the 2020 Daytona 500 ). I just don’t feel like that is acceptable.”
NASCAR made safety enhancements to address airborne wrecks in recent years, and the Team Penske driver praised his car's integrity after the wreck Sunday at Talladega.
“The car did a great job," Logano said. "The last time I flipped it was crushed on my head. This time, I don’t think any of the roll cage crushed at all, so I appreciate what NASCAR’s done. Thank you and the safety team for getting me out of there. There was some vicious hits in this one. Just happy to be alive.”

title: Registered sex offender accused of posing as teenage girl to enroll in high school

The case remains an active and ongoing investigation.”
KGW reports that in 2024, Craig was sentenced to 40 days in jail after claiming to be a “15-year-old homeless teenager named Madison” and enrolled at a high school in Oregon.

title: Penalty-Kick Drama for Houlton, Six Goals for Caribou and Fort Kent Moves On
text:
Houlton Survives Penalty Kicks, Caribou Scores Six as County Soccer Playoffs Continue
Saturday brought plenty of playoff excitement for Aroostook County soccer teams, including a penalty-kick thriller, a six-goal performance and another shutout victory for one of the region's top seeds.
Houlton's boys survived a dramatic shootout against Penquis to advance in the eight-person tournament, while Caribou's boys rolled past Medomak Valley 6-2 in Class B North.
On the girls' side, top-seeded Fort Kent continued its postseason run with a 3-0 victory over Maine Central Institute, while Katahdin's season came to an end in a penalty-kick loss to Penquis.
Three County teams are moving on, and the regional quarterfinals are bringing some interesting matchups.
Houlton Boys Survive Penalty-Kick Thriller Against Penquis
It doesn't get much more dramatic than deciding a playoff game from the penalty spot.
Ninth-seeded Houlton traveled to eighth-seeded Penquis on Saturday for an eight-person boys preliminary matchup, and neither team was able to break through during regulation or overtime.
With the game still scoreless, it came down to penalty kicks.
The Shires converted three attempts to Penquis' two, giving Houlton the victory and a place in the regional quarterfinals.
The result goes into the books as a 1-0 win for Houlton, with the Shires taking the shootout 3-2.
For a team that entered the tournament as the No. 9 seed, it's a big road victory and another opportunity to keep playing.
Caribou's Three Two-Goal Scorers Lead Win Over Medomak Valley
Caribou's boys made the most of their home playoff opportunity Saturday, defeating Medomak Valley 6-2 in a Class B North preliminary matchup.
And the Vikings didn't have to rely on just one scorer.
Louie Hebert, Declan Miller and Carter St. Pierre each scored twice for eighth-seeded Caribou, accounting for all six goals.
Liam Doughty scored both goals for ninth-seeded Medomak Valley.
The victory sends Caribou into the regional quarterfinals, where the Vikings will face top-seeded John Bapst.
It's a familiar opponent for Caribou, but the stakes are considerably higher this time around. The Vikings will need another strong performance to keep their tournament run going.
Fort Kent Girls Shut Out MCI to Advance in Class C North
Top-seeded Fort Kent opened its Class C North postseason with a 3-0 quarterfinal victory over eighth-seeded Maine Central Institute.
The Lady Warriors took care of business at home, earning the shutout and advancing to the regional semifinals.
Fort Kent entered the tournament as the No. 1 seed following a strong regular season, and Saturday's victory keeps the Lady Warriors in the hunt for a regional championship.
With the field narrowing, the competition will only get tougher from here.
Katahdin Girls Fall to Penquis in Penalty Kicks
Katahdin's girls were involved in another dramatic eight-person preliminary matchup Saturday.
The ninth-seeded Lady Cougars traveled to eighth-seeded Penquis, and the two teams remained scoreless through regulation and overtime.
The game eventually went to penalty kicks, where Penquis came away with the victory.
The final is recorded as a 1-0 win for Penquis following the shootout.
It was a difficult way for Katahdin's season to end, especially after keeping Penquis off the scoreboard throughout open play and overtime.

Houlton's boys are moving into the eight-person quarterfinals after their shootout victory, while Caribou's boys will take on No. 1 John Bapst in Class B North.
Fort Kent's girls have already secured a place in the Class C North semifinals after their shutout win over MCI.

text:
Ukraine disputes Elon Musk's claim that its military violated Starlink's terms of service
Ukrainian officials have disputed claims by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk that the country’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service by using the civilian satellite internet network for offensive drone strikes.
Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said long-standing restrictions on the civilian system in Ukraine made such offensive use impossible.
“It’s very strange that Elon Musk doesn’t know about the restrictions on Starlink’s operation in Ukraine,” he wrote in an online post.
SpaceX’s Starlink and its military-focused Starshield service are critical to Ukraine’s wartime connectivity. Earlier this month, Ukrainian drones connected to Starshield lost connectivity at high speeds, disrupting air defenses during daily Russian air attacks. Officials said the so-called speed caps were lifted on Saturday, and the service was restored.
Still, questions have persisted about who ordered the interruptions to satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow’s attacks.
Writing on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that drones operated via the civilian Starlink system had a speed restriction of 70–90 kmh (43-56 mph) within Ukraine and did not work in Russia.
“Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes,” he said.
Musk acknowledged on Saturday that SpaceX had throttled Starlink in Ukraine.
“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”
But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. U.S. President Donald Trump has maintained that he didn't make that call, while Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk.
Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the Ukrainian military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions. They also added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by Trump’s reported deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia that Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.
The US is making new efforts to end the war
The restoration of Starlink service followed a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week, renewing his call on Western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors.
“This week alone, Russia has launched about 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistic missiles, and almost 2,300 strike drones at Ukraine,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post.
He said the attacks — many of them deadly — had affected nine regions of the country, damaging power plants, grain stores, civilian homes and commercial facilities.

title: Thousands of protesters march in cities across Europe
text:
Soldiers guard center of Milan as thousands of protesters march in cities across Europe
Thousands of young people marched Saturday through the streets of several Italian cities, including Milan, Rome and Turin, as authorities deployed large numbers of police and soldiers in a largely successful bid to stave off a repeat of the violent clashes and looting that marred similar protests last week.
Video above: Police in Rome deployed tear gas and water cannons against protesters
The demonstration in Milan remained peaceful, but there were brief clashes with police in both Rome and Turin.
In Milan, thousands of young people marched the streets as soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up, but by late afternoon, most shops had opened, Italian media reported.
Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week. In Milan, police detained several minors as a preventive measure, media reported.
While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities Saturday from Milan to Rome to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana.
The protests encompass a broad range of issues from education and corruption to anti-war movements, pensions and housing.
Army vehicles and boarded-up luxury stores in Milan
In Milan, huge crowds of mostly young people gathered as night fell, chanting insults to Meloni and holding aloft banners such as “No to lies of the state.”
A group of protesters dumped manure outside Italy’s energy regulator and burned a symbolic, oversized electricity bill, images broadcast on local television showed.
Video below: Steelers-Saints game in Paris to proceed despite violent protests
The 500 soldiers deployed to Milan came in addition to hundreds already stationed there, supporting about 5,000 police and other security personnel. Authorities used drone surveillance, checks at railway stations, rapid-response units and online monitoring for potential calls to violence.
A mayoral hopeful, Pierfrancesco Majorino, who announced his candidacy Thursday, joined the marchers and remarked how peaceful the day was, according to Italian media. He will contest a center-left primary in early 2027. Milan's center-left Mayor Giuseppe Sala, who has held the role since 2016, is not running again.
Many stores, particularly luxury boutiques within Milan's fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows. The Apple store also shut down and remained shut even as others reopened.
Rioters last weekend smashed their way into stores, targeting sneakers, athletic wear and sporting goods on streets that run off the city’s central Duomo square.
Security measures extended beyond the city center over concerns protesters could move into other neighborhoods.
The protesters ended their march peacefully Saturday evening outside the Milan Polytechnic, more than 3 kilometers (2 miles) from the city center.
Officials said Saturday they were investigating a 30-year-old freelance journalist said to be the “mastermind” of the newly formed Oct. 17 movement, which has been the main driver of the recent protests in Italy.
Milan police say last week's violence and looting involved about 2,000 very young protesters, many of them “naturalized, second-generation Italians,” alongside foreign nationals. Over two days, police arrested 45 people, including 34 minors.
A group of about 30 far-right activists, described as hooligans linked to Inter Milan soccer club, made a brief appearance chanting anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans but were isolated by police.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the soldiers deployed Saturday were only recently allowed to use plastic restraint ties and only in areas around train stations, not throughout the city. They are not authorized to carry pepper spray or tasers, he said.
Protesters try to force entry into Colosseum in Rome
Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.
A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards. Elsewhere, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters.
“I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study ... and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities,” said Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association.
A separate anti-war march took place in central Rome. Organizers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.
But it was these marchers who briefly clashed with police near the Piazza della Repubblica, even as organizers were trying to hold the crowd back using batons and tear gas. In the end, the protesters pulled back when a water cannon was turned on. They retreated to a location about half a kilometer (mile) away.
Clashes and buildings set on fire in Albania
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom set government buildings on fire and threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 officers patrolled the streets Saturday.
For over a week, protesters have hurled rocks, flares, firebombs and fireworks at police who have used batons and tear gas in clashes in the city center.
High school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama.
A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the prime minister's office turned violent earlier, with some activists lighting fires on the street.
Rama said Saturday his government was preparing a response to the students' demands and called them to a dialogue. He warned that violent protesters will face penalties.
Pensions and housing spark Madrid and Lisbon protests
Thousands of retirees and others marched peacefully in Spain's capital Saturday to demand public pensions aren’t meddled with.
“They are threatening us with privatizing pensions. It’s just another thing they want to profit from," said Maria José Benito, 68.
The protests came ahead of next month’s snap election as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist Party criticized the conservative opposition Popular Party for making overtures about privatizing public pensions. Spain also has been roiled by protests this fall around the issue of housing, as rental and home costs have risen in recent years beyond what many Spaniards can afford.
Taking their cue from Spaniards, protesters in Lisbon demanding affordable housing marched across the city on Saturday.
They have also targeted recent measures announced by the government of Prime Minister Luis Montenegro that include easing the cap on yearly rent increases and facilitating the eviction of tenants who fail to pay rent.
Montenegro defends the measures, saying that they aim at reinforcing trust between tenants and landlords and boosting the rental market. Protesters claim that the measures are not balanced and put tenants in a more vulnerable position.
Nellas reported from Athens, Greece, and Hui reported from London. Associated Press writers Suman Naishadham in Madrid, Giada Zampano in Rome, and videojournalists Niccolò Lupone in Milan, Veronica Sauchelli in Rome, Alicia León in Madrid and Helena Alves in Lisbon contributed to this report.

title: 'Big, furry pillow lounging next to that tree': Man snaps selfie with black bear
text:
'Big, furry pillow lounging next to that tree': Man snaps selfie with black bear
A resident in one Massachusetts town got the shock of his life after he spotted a black bear in his backyard, prompting him to catch a selfie from a safe distance.
A bear has been spotted repeatedly this week in Chelmsford's Westlands neighborhood, surprising many residents in the Massachusetts town.
"I just looked at my neighbor's house, and there’s just this big, furry pillow lounging and sitting next to that maple tree," said Tom Salowsky, who has lived in the area for years.
He continued, saying the bear was "very docile, it was just munching on seed. It was incredible — I mean, to the point that I got a selfie with it, at what? Fifteen, 20 feet? Yeah, that’s pretty cool."
Salowsky sent the photo to his wife, Amanda, who was at work.
"All of a sudden he turned on FaceTime, and I’m like, 'Are you kidding me?'" she said. "And he’s like, 'Can you believe it?'"
The bear’s presence excited the whole family, including their dog Sox, who Salowsky said had been acting unusually during walks in recent days.
"Just making aggressive lunges and excitement I haven’t seen since he was a puppy," he said.
The bear, which has tags on its ears, is likely being tracked by the state.
According to MassWildlife experts, bears are actively searching for outdoor food sources at this time of year.
Residents in the area have since been advised to take in bird feeders, secure garbage and compost, and protect any livestock. They are also advised to give the animals space.

title: Why this Massachusetts independent is traveling for Troy
text:
Charlie Welch of Northampton, Massachusetts, holds a bachelor’s degree in American history from Harvard College and an MBA in finance and economics from New York University. He runs a real estate agency.
I have never before spent my time on politics, yet in addition to canvassing for Troy Jackson, I phone bank for him three nights a week and I will be in Maine on Election Day to serve as a poll observer.
On Saturdays, I phone bank for Roy Cooper, the Democratic Senate candidate in North Carolina. I have donated money to the campaigns of Chris Pappas in New Hampshire and of Cait Conley in New York, both Democratic candidates running to flip or defend a seat in Congress. This is a radical departure for me, a person who has had no political party affiliation and has rarely voted outside of presidential elections.
It’s clear to me that this election is different. In this midterm election, our democracy is on the line. This is a crisis that demands the attention of every voter in this country and transcends our state borders and party affiliations.
In this election, we have two choices. We can endorse one man’s progress in dismantling our democratic form of government or we can defy it and reaffirm our commitment to the principles upon which this nation was founded 250 years ago.
We are immersed in a war with Iran of great consequences, including a higher cost of living and a world economy thrown into turmoil. Far graver is the estimated deaths of more than 9,000 people, including more than 1,700 civilians. More deaths will come as the war lumbers on with no end in sight. Although our nation chose this war, and our nation will inherit its legacy, whose war is it? Our Congress has never approved or supported it, yet we started it and are in it, based on the decision of one man.
Without congressional approval, our current president is feverishly remaking our nation’s capital to his liking. In addition to tearing down the East Wing of our White House and constructing a monstrous addition that will be nearly twice the size of the White House itself, he has begun site work for an arch that will be more than twice the height of our Lincoln Memorial.
He threatens to tear down our Kennedy Center unless he is allowed to put his name on it. Past presidents resisted having their names put on government projects while in office. Our current president insists on it.
He has weaponized our government agencies against us. The examples of this are many, but one of the most outrageous is the arrest of an Olympic athlete to deflect the blame for a botched paint job on our Reflecting Pool.
Recently, he has attacked our free press by banning three media outlets from the White House because he considers their news coverage too negative. He is currently running taxpayer-funded ads that are unequivocally intended to sway voters before the midterm elections, a brazen and illegal use of taxpayer money for partisan propaganda and self-aggrandizement.
Prior to 2024, any one of these events would have set off alarms warning us that the guardrails of our democracy had been breached, but overwhelmed by the sheer volume of abuses and so immersed in the bitter partisanship incited by this man, we have hardly noticed that we have surrendered a large portion of our democracy to him, and what remains is rapidly slipping through our fingers.
On Jan. 6, 2021, the ultimate assault on our democratic form of government took place. Never in our nation’s history has there been a violent attempt to overturn the results of a presidential election. Our current president reaffirmed his disdain for our democracy by pardoning over 1,500 people involved in this attack on our nation’s capital.
Mindful of these events, his relentless attempts to influence our upcoming midterm elections are ominous. The peaceful transfer of power is the very soul of any democracy. Without it there is no democracy.
For the time being, we are all able to vote and our votes are meaningful. The vote you cast on Nov. 3 will be more meaningful than any midterm vote cast in our nation’s history.
We all have our beliefs and our priorities. On Nov. 3, I implore you to be clear on what you are prioritizing, what you are endorsing. Your vote will either encourage the slide of our government into the clutches of a man fond of posting pictures of himself as a king, even a god, or it will defy it.
Our nation has faced and defeated great threats before, and regardless of the outcome of this election, we will do it again. But this Nov. 3 is crucial. Without a Democratic victory, the road back to our democracy will be much longer and more arduous.
Despite the distorted image of American greatness that has been peddled to us in recent years, there is only thing that makes our nation great and that is that our founders introduced to this world a revolutionary form of government, a form of government that we have defended for more than 250 years with our blood and our treasure, a government through which the people themselves guide their destiny, instead of a monarch or a king.
It is our unwavering commitment to that democracy that makes us great. Without it, we are ordinary, at best.
Indeed, I am urging you to vote for the Democratic Party in this election, but please do not make the mistake of thinking that I am merely a Democrat in disguise. As an independent, I have voted with both parties. Currently both parties share some of my views; neither of them share all.
I am well aware that a Democratic victory in November will not cure our wounded democracy, but it will stem the bleeding and keep it alive.
For that, I’m willing to drive a lot longer than three hours.

title: For Maine students, academia must come first

title: Man cooking chicken for roadside barbecue finds dead snake in charcoal bag
text:
NAHIKU, Hawaii (HNN/Gray News) - A Hawaii man was cooking chicken for lunch at a roadside grill when he noticed a slithery surprise in a bag of charcoal.
Roy Hanks was in for a surprise while cooking huli huli chicken just before lunch last Saturday for Hana Hawaiian BBQ, a roadside barbecue at Nahiku Marketplace on the island of Maui.
“My husband was running the grill. He went to throw charcoal on the fire. He opened the charcoal bag and found the snake on top of the bag,” said Sharon Fillazar-Hanks, Roy’s wife and the manager of Hana Hawaiian BBQ.
She said she did not believe her husband at first.
“He sent a picture,” Fillazar-Hanks said. “I thought it was a prank, but it wasn’t. It was real, but it was dead.”
Fillazar-Hanks called the Maui Police Department, who responded and then contacted the Hawaii Department of Agriculture Quarantine Division.
MPD officials said the department told officers the snake could be disposed of.
The department confirmed the charcoal bag was packaged outside of Hawaii.
“It was likely already deceased during the packing process in its state or country of origin,” said Jai Cunningham, Hawaiʻi Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity public information officer. “DAB has seen similar cases with baled hay, where snakes seek shelter in the unprocessed product, are killed during processing and are then unintentionally shipped to Hawaiʻi.”
The snake’s species is unclear. Based on photos, state officials said it is likely a nonvenomous rat snake.
“Some people say possible juvenile copperhead snake. Then, one said a rat snake. I’m like, ‘A snake is a snake. We don’t need it here,’” Fillazar-Hanks said.
