title: Once adrift, Graham Platner’s fleet of volunteers finds new purpose
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On a recent October evening, Kelly Millikan was among a half-dozen volunteers sitting on repurposed church pews inside a small storefront in Portland’s Arts District.
Hunched over a clipboard, Millikan dutifully scrawled a note on the back of a postcard.
“Last we spoke you told us of your plan to vote early at City Hall,” she writes. “Thank you for being an active participant in our Democracy + making your voice heard. Best, Kelly + PPM.”
Each postcard is pre-printed with “People Powered Maine. Organized money always wins. Until organized people show up.” — the calling card of an organization founded by former volunteers for Graham Platner.
When Platner’s meteoric bid against Republican Sen. Susan Collins came crashing down in July, thousands of people inspired by the political newcomer and his progressive policy agenda were set adrift.
But many, like Millikan, are still engaged in the consequential election.
Some have signed on to the Maine People Powered Movement, which rose from the ashes of Platner’s implosion. A few are working independently of any organized group. And others have joined up with the Maine Democratic Party.
Many of those disappointed by Platner’s exit say they have found a renewed purpose their organizing.
“I think it was difficult for a lot of people, not just me,” said Michelle Lesperance, a 69-year-old retired special education teacher from Portland who’s working independently for progressive causes. “We had so many reservations about the party itself, and I continued to have reservations.”
But in the short term, she and the party share the same goals.
“The bottom line is: We all are completely, completely and totally 100% around getting rid of Collins,” Lesperance said.
Volunteers with People Powered Maine are sending the postcards to residents their group has already met through canvassing efforts. Their notes don’t advocate for a specific candidate on the Nov. 3 ballot. That’s by design, said Bente Lundh, a lead organizer with the group.
“Most of the time, as you will see in the instructions, we’re not pushing people one way or another,” Lundh told the assembled volunteers. “We’re trying not to be obnoxious that way.”
With less than two weeks before the midterm elections, People Powered Maine’s softer approach is distinct from other progressive organizing efforts in the state.
Democratic Party organizers are mustering canvassers to ask Mainers to vote for Democrat Troy Jackson over Collins. But People Powered Maine isn’t being quite so blunt. They’re betting that fostering relationships beyond the transactional nature of asking for a vote will lead to lasting change.
Those close to these efforts insist there is no tension between the voter outreach efforts of the Democratic Party and independent groups. But they’re undeniably approaching the campaign in different ways.
PEOPLE POWERED MAINE
Last fall, Platner’s campaign held a series of “Grahamcamps” that trained volunteers in relational organizing, which seeks to build relationships within a community and identify a common concern before trying to persuade someone to support a certain issue or candidate.
A core group of lead organizers attracted to Platner’s theory of politics decided to formalize his approach in August, incorporating People Powered Maine as a 501(c)(4), a type of nonprofit that allows for lobbying and public issue advocacy.
“Graham was much more focused on building that connection with the person you’re knocking at a door with,” said Gioachinno Brennan, a 26-year-old Cumberland resident and former Platner volunteer who now works with People Powered Maine. “The whole message was — the campaign is listening … this is a candidate that wants to address the concerns of the people.”
However, the group isn’t staying agnostic in the state’s biggest race. Last month, organizers created a federal political action committee, Maine People Powered Movement, to advocate for specific candidates who pledge to support the group’s platform and who pass muster with its members.
The group is backing Jackson, co-founder Crystale Lapham said, because he signed onto their policy platform and took questions from members.
Within the last couple of weeks, the group worked the crowds at rallies with Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.
At the Warren rally in Portland’s Deering Oaks, Lapham said the group focused on “tripling.” That’s where volunteers ask attendees to call or text three friends urging them to vote and telling them what issues they find important.
Lapham said the group has a core of 250 or so volunteers and more than 2,000 others who have signed up on its website.
The 501(c)(4)’s canvassing approach is largely one of persuasion. Rather than knocking on the doors of Democrats, hoping to fire up the anti-Trump base, People Powered Maine is reaching out to people who are not enrolled in a political party ahead of the midterms. Unenrolled voters comprise nearly a third of the state’s registered voters, making them the second-largest voting bloc behind Democrats in Maine.
Lapham said nearly a third of those unenrolled voters are undecided about the U.S. Senate race, according data from the group’s canvassers. (Formal polls show a far lower share of undecided voters.)
“A lot of the people are saying, ‘This is the first time anybody’s knocked on my door to talk about Troy,'” said Lapham, a 44-year-old Falmouth resident. “So we know that we’re talking to the right doors.”
The group is being assisted by Ronnie Cho, a former statewide organizer for Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign. Cho said Obama had a field operation that was separate from the Democratic Party — and it was key to his resounding victory in Maine.
“One of the biggest takeaways I got from that campaign was how important it was to talk to people beyond party affiliation,” Cho, 43, said.
“We had offices that were not co-located with the Maine Democratic Party, because we knew that we needed to make this place welcome and open for folks of all political stripes. … And I haven’t seen enough of that kind of intentionality when it comes to organizing.”
PARTY EFFORTS
The Maine Democratic Party says it has built the largest canvassing operation in state history.
On Tuesday, the party announced it has made more than a million attempted voter contacts, with canvassers knocking on more than 230,000 doors and making 790,000 phone calls. The party has opened 25 field offices in all 16 counties, trained more than 290 volunteer leaders and surpassed 18,000 volunteer shift sign-ups, it said.
The party said more than 2,200 former Platner volunteers have signed up for at least one volunteer shift.
That effort is geared toward electing Democrats up and down the ballot on Election Day. The party says 30% of their canvassing targets are unenrolled voters — meaning their efforts aren’t strictly partisan, either.
Collins’ campaign did not respond to specific questions about its canvassing operations. But spokesman Shawn Roderick said in a written statement that canvassing is being done by both campaign volunteers and the Maine Republican Party.
An outside group, Stronger Maine, has also been canvassing on Collins’ behalf for months.
SOME STILL ADRIFT
Some former Platner volunteers say they haven’t found a home since the campaign ended.
Among this group of expats is Erin Evans, who has offered her Portland house as a base for canvassing and making homemade campaign throughout the political season.
Evans wanted Nirav Shah to replace Platner on the Democratic ticket, but her candidate was out-organized by Jackson with the help of labor unions during the Democrats’ second, truncated mini-primary in July. But she’s still engaged in campaigning.
“I am 50,000% onboard with Troy Jackson and Matt Dunlap,” Evans said, also referring to the Democrat running for the 2nd Congressional District seat. “And so are all of my Graham friends.”
Evans and some other like-minded former Platner volunteers said they didn’t like the top-down approach of the Maine Democratic Party’s campaign apparatus. Instead, they preferred the flexibility, creativity and community that infused Platner’s campaign.
“I’m not satisfied with either party,” said Jeanne McCliment, a 76-year-old independent who volunteered for Platner. “For me, the Democratic Party is the least worst.”
PLAYING THE LONG GAME
With so much at stake in November, it may seem strange to some how, in many ways, People Powered Maine is already looking beyond the midterms. But this outlook is part and parcel with the group’s theory of politics. They plan to stay active after the election so they can try to make inroads with people who don’t share their views.
“We have a huge resource,” said 24-year-old volunteer Lucy Climer-Kennedy, a Portland transportation planner. “People power.”
On a recent fall day, their unorthodox approach took them to Jonesport, a small Down East town more than 200 miles from Portland. There, Donald Trump and Collins each won their most recent elections with nearly 70% of the vote.
The group did not go there to talk politics or gin up support for Jackson or any other candidate. It was there to provide financial assistance to lobstermen at a local cooperative.
After a long morning of hauling lobster traps, Maurice Alley was greeted at the docks by Suzanne Carver, a fellow resident of nearby Beals and a People Powered Maine member.
As Alley’s crew sorted lobsters into crates and topped off his fuel tank, Carver told the 78-year-old skipper of the F/V Renegade that her group provided up to a couple hundred dollars for each member of the Beals-Jonesport Co-Op to help with the high cost of diesel.
For Alley, it was a pleasant surprise. Oftentimes, lobstermen arrive at the docks only to find that gas prices have gone up and the price of lobster has gone down.
Barely audible over the loud rumble of his diesel engine, Alley lamented that people in power are eager to help farmers affected by high prices, but lobstermen are often forgotten.
Nearby, the organizing group unfurled a banner reading “Working Mainers left holding a bill.” It detailed the increased costs of diesel, heating oil, gasoline and health insurance. Another volunteer offered Alley and his crew slices of pizza and cold drinks, which he accepted.
Before shoving off, Alley was asked about the assistance he received.
“Well, I like that,” he said. “It’s not that farmers’ aid, but at least it’s something.”
Carver, a former Platner volunteer, was careful not to talk politics or specific candidates on the docks. She said she’s only there to help her community.
Tensions rose when more reporters arrived with cameras. One reporter asked Carver about the upcoming elections and specific candidates. Within 30 minutes, journalists were asked to leave the docks by the manager.

title: Some schools are banning caffeine pouches. Here's what parents and students should know
text:
Some schools are banning caffeine pouches. Here's what parents and students should know
Coffee, energy drinks and soda are not the only ways young people are getting their caffeine fix. Another product catching the attention of health experts, school officials and parents doesn’t come in a cup or a can. It comes in a pouch.
Caffeine pouches, small packets placed in the mouth between the lip and gum, are marketed as a portable and discreet way to boost energy and focus. Some contain as much as 200 milligrams of caffeine or about the amount in two cups of coffee, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. Health experts warn that consuming too much caffeine can cause serious side effects, including increased heart rate, especially in children and teens.
Related video above: Doctor shares advice for parents of teens who say they need caffeine to get through the day
The pouches also closely resemble nicotine products, raising concerns among school officials about student health and the difficulty of distinguishing between the products. Some K-12 school districts across the U.S. have responded by banning them, even though there is no federal minimum purchase age for caffeine pouches.
Here’s what to know about the pouches, their potential risks and how schools are responding.
Caffeine pouches have a variety of nicknames
Caffeine is a stimulant that increases alertness, energy and brain activity. It can be safe for most healthy people in moderate amounts. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said amounts up to about 400 milligrams per day, roughly two to three 12-ounce (about 354.8 milliliters) cups of coffee, are not generally associated with health problems.
Caffeine pouches are small packets designed to release caffeine through the tissues in the mouth. The amount in each pouch depends on the brand.
The main concern is consumption by children. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, caffeine from the pouches is absorbed into the bloodstream and the effects are felt in minutes.
The pouches do not require spitting and are sold in multiple flavors, such as coffee, mint, fruit and seasonal options like pumpkin spice. Some health officials worry they can be mistaken by young consumers for candy or gum.
Unlike with caffeinated beverages, children and teens may use caffeine pouches more discreetly. The pouches are sometimes referred to on social media as lip pillows, lip cushies and upper or lower deckies, depending on where they are placed in the mouth.
Consumer trade groups and caffeine pouch makers, including ALP Pouch, declined to speak to The Associated Press about the products.
Caffeine has a range of possible side effects
Health organizations, including Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Columbus, Ohio, say too much caffeine can cause significant side effects, including tremors, anxiety, difficulty sleeping, seizures and other complications. Caffeine can remain in the body for more than eight hours depending on the person's metabolism, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics’ Committee on Nutrition. When the effects of caffeine wear off, people can experience headaches, irritability and tiredness. The academy says avoiding caffeine is the best choice for children.
Caffeine pouches may worsen anxiety and sleep problems among teenagers already facing academic and social pressures, potentially affecting their mental health, academic performance and development, said Rob van Dam, a professor of exercise and nutrition sciences at George Washington University in Washington.
“You can get into a vicious cycle where kids just don’t get enough sleep for their normal development and mental health,” he said.
Health experts also worry that teenagers may lose track of their total caffeine consumption, particularly when combining pouches with energy drinks and other caffeinated foods and beverages.
Parents concerned about excessive caffeine consumption can contact the Poison Control Center Hotline at 1-800-222-1222. Seizures, difficulty breathing, collapse or severe heart-related symptoms warrant emergency medical attention, experts say.
Some schools are banning use of caffeine pouches by students
Nearly two-thirds of young people ages 12 to 19 consumed caffeine on a given day, according to a July report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Their average daily intake was about 31 milligrams, far less than the amount found in some caffeine pouches.
Some K-12 schools have taken precautionary measures to restrict use, such as banning caffeine pouches altogether, over concerns about student health, classroom distractions and the difficulty of distinguishing them from nicotine products. It remains unclear whether usage is increasing among American students, although some schools have reported seeing more of the products on campus.
School districts in New York, Kansas, Pennsylvania and Missouri have included caffeine pouches in student conduct policies or prohibited their use on campus. Other schools, including Onsted Middle School in Michigan and North Middle School in Wisconsin, have warned families to leave the products at home.
Holton High School in Kansas says staff cannot reliably determine what substances are inside the pouches, so they prohibit the products under its rules against tobacco and simulated tobacco products. Violations could result in disciplinary action or citations from law enforcement.
In New York, Peru Central School District officials also raised concerns about the nearly identical appearance of caffeine and nicotine pouches during a May 2025 school board meeting. The district’s code of conduct now prohibits caffeine pills and pouches on school grounds.
“The real issue for us as a school, in the middle and high schools in particular, is that when students are using pouches it’s impossible for us to know what the pouch is,” Joha Battin, associate director of student services for the school district, said during the meeting.
Federal nutrition standards generally prohibit schools from selling caffeinated beverages to elementary and middle school students during the day, but those rules do not restrict what students bring from home, leaving districts to decide whether caffeine pouches belong in classrooms and how to enforce restrictions on products that closely resemble nicotine pouches.

title: ICE said a man jumped on the hood of their vehicle. Video — and police — say otherwise
text:
ICE said a man jumped on the hood of their vehicle. Video — and police — say otherwise
DHS accuses man of "flopping for the camera."
ICE said a man jumped on the hood of their vehicle. Video — and police — say otherwise
DHS accuses man of "flopping for the camera."
A 37-year-old man was struck by a federal immigration vehicle Tuesday morning while documenting ICE activity, an incident captured on multiple videos and under investigation by Woodland, California, police.
The Department of Homeland Security responded by saying the man had jumped on the vehicle’s hood. But local police raised doubts about federal officials’ account as they announced a criminal investigation into Tuesday morning’s incident involving the pedestrian
The man, identified as Antonio Moreida, sustained minor injuries. He was evaluated at the scene by medical personnel before being taken to the hospital.
Woodland police said the vehicle that struck him was a Chevrolet Tahoe operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who were conducting an operation in the area.
The ICE driver immediately notified Woodland police dispatch of the collision and cooperated with investigators, police said.
"I heard the engine because it was smashing down the street, and that's how I turned my focus from that to the vehicle, and just like that, they closed in on me," Moreida told sister station KCRA 3.
The Department of Homeland Security said "ICE did not hit a pedestrian" and accused Moreida of "flopping for the camera."
The Woodland Police Department disputed DHS's claims, saying they're "inconsistent" with video evidence reviewed by its investigators.
Videos show different angles of the incident
Video shared by the advocacy group NorCal Resist shows two unmarked SUVs passing each other. The camera follows one SUV as it drives away, showing its brake lights before it swerves to the left. The footage captures the moment Moreida, who is in the roadway, falls to the ground and rolls onto his back as the SUV continues driving.
Another angle from a home surveillance camera shows Moreida walking alongside and touching one of the SUVs before it drives out of frame. He then continues walking in the middle of the street, holding a GoPro camera. Moments later, another SUV enters the frame, its engine revving before it swerves and strikes Moreida with its right front side. The vehicle then drives away.
Moreida and a witness speak out
Moreida said he was at the scene to document the activity of ICE agents when the collision occurred.
"Definitely seemed to swerve into me rather than try to avoid me based off of where I was in the street," he said.
Steve Hanes, a Woodland resident who witnessed the incident, described what he saw.
"He went right up to the car and was taking pictures on his phone. I guess they didn't really like that because they said to step away, so he stepped away, he went down there, and then I heard a car accident, like skid marks, and some car hit the guy who was taking pictures here," Hanes said.
Moreida explained that his GoPro camera served to document ICE activity and to record what happened in case something went wrong.
"Getting hit by a moving vehicle isn't something you just brush off, so definitely feel sore and got my knees scraped up, my hands scraped up, you know that hit I took it to the chest, so once I fell, I rolled, the wind was knocked out of me," he said.
Woodland police give an update on the investigation
Woodland police said Tuesday evening that investigators worked throughout the day to gather evidence, take statements and review relevant audio and video.
"As part of that work, investigators obtained and reviewed additional video footage showing multiple perspectives of the incident, including the interaction between the pedestrian and federal personnel in the minutes before the collision," Woodland police said. "This footage is being reviewed alongside other evidence to help establish the full sequence of events, including the actions of both the pedestrian and the driver."
Woodland police said they did not participate in the federal operation and will investigate the collision independently and submit a complete investigation to the district attorney's office for review.
“I’ve seen the video myself, and I find it very troubling. I understand why people in our community are upset and worried,” Woodland Police Chief Ryan Kinnan said in a statement. “Our responsibility is to conduct a thorough and impartial investigation to establish the facts. We recognize the concerns surrounding federal law enforcement activity in Woodland, and the safety and well-being of our community members remain a priority.”
DHS says 'ICE did not hit a pedestrian'
KCRA 3 reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security for comment multiple times on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, DHS shared this statement: "This is false. ICE did NOT hit a pedestrian. An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes. The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department. Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation."  
Woodland police said Wednesday claims made in the DHS statement are "inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed" by the department's investigators.
Police said investigators established the following based on video evidence:
- The pedestrian was struck by a vehicle driven by an ICE agent
- The pedestrian did not jump onto the hood of the vehicle
- The pedestrian did not slide off the hood of the vehicle
- The driver applied the brakes before the collision
- The driver remained near the scene, contacted Woodland police and cooperated with officers during the initial investigation
Defense attorney says the federal government could take over the case
The Yolo County District Attorney's Office said it could not comment at this time as the matter is under active investigation by Woodland police.
Sacramento defense attorney Mark Reichel said from watching the videos he thought this could be a case of assault with a deadly weapon, and federal agents could be charged by the state.
But even if the district attorney decided to file charges, the case may not go before a judge because the federal government could take over the prosecution, he said.
"If the DA in Yolo County files a criminal charge, and the U.S. attorney here in Sacramento can come in federally, take the case to federal court, and then prosecute it themselves. And if the Trump administration is saying do not prosecute, we know they're not going to," Reichel said.
Reichel also said identifying the agent who was driving could be difficult. He noted that if the federal government does not release the agent's identity, there would be no one to prosecute.
Local, state, federal officials speak out
U.S. House Rep. Mike Thompson, who represents the Woodland area, issued the following statement.
"ICE cannot continue to terrorize our communities. I am in communication with local law enforcement, who have informed me that ICE was operating the vehicle in question and that an investigation is underway. No one is above the law. ICE's actions have contributed to growing distrust and fear within our communities, making transparency and accountability all the more critical. Members of our community need to feel safe."
Assemblywoman Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said on social media, "Our community deserves answers and accountability."
Woodland Mayor Tom Stallard joined Thompson, Aguiar-Curry, Moreida and others at a news conference Wednesday to speak about the situation.
"It's a very sad occasion that brings us together," Stallard said. "I can only let you know I'm beyond anger. I'm at the point of outrage, to the point where I couldn't even sleep last night thinking about this, realizing the people in our community are living in fear because of this effort by ICE to do whatever objective they're trying to do, but doing it in the most hateful, mean, incomprehensible method."
Angel Barajas, who represents District 5 for the Yolo County Board of Supervisors, said a request was made to ask the Woodland Police Department and the Yolo County District Attorney's Office whether charges should be filed in connection with the incident.
ICE has reduced the amount of training for officers, including in vehicle operations and how to deal with confrontations, said Schwank, who is now an agency whistleblower after resigning in February.
On Saturday, ICE said it is instituting additional training for officers.
“ICE training will now be extending to 72 days. The change, effective June 2, 2026, will apply to all new academy classes beginning July 1, 2026. All graduates of the previous academy curriculum will attend follow-on training at the Advanced Field Officer Training Program,” an ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CNN. “As we have said all along, ICE training does not end when recruits graduate from the academy. ICE officers go through a rigorous on-the-job training and mentorship. This additional training is tracked online and monitored closely.”
CNN contributed to portions of this report.

title: Is it Nov. 4 yet? What about now?
text:
Eddie Adelman is a writer who lives in Belfast. His book of columns and short essays is titled “Don’t Get Me Started.”
I don’t know about you, but I’ve got Wednesday, Nov. 4, circled on my calendar. That’s the day after Election Day, when all the political ads expire, the lawn signs begin to come down and the robocalls cease and desist. And let’s not forget the political junk mail.
I am neither a Democrat nor a Republican. As a proud independent, you could say I’m an equal opportunity skewer.
But before I do any skewering, let me say how blessed I am to live in a country where I can write a piece like this without fear of being abducted from my home in the middle of the night and imprisoned, tortured or killed.
For the brave citizens in places like Russia, North Korea and Iran willing to risk everything standing up to tyranny, I can only bow my head in humility and utter veneration.
And with that, back to the skewering. As far as I can tell, the No. 1 goal of every elected official is simple: Get reelected at all costs.
Power is intoxicating, as the senators in ancient Rome knew all too well while they luxuriated in their executive bath houses. Nowadays, getting reelected is a full-time job. There’s always a new gunslinger ready and willing to face off in the middle of town. And let’s face it, we all love a “Gunsmoke” moment.
Sadly, it’s the moments leading up to that face-off that cause trouble.
Let’s start with political advertising. It’s been estimated that the total cost for the 2024 presidential and congressional election campaigns was about $16 billion. Sixteen billion dollars. And that doesn’t even take into account the cost of local and state elections.
Who knows what the total price tag will be for the 2026 campaigns?
Think about how much low-income housing all this money could buy. In a single election cycle, we could take a significant bite out of the homeless crisis here in America.
Of all the billions of dollars raised and spent, a sizable chunk will be spent on TV ads.
If I’m not mistaken, there was a time when TV ads didn’t mention the competition. Tide never mentioned Cheer. Ford never mentioned Chevy. Pepsi never mentioned Coke.
I believe the same was true for political ads. We were content to see the candidates posing in the backyard with his or her family in front of a swing set, surrounded by impossibly cute kids and stout, hard-working immigrant parents. Kiss those days goodbye.
Nowadays, candidates take turns disparaging, even demonizing, their opponents. Not only do these ads cancel each other out, but they ruin the TV watching experience. It’s enough to drive the average citizen to pick up a book.
And political junk mail? Please. Has anyone ever read one of those mailings and thought, “That does it. I’m changing my vote.” Hello, recycling bin.
Road signs. Lawn signs. Hats. T-shirts. Bumper stickers. Don’t get me started. Election Day is just around the corner. And as far as I’m concerned, it can’t get here soon enough.
I’m Eddie Adelman and I approved this column.

title: War in Yemen Reaches Bates Students
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bates students are feeling the pressure at the pump. Louisa Kraus ’30, who drove to a concert in Boston last week, said it cost her about $40 round trip.
She added, “Thankfully I have really good friends, so if I’m driving them places they’ll chip in for gas, but [I’m] definitely less likely to drive as long because of the gas [price].”
Kraus’ story is an all-too-common reality for Bates students. Gasoline prices have increased by an average of $1.35 per gallon since this time last year. Similarly, diesel has increased by an average of $2.63 per gallon, according to AAA.
Collin Marshall ‘30 said that the higher prices have impacted his driving habits. Before, he would always make sure to have a full tank; now, with the higher prices, he “waits until [his car is] basically empty” to refill.
Prices began increasing after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February 2025. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs reported that the war has since killed over 3,400 Iranian civilians and an unknown number of Iranian soldiers.
In response, Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, heavily restricting Persian Gulf oil exports. This forced the Gulf states to find alternative routes to export their oil, reducing international supply.
Because oil is an essential commodity for almost every industry, the price of oil has risen.
Compounding this, Ansar Allah, the governing majority of Yemen, recently began bombing Saudi oil sites and tankers in retaliation for a Saudi attack on a Yemeni airport. This further restricted the already strained fuel supply routes. Earlier this month, President Trump accused Ansar Allah of trying to drive up gas prices, promising that he will “never forget” their recent actions.
What is Ansar Allah?
Ansar Allah (“supporters of God”) began as a Yemeni paramilitary group under the leadership of the al-Houthi family, who continue to dominate Yemeni politics.
They draw much of their support from the Zaidi Shia population of northwestern Yemen, which has religious ties to Iran.
Ansar Allah gained national prominence by promising to fight the corruption of the American-backed Yemeni ruler Ali Saleh, who resigned following an assassination attempt in 2011.
In 2014, Ansar Allah seized the Yemeni capital of Sana’a and has since then governed most of the densely populated northwestern region of Yemen.
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates then invaded Yemen with American support, in an attempt to drive Ansar Allah from power.
The war has been characterized by widespread murder of Yemeni civilians by the American coalition, with hospitals, schools, and funeral processions repeatedly targeted by American forces.
Doctors Without Borders reported that American coalition forces bombed their hospitals after they received their exact locations.
This, combined with an embargo on Yemen by Saudi Arabia, led to the deaths of over 377,000 Yemenis, according to a U.N. Development Programme report.
Despite this, Ansar Allah has maintained control of Sana’a and a majority of the densely populated northwest.
Ansar Allah’s Foreign Policy
Ansar Allah has ideological and religious similarities with the Islamic Republic of Iran, and both have common enemies in the United States and Saudi Arabia.
Together with Iran, Ansar Allah is considered among the most powerful members of the “Axis of Resistance,” an anti-American alliance which also includes numerous smaller military groups such as Hamas and Hezbollah.
Ansar Allah began to increase its international repute in 2023 when it began attacking ships in the Red Sea in order to protest the Gaza Genocide.
The Biden and then Trump administrations began bombing Yemen to try to protect Israeli-affiliated ships.
Since 2024, the United States has lost over $7 billion in munitions and equipment, according to a report by the American think tank Defense Priorities.
While only moderately damaging Ansar Allah’s military capabilities, the United States and its allies have killed several hundred civilians.
This had the unintended consequence of increasing Ansar Allah’s domestic and international standing, with many analysts labeling the campaign a defeat for the United States.
2025-Present: The American Attacks on Iran
On Sept. 10, 2026, an unknown actor bombed the East-West Pipeline as Ansar Allah soldiers advanced in Yemen.
This forced Saudi Arabia to halt most of its oil exports; the kingdom said it had only five days of fuel left in export hubs on Sept. 13.
Though the Saudis have since resumed limited operations using the pipeline, this attack demonstrates a key vulnerability for the kingdom, likely to keep prices high even after the pipeline resumes full operations. Ansar Allah has since bombed Saudi Aramco facilities and the capital, Riyadh.
Not Just Gas Prices
According to an outlook report from the Maine Department of Administrative and Financial Services, Maine was already “facing significant economic uncertainty” before the war began, and the effects of higher fuel prices are likely to hurt the state more than others.
This is primarily because of Maine’s geography, as it is relatively remote from other parts of the country.
A report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture found that food prices are especially impacted by changes in fuel costs because the majority of staple crops (such as onions and potatoes) are grown in states such as Idaho.
Maine could see increased food prices because of the state;s distance from the agricultural heartland. Fuel prices have also become a flashpoint in the 2026 midterms as Maine prepares for winter heating.

NEWPORT, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A large fire at a seafood processing plant prompted evacuations in Newport, Oregon, over concerns that the smoke contained ammonia.
Crews battled a large structure fire that broke out at a freezer building in the Pacific Seafood plant on the historic Newport Bayfront Sunday morning. According to the City of Newport, about 30 to 40 people were at work in the building at the time, but all were able to get out safely.
One firefighter was taken to the hospital and treated for exhaustion.
The City of Newport issued an evacuation order for people within a 1-mile radius of the processing plant. However, later in the day, officials said crews mitigated the risks of a tank leaking ammonia and reduced the evacuation zone to just a couple of blocks because of smoke.
Ammonia is a colorless gas with a sharp odor. High levels of exposure can cause skin, eye and throat irritation, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Authorities said the main concern now is toxic smoke created by the fire.
Authorities urge everyone in the area to stay inside if possible, and to wear a mask if they have to go outside.
An evacuation shelter had been set up at a local church.
Fuller said the cause of the fire has not been identified yet, but crews remain on the scene.
No civilian injuries have been reported at this time, according to city officials.
Newport is located about 132 miles southwest of Portland, Oregon, and has a population of about 10,000 people. Its bayfront is a popular tourist attraction featuring shops, restaurants and tours.
Fuller said a “good chunk” of the small town was impacted by the evacuation, including businesses and residences. The Newport aquarium announced it was closing for the rest of Sunday as a result of the evacuations.
Pacific Seafood released a statement about the fire on Sunday evening, in which Vice President Ashton Meier thanked the emergency responders who have been working to knock down the flames:
“Pacific Seafood is devastated by today’s fire in Newport. Although we are still working with emergency response officials to determine the full extent of the damage, we expect that it will be a major loss.

title: Portland’s Sacred Heart Church holds final Mass
text:
PORTLAND — The sun cast a stained glass rainbow across Catherine Bernier’s pew. Her feet rested on pale ovals scuffed into the dark floorboards by hundreds of parishioners over the last 130 years.
“This is not easy,” the Very Rev. Seamus P. Griesbach said to his parish at Portland’s Sacred Heart Church.
Bernier rested her head on her mother’s shoulder and wiped her tears as she listened to the service, just as she had countless times before.
But this was the last time she and her parish would sit in the pews of the ornate Mellen Street building.
Just over two weeks ago, the Portland Peninsula and Island Parishes announced the closure of Sacred Heart and St. Dominic Parish. The 1896 building is aging faster than the Portland Diocese can keep up with, and repairs would come with a $6 million price tag.
The diocese doesn’t have a plan for the building yet, but will make decisions on its fate in the coming months.
“I wish we could just take it, pick it up and put it somewhere else where it wasn’t falling apart,” Griesbach said later. “It’s in a bad place, where the foundations are collapsing, and where everything’s been going against this building for a long time.”
He pointed up at the meticulously detailed plaster, and at the stained glass windows. It’s beautiful, Griesbach said.
At the top of an ornate pillar next to the altar, the ceiling is beginning to crack. Griesbach wishes he knew why this had to happen at Sacred Heart.
Hundreds of people gathered on Sunday, filling the pews to say goodbye to the building as the band played hymns with Latin and African roots. For years, the church has offered a safe place for immigrants to worship, like Nene Mokamia and her family.
When Mokamia found the church after moving from the Democratic Republic of Congo a few years ago with her husband and daughter, she said it felt like home. Her family was welcomed immediately.
Mokamia was a reader for her parish in the Congo. She didn’t know if she’d be able to find the same opportunity in Portland, but Sacred Heart’s combined French and English Mass gave her a way.
“We found peace. We found love at this church,” Mokamia said.
She and the Berniers agree that the church’s closure is upsetting. But for them, losing the building to age is easier knowing that the spirit of their parish will live on.
The diocese said in its announcement that the English and French Mass is moving to St. Pius X Church and the Spanish-language Mass will be held at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception.
“It’s devastating to say goodbye to the physical place, but the spirit of it is why we’re all here and that’s going to go with us,” Catherine Bernier said. “People will persevere in faith, and there’s a great deal of love.”
As the service ended Sunday, parishioners stood from their pews with outstretched arms swaying with the band. They clapped to the beat, some letting out a cathartic shriek as they said their goodbyes.

title: Carrying his badge: Daughter of fallen sergeant continues his legacy as a deputy
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - Six years after losing her father, a South Carolina deputy says she has found him again — as she wears the same badge he wore before he was killed in the line of duty.
Sgt. Conley Jumper with the Greenville County Sheriff’s Office was killed in the line of duty in October 2020 during a traffic stop on Interstate 85. He left behind a wife and a daughter who once planned to become a lawyer.
Now, his daughter wears her father’s badge.
A father who kept his two worlds separate
In her first interview since joining the Greenville County Sheriff’s Office in her father’s honor, Deputy Cat Jumper said she does not remember growing up around danger. She remembers a man in uniform arriving to catch the end of her volleyball games.
“I loved seeing him — I’d be playing volleyball, and you see this big guy coming in in the same uniform. You’re like, ‘Oh, that’s my dad right there.’ You know, it’s just cool,” Cat Jumper said.
For 28 years, Sgt. Conley Jumper worked Greenville County’s streets, most recently as a K-9 handler and in the department’s school enforcement division. At home, Cat Jumper said, he kept that world separate from his family.
“He kind of shielded me from kind of realization of what law enforcement is and kind of the dangers that occur... even through high school, I did not know. Even through a little bit of college, I did not know. He did a good job at kind of shielding me from that evil,” she said.
A different path before her father’s death
Cat Jumper was a pre-law student at Wofford College, aiming for law school and a career in criminal law.
“At the time before his death, I had different aspirations, different kind of goals. Law enforcement wasn’t really an interest at that time,” she said.
That changed on Oct. 20, 2020, when her father was killed during a traffic stop on Interstate 85.
“I remember it very vividly... it’s gonna be one of those memories that kind of stick in your head, and it’s gonna stay. I remember everybody there, where I was, what I was doing. It’s just an awful feeling,” Cat Jumper said.
Finding a new direction
Cat Jumper said her shift away from law school did not happen overnight. It grew out of what she saw in the months after her father’s death — and how the Greenville County Sheriff’s Office supported her family.
“I saw the camaraderie, everything the sheriff’s office did for us, did for my mom and I, my family... I start being around the sheriff’s office more as a 19, 20-year-old kid, and it’s like this is comfortable. This is home. Being around these people make me happy, make me feel secure and safe,” she said.
Letters arrived after Conley Jumper’s death from people her father had touched while working off-duty side jobs in neighborhoods across the county.
“One letter that we had was a grandma wrote to us stating how he made an impact on their grandson... how he would let them play with the dogs while he was working side jobs over there and just how that interaction with police changed their grandson’s view on police and how it made her feel safe in that community,” Cat Jumper said.
“Knowing that you can make a difference — whereas if I were to sit behind a desk, it’s kind of harder to do,” she said.
Patrolling the same neighborhoods
Cat Jumper moved from the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division in Greenwood to the Greenville County Sheriff’s Office in 2025. Today, she patrols some of the same neighborhoods her father once worked.
“Funny enough, I actually work those same areas. So, I will come across people, and they see my name tag and make that connection,” she said. “Me and your dad had some issues, but he was a cool guy... it’s rewarding. That is absolutely rewarding to me — to have someone make that connection and tell me that experience.”
“It’s like he was out with this person at one point in time. Now, I’m out with this person at this time. So, it’s kind of special... it’s all mutual respect, all the way around,” she said.
Family support
Cat Jumper said her mother, Sara, has been the family’s support through the transition, including when she told her mother she was going to the academy.
“She’s a trooper. She’s been the rock the entire time... it took her by surprise, but she also deep down knew that this was going to happen,” Cat Jumper said.
Marking the anniversary
Cat Jumper and her mother have chosen to treat the anniversary of her father’s death as an ordinary day.
“The easiest part is kind of let it be a normal day, as weird as that sounds,” she said. “When you have such a profound loss, it’s like it’s always gonna be there. And it’s ups and downs, and you’re always gonna have that pain.”
She said wearing the uniform has had an effect her family did not expect.
“My family was concerned that it would be the opposite, but it has helped because I’m able to be closer to him in an indirect way. So, being in this uniform, I take pride in it. I do,” she said. “I’m gonna treat people with respect — how I would like to be treated. How I would like my dad to be treated is how I treat people. And I knew that he did the exact same thing.”
Six years after losing her father, Cat Jumper says she has found him again — on patrol, in a name tag and in the small kindnesses he taught her without ever meaning to.
Conley Jumper’s name lives on across Greenville County, including at the Sgt. William Conley Jumper Jr. School Security Center in Taylors, dedicated last October in honor of his decade in school enforcement.

title: Obituary: Paul Butler
text:
FALMOUTH – After a brief illness, Paul Butler passed peacefully, surrounded by his family on Oct. 21, 2026.
Paul and his twin brother, Willard “Bill” Richardson were born in New York City, N.Y. on March 18, 1933. The boys were raised in New York City, and then Portland, Maine. They spent their summers at Camp Hinds in Raymond and at their family cottage on Highland Lake in Falmouth. Paul loved to tell stories of he and his brother delivering newspapers by boat to the residents of the lake and of their adventures with Blackie, their beloved black labrador.
He attended Deering High School where he was president of the student council. He was always “loyal to the purple” throughout his life and continued to be active in organizing class reunions. When he was not able to attend the annual Deering/Portland Thanksgiving Day football game, he was eager to hear the score. He earned his Eagle Scout with the Boy Scouts, ran track and was active in school committees.
After high school, Paul attended the University of Maine at Orono where he met the love of his life, Jan Bishop. He was a member of the Honorary Society of Sophomore Owls and Sigma Chi fraternity where he met some of his lifelong friends.
Following graduation, he spent six months in officer training at Fort Benning in Georgia before returning to Maine to marry Jan in August 1956. They moved to Hartford, Conn. after the wedding and started his career at Connecticut General Life Insurance Company. Their first daughter, Brenda, was born in Hartford, Conn. in 1959.
In 1960 the family returned to Maine and Paul went to work for his father-in-law, M. Stanley Bishop. He went on to be president and owner of A. R. Bishop and Son until he retired in 1994. Paul grew the company from its original home on Commercial Street to a new facility and retail shop in South Portland. Throughout the years, Paul established and fostered relationships and friendships with the owners, chefs and buyers of the many restaurants, hotels, schools, children’s summer camps, and ski resorts that he faithfully serviced over the years.
Three more daughters, Julie, Jill and Gail joined the family while they resided in South Portland. In 1974 they built a home in Cape Elizabeth where they lived for the next 45 years. The Butler dogs, Prince, Shep and Buffer were always an integral part of the family. Wherever their home was, neighborhood friends became an important part of their lives.
Paul joined the South Portland/Cape Elizabeth Rotary Club in 1974. He served as president in 1980-’81, as club secretary from 1996-2013 and was proud of 37 years of perfect attendance. He became a Paul Harris Fellow in 1986. Many of his fellow rotarians became some of his closest friends. Some of his favorite fundraising activities included Christmas tree sales, Family Fun Day at Fort Williams and serving at the local food kitchens.
After retiring in 1994 Paul and Jan enjoyed traveling with family and friends, playing golf and bowling in local leagues. He continued to volunteer at the South Portland Food Pantry and served as treasurer of the First Congregational Church in South Portland. They especially enjoyed spending their winters on Florida’s Gulf coast and family time in Bethel in the summer. Of all the new and exciting things they did in retirement, watching their grandchildren grow up was certainly the highlight. Paul and Jan were actively involved in their activities over the years and were an influential part of them growing into the remarkable young adults they have become.
2019 saw a move to Ocean View in Falmouth. Paul celebrated his 90th birthday in 2023 and on Aug. 11, 2026, Jan and Paul celebrated their 70th wedding anniversary.
Anyone who knew Paul wouldn’t be surprised that he fought to the end and did nothing but give his daughters and caregivers a hard time, in his loving and humorous way. When appropriate, he loved to kid around with family members, friends and anyone willing to join in. We will miss the stories we have heard over and over again but never get tired of hearing.
Paul is survived by his beloved wife, Jan; and their three daughters, Julie Butler of Standish, Jill Butler Mack (David) of Framingham, Mass. and Gail Butler White (Alan) of Windham; twin brother, Willard Richardson Butler (Carol) of Richmond, Va.; four grandchildren, Kelsey White, Grace Mack (Tom Tryon), Caroline Mack and Benjamin White; his niece, Melissa Butler and nephew, Mark Butler.
Paul was predeceased by his daughter, Brenda Ann; his parents Guy and Dorothy Bulter and his stepmother, Nancy Butler.
Paul valued his friendships and was especially grateful for those who have stayed in touch over the years. The family would like to extend its deepest appreciation to medical staff at Northern Light Mercy Hospital and to Northern Light Hospice for their compassion and support.
A service will be held at the First Congregational Church in South Portland on Saturday, Oct. 31 at 11 a.m. Reception to follow in the Wright Pavilion.

title: Sri Lanka provides medical help, repatriates Iranian sailors stranded in Indian Ocean
text:
Sri Lanka provides medical help, repatriates Iranian sailors stranded in Indian Ocean
Sri Lanka has responded to a distress call and provided medical help to 40 Iranian sailors from ships anchored close to the island’s waters before repatriating them to Tehran, a spokesperson said Sunday.
The sailors were brought to the island’s southern port of Galle on Saturday after Sri Lankan authorities received a distress call seeking medical help, said Thushara Rodrigo, the foreign ministry spokesperson.
He said he doesn’t have details about which ships the sailors came from. He said they were transported to the shore by vessels arranged by the Iranian Embassy and local shipping agents. The ministry handled the immigration and institutional formalities.
Related video: Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
After initial medical treatment, they left Sri Lanka early Sunday, added Rodrigo.
The Iranian oil tankers have been anchored off Sri Lanka for the past several months after the U.S. resumed its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving dozens of Iranian vessels stranded and unable to return home.
The plight of these sailors has been a growing issue over the past weeks after Sri Lankan authorities acknowledged that there were 19 ships stationed about 24 nautical miles from its coast and that they have reported shortages of food, water and fuel.
Two weeks ago, the Sri Lankan government said it had no immediate plans to help the ships, saying that Sri Lanka will put its national interest first before considering any help, and the companies that supply ships are aware of possible secondary sanctions from the United States.
This latest development comes nearly seven months after a U.S. torpedo attack sank the Iranian naval ship IRIS Dena, killing 87 sailors.
The ship was returning home after taking part in a naval exercise at invitation from India. A second Iranian ship was brought to a Sri Lankan port after its crew reported technical problems.
The wounded sailors who were treated in Sri Lankan hospitals and those rescued from the second ship were safely repatriated to Iran.
Sri Lanka is emerging from an economic crisis and both the U.S. and Iran are crucial trading partners. The U.S. played an important role in assisting with an International Monetary Fund bailout deal and helping the agricultural sector to avert a food crisis.

Bryan MacFarlane, 41, was part of a gathering of the deaf community playing cornhole at Schemengees Bar & Grille. He had recently moved back to Maine after becoming the first deaf person to obtain a commercial driver's license in the state of Vermont.
Keith Macneir
Keith Macneir, 64, was killed in the shooting at Schemengees Bar & Grille. A native of Fort Lauderdale, Florida, Macneir was in Lewiston to celebrate his birthday with his son. He was waiting for his son at the restaurant when the gunman entered and opened fire.
Ronald Morin
Ron Morin, 55, was fatally shot at Schemengees Bar & Grille. The husband and father of two worked for Coca-Cola for more than 30 years. He was one of eight siblings.
Joshua Seal
Josh Seal, 36, was a husband, a father of four and a tireless advocate for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing community. He was among the victims who were shot at Schemengees.
A skilled sign-language interpreter, Seal was widely known as the American Sign Language interpreter for former Maine CDC director Dr. Nirav Shah’s COVID-19 pandemic briefings. He worked for the Maine Center for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing as an educational technician at Portland's East End Community School for seven years. He was also the director of interpreting services for the Pine Tree Society and founded the Camp Dirigo Experience for deaf children and teenagers.
Arthur Strout
Artie Strout, 42, was a husband and shared a blended family of five children with his wife. He was shot and killed at Schemengees Bar & Grille.
Robert & Lucille Violette
Bob and Lucy Violette were fatally shot at Just-In-Time Recreation. Lucy was 73 years old and Bob was 76 years old.
Friends say Bob Violette should be remembered as a wonderful person who died trying to protect children.
"I have no doubt that he was protecting those kids 'til the end. He is just such a good man, that he deserves people to know about him and what he meant to everyone," Brandon Dubuc said.
Lewiston Public Schools Superintendent Jake Langlais described Lucy as "one of the kindest people I have ever met."
"She supported youth, their development, loved bowling, a good laugh, and was a valued member of the business office at Lewiston Public Schools," Langlais said. "Lucy served the public for over 52 years. Lucy was a mentor providing various levels of guidance and care to many from youth bowling, life mentoring, and so much more."
Stephen Vozzella
Steve Vozzella, 45, was part of a gathering of deaf people playing cornhole at Schemengees Bar & Grille. He and his wife, Megan, had a young daughter and got married less than a year before the shooting. Vozzella was also the father of an adult son.
The Massachusetts native worked as a U.S. Postal Service letter carrier in Boston for more than two decades before he moved to Lewiston in 2022.
Jason Walker
Jason Walker, 51, was fatally shot at Just-In-Time Recreation. The husband and father of two was killed as he charged at the gunman in an attempt to disarm him. He joined the Maine National Guard after graduating high school and was a member of the Sabattus Historical Society.
Joseph Walker
Joe Walker, 57, the manager of Schemengees Bar & Grille, was killed in the shooting.
Maine State Police said Walker had grabbed a kitchen knife and was apparently running toward the shooter to stop him when he was shot twice in the stomach.
When asked if he was surprised to hear his son attempted to run to the shooter, his father – Auburn City Councilor Leroy Walker Sr. — said: "No, not at all. I know he would have done that to protect his people."
Aaron Young
Aaron Young, 14, and his father, Bill, were both killed at Just-In-Time Recreation.
“I knew it would hit me when I got here, and he wasn’t here to greet me with a huge smile and a hug when we got in," said Aaron's sister, Kayla Putnam. "My mom just keeps saying, 'He gives the best hugs.'"
Aaron was a son, brother and beloved classmate. Both he and his father were killed in the deadly rampage.
“He was an honor student there. He was really proud of his grades, and his friends really miss him,” Putnam said.
William Young
Bill Young, 44, was a father and an auto mechanic. He and his son, Aaron, were both killed at Just-In-Time Recreation.
Kayla Putnam, Bill Young's stepdaughter, said he was the rock of the family.
“He’s going to be very missed,” Putnam said. “It’s going to be very hard for the family right now to deal without him because he was kind of the center of the family and everything. We are going to have a lot to deal with and plan and make sure everyone is taken care of.”

title: Letter on Susan Collins and Navatek doesn’t wash

title: VIDEO: Deer crashes through window after entering apartment unit
text:
'Certainly unusual:' Video captures deer leaping through window after entering apartment
A deer was caught on camera leaping out of a window after entering a lower-level residence at an apartment building in Wisconsin.
The Appleton Police Department shared body camera video, showing authorities looking through a glass door and into the apartment in search of the deer.
The deer was then captured breaking through a side window of the unit and running away from officers.
Watch body cam footage in the play finder above
Authorities said the resident was not home at the time of the incident.
The landlord and resident have since addressed the broken windows and made sure no other issues were found inside the apartment, police said.
Appleton police are now issuing a reminder to be aware of deer on the move this time of year.
"While a deer entering an apartment is certainly unusual, increased deer movement this time of year is not. Wisconsin DNR identifies October and November as the months when most deer-vehicle collisions occur, as deer become more active during the fall breeding season. Deer are also most active around dawn and dusk," the department said in a Facebook post.
"Drivers should slow down, remain alert and scan the roadsides for deer, particularly during the morning and evening hours," the department continued. "If you see one deer cross the road, be alert for others that may follow."

title: Man allegedly attacked fellow Uber passenger for taking up too much space in shared ride
text:
OCALA, Fla. (WCJB/Gray News) - A Florida man was arrested after he allegedly attacked another man he said was taking up too much space in their shared Uber.
Deputies with the Marion County Sheriff’s Office responded to a Walmart in Ocala last Saturday after a report of a disturbance. There, they spoke with 60-year-old Burton McDonald and the 65-year-old victim.
The victim said he and McDonald got into an argument over the amount of space the victim’s items were taking up in the shared Uber ride. It was after this argument that McDonald allegedly battered the victim.
McDonald was being held at the Marion County Jail with a $1,000 bond. Online records show he is scheduled to appear in court in November.

title: Obituary: Marion Macbeth Conley
text:
SEBASTIAN, Fla. – Marion Macbeth Conley (Woodworth), born on Sept. 27, 1944, in South Portland, passed away peacefully on Oct. 8, 2026 in Peachtree City, Ga., at the age of 82.
Marion liked to be on the move. She was an avid tennis player and played competitively with various groups in Maine and Sebastian, Fla. for 45 years. title: New York's archdiocese and survivors of clergy abuse agree to $800 million legal settlement
text:
New York's archdiocese and survivors of clergy abuse agree to $800 million legal settlement
The Archdiocese of New York and attorneys for about 1,300 parishioners who said they were sexually abused by clergy have agreed to an $800 million settlement of their legal claims, the second-largest involving a Catholic archdiocese in the U.S.
Archbishop Ronald Hicks sent an email Saturday to clergy confirming the settlement after attorneys for the survivors of alleged abuse announced it. Hicks said the agreement will not be final until the parties sign it, an action scheduled for the week of Nov. 6.
The only larger settlement over sexual abuse claims in the U.S. was by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, which agreed in 2024 to pay $880 million to 1,000 abuse victims, in addition to $740 million in claims it had paid previously. In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to a $395 million settlement over about 500 lawsuits filed over clergy abuse, and in December 2025, a federal judge approved a settlement in which the Archdiocese of New Orleans agreed to pay at least $230 million to abuse victims.
The agreement with the New York archdiocese would end more than seven years of lawsuits. The parties agreed to a framework for an agreement in May that required everyone who filed a claim to sign off.
“The unanimous agreement of survivors who filed claims against the Archdiocese of New York marks a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice,” Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing people who filed more than 1,000 of claims against the Catholic Church in New York state, said in a statement. “Through their courage, sacrifice, and determination, survivors have helped bring about a reckoning and a meaningful step toward accountability.”
The Archiocese of New York covers the city's boroughs of the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island as well as seven counties to the north of New York City and is home to about 300 churches, more than 150 parochial schools and 2.5 million Catholics.
In his email to clergy, Hicks said that if church members ask about the settlement, “please let them know that much progress has been made.”
“We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors,” he wrote. “This agreement will also allow the archdiocese to turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children.”
A New York law enacted in 2019 allows survivors of child sexual abuse to file lawsuits against their abusers and institutions that shielded them until they turn 55. People who had already had turned 55 when the law was enacted also were given until August 2021 to file lawsuits, no matter when the alleged abuse occurred.
“This is an extraordinary achievement for the survivors,” said Trusha Goffe, an attorney in Anderson’s firm. "The survivors remained resolute through years of litigation to reach this monumental settlement.”

title: At 6-feet-9, Cooper Black makes NHL history in debut vs. Penguins
text:
Florida Panthers rookie goalie Cooper Black — all 6-feet-9 of him — makes NHL history in debut
Florida Panthers goalie Cooper Black skated onto the PPG Paints Arena ice alone during pregame warmups on Thursday night, a time-honored hockey tradition given to rookies everywhere.
It took Black fewer strides to make the memorable lap than most.
Video above: Kyle Busch honored during Game 1 of NHL Conference Finals between Canes and Canadiens
Call it one of the upsides of being 6-foot-9.
Black made NHL history in his first career start when he became the tallest goaltender to ever appear in a regular-season game. Black is listed as two inches taller than Ben Bishop, Ivan Fedotov, Mads Sogaard and Mikko Koskinen, all 6-7.
The 25-year-old from Alpena, Michigan, who started playing when he was 8 and had a 5-inch growth spurt between his junior and senior years in high school when he shot up from 6-0 to 6-5 and kept right on going, made 18 saves in a 4-0 loss.
“It’s cool right, growing up, all the guys you kind of saw and watched as a kid, even as a goalie,” Black said. "Cool experience to play against the guys, would have been nicer to win.”
Black, called up from Florida's AHL affiliate in Charlotte recently after Jacob Markstrom went down with a shoulder injury, stopped Pittsburgh Penguins defenseman Kris Letang with his blocker pad on a wrist shot about two minutes in. He also turned aside a breakaway opportunity by Penguins forward Rickard Rakell before giving up a goal to 5-9 Pittsburgh forward Nick Robertson, who beat Black to the glove side.
Panthers head coach Paul Maurice praised Black's development in recent years. Florida signed Black as an undrafted rookie free agent in 2024. Black blossomed last season in Charlotte, posting a 25-13-4 record with a 2.47 goals-against average and a .903 save percentage.
Video below: Hockey player medically airlifted after suffering injuries during game
“A man that size, it takes a long time to grow into that body,” Maurice said with a smile before the game, adding with a laugh, “I think he’s done.”
Black became the first player in Savannah Ghost Pirates franchise history to reach the NHL. The Ghost Pirates are an ECHL affiliate of the Panthers.
Black, 25, played seven games for Savannah during the 2024-25 season. He posted a 4-3-0 record, a 3.07 goals-against average and an .886 save percentage.
He also appeared in 63 American Hockey League games with the Charlotte Checkers, compiling a 38-19-6 record with a 2.39 goals-against average and a .904 save percentage.
Before turning professional, Black played 60 games at Dartmouth College. He finished his collegiate career with an 18-31-9 record, a 2.82 goals-against average and a .904 save percentage.
